docs.title: About this book
docs.text: A complete first course in organic chemistry: bonding and shape, naming, stereochemistry, acids and bases, curly-arrow mechanisms, the reactions of hydrocarbons and of the main functional groups, spectroscopy, polymers and biomolecules, and safe, green laboratory practice, with worked examples, exercises and quizzes.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Acids and Bases in Organic Chemistry
docs.text:
Proton transfer, pKa and the structure of the conjugate base

Acid–base reactions are the simplest reactions in organic chemistry and among the most important. Many reactions start with a proton transfer, many end with one, and the same ideas that decide how strong an acid is (where a negative charge can sit comfortably, how far it can spread) decide the course of reactions throughout the book. This chapter sets out the Brønsted–Lowry and Lewis definitions, the pKa scale, how to predict the direction of an acid–base reaction, and the structural factors that make one acid stronger than another.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  • identify acids, bases and conjugate pairs, and show proton transfer with curly arrows;
  • use pKa values to compare acid strength and to predict the position of an acid–base equilibrium;
  • explain differences in acidity using the atom bearing the charge, resonance, inductive effects and hybridisation;
  • compare the strength of bases using the pKa of their conjugate acids;
  • predict which form of an acid or base predominates at a given pH;
  • recognise Lewis acids and bases and connect them to electrophiles and nucleophiles.

docs.title: 4.1 Brønsted–Lowry acids and bases
docs.text:
In the Brønsted–Lowry definition, an acid is a proton donor and a base is a proton acceptor. (A "proton" here means a hydrogen ion, H⁺, a hydrogen atom without its electron.) When an acid HA gives its proton to a base B, the acid becomes its conjugate base A⁻ and the base becomes its conjugate acid BH⁺:

\[ \mathrm{HA + B \rightleftharpoons A^- + BH^+} \]

Every acid–base reaction involves two conjugate acid–base pairs: HA/A⁻ and BH⁺/B. The members of a pair differ by one proton.

A base needs a pair of electrons with which to take the proton, usually a lone pair on oxygen or nitrogen, or a negative charge. This is why curly arrows describe acid–base reactions so well. One arrow starts at the lone pair of the base and points to the proton; a second arrow starts at the H–A bond and points to A, showing the bonding pair staying behind on A as the new lone pair.

Figure 4.1 Proton transfer with curly arrows. The reaction of hydroxide ion with ethanoic acid drawn with curly arrows. A lone pair on hydroxide forms a new bond to the acidic proton, and the electrons of the O–H bond move onto the oxygen of the acid, which becomes the ethanoate ion. The products are the conjugate base of ethanoic acid and the conjugate acid of hydroxide, water.

Caution: arrows show electrons, not protons

A curly arrow always shows the movement of an electron pair. It never shows a proton (or any atom) moving. In a proton transfer, draw the arrow from the lone pair of the base to the H, not from the H to the base.

Water can act as either an acid or a base (it is amphoteric): it donates a proton to ammonia, giving hydroxide, and accepts one from hydrogen chloride, giving the hydronium ion, H₃O⁺. Many organic molecules are amphoteric too. Ethanol is a weak acid towards a strong base and a weak base towards a strong acid.

docs.title: 4.2 Measuring acid strength: Ka and pKa
docs.text:
The strength of an acid in water is measured by the equilibrium constant for its ionisation, the acid dissociation constant \(K_\mathrm{a}\):

\[ \mathrm{HA + H_2O \rightleftharpoons A^- + H_3O^+} \qquad K_\mathrm{a} = \frac{[\mathrm{A^-}][\mathrm{H_3O^+}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]} \]

Ka values range over more than fifty powers of ten, so they are converted into a logarithmic scale, just as hydrogen-ion concentrations are converted into pH:

\[ \mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a} = -\log_{10} K_\mathrm{a} \]

The smaller the pKa, the stronger the acid. Because the scale is logarithmic, a difference of one pKa unit means a tenfold difference in Ka: ethanoic acid (pKa 4.8) is about one hundred thousand times more acidic than phenol (pKa 10).

Figure 4.2 The pKa scale. Approximate pKa values on a single scale. Strong acids such as HCl lie to the left, with negative pKa values; very weak acids such as alkanes lie to the far right. Every acid on the scale has a conjugate base whose strength runs the other way: the weaker the acid, the stronger its conjugate base. Acid Conjugate base Approximate pKa HCl Cl⁻ −7 H₃O⁺ H₂O −1.7 CH₃COOH (ethanoic acid) CH₃COO⁻ 4.8 NH₄⁺ NH₃ 9.2 C₆H₅OH (phenol) C₆H₅O⁻ 10 CH₃NH₃⁺ CH₃NH₂ 10.6 H₂O OH⁻ 15.7 CH₃CH₂OH (ethanol) CH₃CH₂O⁻ 16 CH₃COCH₃ (C–H next to C=O) ⁻CH₂COCH₃ 19 HC≡CH HC≡C⁻ 25 NH₃ NH₂⁻ 38 CH₂=CH₂ CH₂=CH⁻ 44 CH₄ CH₃⁻ 50

Table 4.1. Approximate pKa values worth remembering. Values above about 16 cannot be measured in water and are estimated by other methods; treat them as a guide to order of magnitude.

Note: the pKa of water

Some books give the pKa of water as 15.7 and others as 14.0. The difference comes from how the concentration of water itself is treated in the equilibrium expression. This book uses 15.7, which makes water directly comparable with alcohols, but the conclusions never depend on the choice.

docs.title: 4.3 Predicting the direction of an acid–base reaction
docs.text:
An acid–base equilibrium always lies on the side of the weaker acid and the weaker base. Put simply, the proton ends up on the strongest base available.

To predict the outcome of a reaction:

  1. Identify the acid on each side of the equation.
  2. Look up (or estimate) their pKa values.
  3. The equilibrium favours the side with the acid of higher pKa (the weaker acid).

The equilibrium constant for the reaction is approximately \(10^{\Delta}\), where \(\Delta\) is the pKa of the product acid minus the pKa of the reactant acid.

Example 4.1: Will hydroxide deprotonate ethanoic acid? Will it deprotonate ethyne?

Ethanoic acid + hydroxide → ethanoate + water. The acid on the left has pKa 4.8; the acid on the right (water) has pKa 15.7. The weaker acid is water, on the right, so the reaction goes essentially to completion. K ≈ 10^(15.7 − 4.8) ≈ 10¹¹. This is why carboxylic acids dissolve in aqueous sodium hydroxide.

Ethyne + hydroxide → ethynide + water. The acid on the left (ethyne) has pKa 25; the acid on the right (water) has pKa 15.7. Now the weaker acid is on the left, so the equilibrium lies far to the left: hydroxide is not a strong enough base. To remove the proton from ethyne we need the conjugate base of a much weaker acid, such as the amide ion NH₂⁻ (the conjugate base of ammonia, pKa 38).

Key idea

A base can effectively remove a proton from any acid whose pKa is lower than the pKa of the base's own conjugate acid. Read Table 4.1 this way: each conjugate base in the table can deprotonate every acid above it.

docs.title: 4.4 What makes an acid strong?
docs.text: An acid is strong when its conjugate base is stable. Everything that stabilises the negative charge left behind in A⁻ makes HA more acidic. Four structural factors matter, roughly in this order of importance.

docs.title: 1. The atom that carries the charge
docs.text:
Across a row of the periodic table, acidity increases with electronegativity. A more electronegative atom holds a negative charge better:

\[ \mathrm{CH_4\ (50) < NH_3\ (38) < H_2O\ (15.7) < HF\ (3.2)} \]

Down a group, acidity increases with the size of the atom, even though electronegativity decreases. HF (pKa 3.2) is far weaker than HCl (−7), HBr (−9) and HI (−10). In a larger atom the charge is spread over a larger volume, and the H–X bond is longer and weaker. Similarly, thiols (R–SH, pKa about 10) are more acidic than alcohols (R–OH, pKa about 16).

docs.title: 2. Resonance
docs.text:
If the negative charge of the conjugate base can be delocalised by resonance, it is stabilised, and the acid is stronger. Compare ethanol (pKa 16) with ethanoic acid (pKa 4.8). Both lose a proton from an O–H group. In ethoxide, CH₃CH₂O⁻, the charge stays on one oxygen. In ethanoate, the charge is shared equally between two oxygens through two equivalent resonance contributors (Figure 1.4). That sharing makes ethanoic acid about 10¹¹ times more acidic.

Phenol (pKa 10) lies between the two. When phenol loses its proton, the negative charge can spread from oxygen into the benzene ring, onto the two ortho carbons and the para carbon.

Figure 4.3 Resonance in the phenoxide ion. Resonance contributors of the phenoxide ion. Curly arrows move a lone pair from oxygen into the ring and push the ring's π electrons along, so the negative charge appears in turn at the ortho carbon, the para carbon and the other ortho carbon. Delocalisation makes phenol about a million times more acidic than an alcohol, though much less acidic than a carboxylic acid, where the charge is shared between two electronegative oxygens.

The phenoxide charge is spread over four atoms, but three of them are carbon, which holds negative charge less well than oxygen. In ethanoate both atoms sharing the charge are oxygen. That is why phenol is a weaker acid than a carboxylic acid.

A group that can accept electrons by resonance strengthens the acid further. 4-Nitrophenol (pKa about 7.2) is a much stronger acid than phenol, because the nitro group at the para position can take the negative charge onto its own oxygens.

docs.title: 3. Inductive effects
docs.text:
Electronegative atoms pull electron density through σ bonds. This inductive effect spreads the negative charge of a nearby anion and stabilises it. Each chlorine added to ethanoic acid makes the acid stronger:

Acid pKa CH₃COOH 4.76 ClCH₂COOH 2.86 Cl₂CHCOOH 1.29 Cl₃CCOOH 0.65

Table 4.2. The inductive effect of chlorine on the acidity of ethanoic acid.

The inductive effect falls off quickly with distance, because it is passed along σ bonds. Butanoic acid has pKa 4.82. A chlorine on the carbon next to the COOH group (2-chlorobutanoic acid) lowers it to 2.86, one carbon further away (3-chlorobutanoic acid) to 4.05, and on the far end (4-chlorobutanoic acid) only to 4.52.

Alkyl groups have a weak opposite effect: they are slightly electron-donating, which destabilises an anion. This is one reason why ethanoic acid (4.76) is weaker than methanoic acid (3.75).

docs.title: 4. Hybridisation
docs.text:
The more s character in the orbital holding the lone pair of the conjugate base, the more stable the anion. An s orbital is closer to the nucleus than a p orbital, so electrons in it are held more tightly. sp orbitals have 50% s character, sp² 33% and sp³ 25%. Hence:

\[ \mathrm{HC{\equiv}CH\ (25)\ \ \gg\ \ CH_2{=}CH_2\ (44)\ \ >\ \ CH_3CH_3\ (about\ 50)} \]

Terminal alkynes are acidic enough to be deprotonated by the amide ion, a fact used to make new carbon–carbon bonds in Chapter 7.

Key idea: ARIO

To compare two acids, look at their conjugate bases and ask, in order: which Atom carries the charge? Is there Resonance? Are there Inductive effects? In what Orbital (hybridisation) is the lone pair? The first factor that differs usually decides.

Example 4.2: Ranking acids

Rank in order of increasing acidity: ethanol, ethanoic acid, phenol, 2,2,2-trifluoroethanol (CF₃CH₂OH).

All four lose a proton from O–H, so the atom is the same. Ethanoic acid has the best resonance (two oxygens) and is the most acidic. Phenol has resonance into the ring and comes next. Ethanol and trifluoroethanol have no resonance; the three fluorines of trifluoroethanol stabilise the anion inductively, so it is more acidic than ethanol (its pKa is about 12.4).

Increasing acidity: ethanol < trifluoroethanol < phenol < ethanoic acid.

docs.title: 4.5 Bases and the pKa of the conjugate acid
docs.text:
The strength of a base is described by the pKa of its conjugate acid, sometimes written pKaH. The higher the pKa of the conjugate acid, the stronger the base, because a strong base holds onto the proton it gains.

Base Conjugate acid pKa of conjugate acid Comment CH₃NH₂ (methanamine) CH₃NH₃⁺ 10.6 alkyl group donates electrons NH₃ NH₄⁺ 9.2 reference C₅H₅N (pyridine) C₅H₅NH⁺ 5.2 lone pair in an sp² orbital C₆H₅NH₂ (aniline) C₆H₅NH₃⁺ 4.6 lone pair delocalised into the ring CH₃CONH₂ (ethanamide) CH₃C(OH)=NH₂⁺ about −0.5 lone pair delocalised onto C=O

Table 4.3. Nitrogen bases. The same factors that stabilise anions also explain base strength: a lone pair that is delocalised or held in an orbital with more s character is less available for a proton.

Amines are the most important organic bases (Chapter 13). Amides contain nitrogen too, but they are hardly basic at all, because the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised onto the carbonyl oxygen by resonance. Strong bases used in the laboratory include sodium hydroxide, alkoxides such as sodium ethoxide, sodium amide (NaNH₂) and sodium hydride (NaH), whose hydride ion H⁻ is the conjugate base of H₂ (pKa about 35).

Caution: strong base, not 'strong acid's conjugate'

The conjugate base of a strong acid is a weak base: Cl⁻ from HCl has no useful basicity at all. The conjugate base of a weak acid is a strong base: NH₂⁻ from NH₃ is very strong. Keep the see-saw in mind.

docs.title: 4.6 Acids and bases at a given pH
docs.text:
In biology and in the laboratory we often need to know which form of a compound is present at a particular pH. The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation relates the ratio of the two forms to the pH:

\[ \mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a} + \log_{10}\frac{[\mathrm{A^-}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]} \]

Three useful consequences follow:

  • When pH = pKa, the acid is exactly half ionised.
  • When the pH is below the pKa, the protonated form (HA) predominates; when it is above, the deprotonated form (A⁻) predominates.
  • Each unit of pH away from the pKa changes the ratio by a factor of ten.

Example 4.3: An amino acid at pH 7

In the body (pH about 7.4), a carboxylic acid group (pKa about 2 in an amino acid) is far above its pKa: it is almost entirely in the form COO⁻. An amino group whose conjugate acid has pKa about 9.5 is below its pKa: it is almost entirely in the form NH₃⁺. So an amino acid such as glycine exists in water near neutral pH as a zwitterion, ⁺H₃N–CH₂–COO⁻, carrying both a positive and a negative charge (Chapter 15).

The same reasoning underlies a standard separation in the laboratory, acid–base extraction. A carboxylic acid dissolved in an organic solvent with a neutral compound can be removed by shaking the solution with aqueous sodium hydrogencarbonate: the acid is converted into its water-soluble carboxylate salt and moves into the aqueous layer, while the neutral compound stays behind. Acidifying the aqueous layer then gives back the free acid.

docs.title: 4.7 Lewis acids and bases
docs.text:
The Lewis definition is broader. A Lewis base is an electron-pair donor, and a Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor. Every Brønsted base is also a Lewis base, and H⁺ is one particular Lewis acid. But many Lewis acids contain no proton at all. They are species with an empty orbital or a low-lying vacant orbital:

  • Boron trifluoride, BF₃: boron has only six valence electrons and an empty p orbital. It accepts a lone pair from an ether or an amine to form an adduct, such as F₃B⁻–O⁺(CH₂CH₃)₂.
  • Aluminium chloride, AlCl₃, and iron(III) bromide, FeBr₃: used as catalysts in the substitution reactions of benzene (Chapter 8).
  • Metal cations such as Mg²⁺ and Zn²⁺, which bind lone pairs.
  • Carbocations, such as (CH₃)₃C⁺, which have an empty p orbital on carbon.

The Lewis picture leads directly to the most important idea in the study of reactions. A Lewis base attacking a carbon atom is called a nucleophile, and a Lewis acid, or any species with an electron-poor atom that can accept a pair, is called an electrophile. Chapter 5 develops this language and uses it to describe reaction mechanisms.

docs.title: 4.8 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Brønsted–Lowry: acids donate protons, bases accept them. Each acid has a conjugate base and each base a conjugate acid.
  • Curly arrows run from the lone pair of the base to the proton, and from the H–A bond to A.
  • \(\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a} = -\log K_\mathrm{a}\). Lower pKa means a stronger acid; each unit is a factor of ten.
  • An acid–base equilibrium favours the weaker acid and weaker base.
  • Acidity rises with the electronegativity and size of the atom carrying the charge, with resonance delocalisation of the charge, with electron-withdrawing groups nearby, and with s character of the lone-pair orbital.
  • Base strength is measured by the pKa of the conjugate acid: higher means stronger.
  • Below its pKa an acid is mainly protonated; above it, mainly ionised.
  • Lewis acids accept electron pairs and Lewis bases donate them; nucleophiles and electrophiles are the reacting partners of Chapter 5.

docs.title: 4.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Identify the acid, base, conjugate acid and conjugate base in: CH₃NH₂ + CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃NH₃⁺ + CH₃COO⁻. Draw the curly arrows. Which side does the equilibrium favour?

Answer

CH₃COOH is the acid and CH₃NH₂ the base; CH₃NH₃⁺ is the conjugate acid of methanamine and CH₃COO⁻ the conjugate base of ethanoic acid. Arrows: from the nitrogen lone pair to the acidic H of the COOH group, and from the O–H bond onto the oxygen. The acids are CH₃COOH (pKa 4.8) and CH₃NH₃⁺ (10.6). The weaker acid is CH₃NH₃⁺, on the right, so the equilibrium lies to the right (K ≈ 10^5.8).

Exercise 2

Which of the following bases can deprotonate ethanol (pKa 16) essentially completely? (a) NaOH; (b) NaNH₂; (c) NaH; (d) NaHCO₃ (the conjugate acid, H₂CO₃, has pKa 6.4).

Answer

A base deprotonates ethanol completely only if its conjugate acid is much weaker than ethanol (pKa well above 16). (a) No: water (15.7) and ethanol (16) are nearly equal, so an equilibrium mixture results. (b) Yes: ammonia has pKa 38. (c) Yes: H₂ has pKa about 35, and the H₂ escapes as a gas, which drives the reaction to completion. (d) No: H₂CO₃ (6.4) is a far stronger acid than ethanol.

Exercise 3

Explain why ethanoic acid (pKa 4.8) is a much stronger acid than ethanol (pKa 16), even though both lose a proton from an O–H group.

Answer

Compare the conjugate bases. In ethanoate the negative charge is delocalised by resonance over two equivalent oxygen atoms; in ethoxide it is localised on one oxygen. Delocalisation stabilises ethanoate, so ethanoic acid gives up its proton more readily. In addition, the C=O group withdraws electrons inductively from the O–H oxygen.

Exercise 4

Rank each set from least to most acidic and give the main reason: (a) CH₃OH, CH₃NH₂, CH₃SH; (b) CH₃CH₂COOH, CH₃CHFCOOH, FCH₂CH₂COOH; (c) CH₃CH₃, CH₂=CH₂, HC≡CH.

Answer

(a) CH₃NH₂ < CH₃OH < CH₃SH. O is more electronegative than N; S is in the next row down, and its larger size stabilises the anion better than O does (thiols have pKa about 10).

(b) CH₃CH₂COOH < FCH₂CH₂COOH < CH₃CHFCOOH. Fluorine withdraws electrons inductively; its effect is greater the closer it is to the carboxylate.

(c) CH₃CH₃ < CH₂=CH₂ < HC≡CH. The lone pair of the conjugate base is in an sp³, sp² and sp orbital respectively; more s character stabilises it.

Exercise 5

Which is the stronger base in each pair? (a) CH₃O⁻ or CH₃COO⁻; (b) NH₃ or H₂O; (c) aniline or cyclohexylamine (C₆H₁₁NH₂, pKa of conjugate acid 10.6).

Answer

(a) CH₃O⁻: its conjugate acid, methanol, is much weaker (pKa about 15.5) than ethanoic acid (4.8). (b) NH₃: the pKa of NH₄⁺ (9.2) is far higher than that of H₃O⁺ (−1.7). (c) Cyclohexylamine (10.6 against 4.6): in aniline the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring and is less available for a proton.

Exercise 6

Benzoic acid has pKa 4.2. (a) What is the ratio [C₆H₅COO⁻]/[C₆H₅COOH] at pH 7.2? (b) At pH 2.2? (c) Use your answers to explain how benzoic acid can be separated from naphthalene (a neutral hydrocarbon) dissolved in ethoxyethane.

Answer

(a) pH − pKa = 3, so the ratio is 10³ = 1000: the acid is almost entirely ionised. (b) pH − pKa = −2, so the ratio is 10⁻² = 0.01: almost entirely the neutral acid.

(c) Shake the ether solution with aqueous sodium hydrogencarbonate (pH a little above 8). Benzoic acid is converted into sodium benzoate, which is ionic and moves into the water; naphthalene stays in the ether. Separate the layers, then acidify the aqueous layer to a low pH: benzoic acid, now un-ionised and poorly soluble in water, comes out of solution and can be collected.

Exercise 7

Classify each species as a Lewis acid, a Lewis base or neither: BF₃, NH₃, AlCl₃, CH₄, H₂O, Fe³⁺, (CH₃)₃C⁺.

Answer

Lewis acids (electron-pair acceptors): BF₃, AlCl₃, Fe³⁺, (CH₃)₃C⁺. Lewis bases (electron-pair donors): NH₃, H₂O. Neither: CH₄, which has no lone pairs and no empty low-energy orbital. (Water can also act as a Brønsted acid, but in the Lewis sense it is a donor.)

docs.title: 4.10 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of acids and bases

Exercise 1

Which acid is the strongest?

  1. ethanol (pKa 16)
  2. phenol (pKa 10)
  3. ethanoic acid (pKa 4.8)
  4. water (pKa 15.7)
Answer

ethanoic acid (pKa 4.8)

Exercise 2

An acid-base equilibrium lies on the side of

  1. the stronger acid
  2. the weaker acid
  3. the more concentrated species
  4. the side with more molecules
Answer

the weaker acid

Exercise 3

Acid A has pKa 3 and acid B has pKa 6. By what factor is A stronger than B?

Answer

1000 / a thousand / 10^3

Exercise 4

Trichloroethanoic acid is a much stronger acid than ethanoic acid mainly because of

  1. resonance
  2. the inductive effect
  3. hybridisation
  4. hydrogen bonding
Answer

the inductive effect

Exercise 5

Which base is strong enough to deprotonate ethyne (pKa 25)?

  1. NaOH
  2. NaHCO₃
  3. NaNH₂
  4. CH₃COONa
Answer

NaNH₂

The conjugate acid of NH₂⁻ is NH₃ (pKa 38), a weaker acid than ethyne.

Exercise 6

At pH 2, a carboxylic acid with pKa 4.8 is mainly

  1. ionised
  2. un-ionised
  3. exactly half ionised
Answer

un-ionised

Exercise 7

BF₃ is best described as

  1. a Brønsted acid
  2. a Lewis acid
  3. a Lewis base
  4. a Brønsted base
Answer

a Lewis acid

docs.title: Chapter 10: Alcohols, Ethers and Epoxides
docs.text:
Compounds with C–O single bonds

Alcohols are everywhere: ethanol in drinks and fuels, glycerol in fats, cholesterol in cell membranes, the many OH groups of sugars. They are also among the most useful compounds in the laboratory, because the OH group can be turned into almost any other functional group. Ethers, in which oxygen joins two carbon groups, are much less reactive and are valued as solvents. Epoxides are ethers in a strained three-membered ring, and that strain makes them reactive in ways ordinary ethers are not. This chapter covers the properties, preparation and reactions of all three, building on the substitution and elimination mechanisms of Chapter 9.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  • explain the physical properties of alcohols and ethers in terms of hydrogen bonding;
  • describe the acidity and basicity of alcohols and the formation of alkoxides;
  • list the main ways of making alcohols;
  • convert alcohols into haloalkanes and sulfonate esters, choosing suitable reagents;
  • write the mechanism of acid-catalysed dehydration and predict its products;
  • predict the products of oxidising primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols;
  • make ethers by the Williamson synthesis and describe their cleavage by HI or HBr;
  • prepare epoxides and predict the regiochemistry and stereochemistry of their ring opening under basic and acidic conditions.

docs.title: 10.1 Alcohols: structure and properties
docs.text:
An alcohol has an OH group bonded to an sp³ carbon. The oxygen is sp³ hybridised, with two lone pairs, and the C–O–H angle is close to the tetrahedral angle (about 109° in methanol). Alcohols are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary by the carbon carrying the OH (Section 2.1). An OH group on a benzene ring makes a phenol, which behaves differently (Section 4.4 and below).

The O–H group dominates the physical properties:

  • Hydrogen bonding between molecules gives alcohols much higher boiling points than alkanes, ethers or haloalkanes of similar molar mass. Ethanol (46 g mol⁻¹) boils at 78 °C, propane (44 g mol⁻¹) at −42 °C.
  • Solubility in water: alcohols hydrogen bond to water. Methanol, ethanol and propanol mix with water completely; solubility falls as the hydrocarbon chain lengthens. Each OH group can carry roughly three or four carbons into solution, so diols and triols such as glycerol are very soluble.

docs.title: Acidity and basicity
docs.text:
Alcohols are weak acids (pKa about 15.5 for methanol, 16 for ethanol, 18 for 2-methylpropan-2-ol), similar to water. Alkyl groups make the conjugate base less stable, and bulky alkoxides are poorly solvated, so acidity falls from methanol to tertiary alcohols. Alcohols react with sodium metal, giving hydrogen gas and a sodium alkoxide:

\[ \mathrm{2\,CH_3CH_2OH + 2\,Na \rightarrow 2\,CH_3CH_2O^-Na^+ + H_2} \]

The reaction is gentler than that of sodium with water, and the fizzing is a simple test for an OH group (in a dry, neutral compound). Alkoxides are strong bases and good nucleophiles, used throughout this chapter. Sodium hydride, NaH, is a convenient alternative way to deprotonate an alcohol.

Alcohols are also weak bases. Their oxygen lone pairs accept a proton from strong acids, giving an oxonium ion, R–OH₂⁺. Protonation is the key that unlocks most alcohol reactions, because it turns the very poor leaving group HO⁻ into the good leaving group H₂O.

Phenols (pKa about 10) are about a million times more acidic than alcohols, because the phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance with the ring (Figure 4.3). Phenols dissolve in aqueous sodium hydroxide, whereas simple alcohols do not ionise appreciably in it.

docs.title: 10.2 Making alcohols
docs.text:
Alcohols are made by several routes, most of which are described elsewhere in the book:

Method Example Chapter Acid-catalysed hydration of an alkene (Markovnikov) propene → propan-2-ol 7 Hydroboration–oxidation of an alkene (anti-Markovnikov) propene → propan-1-ol 7 SN2 substitution of a haloalkane by hydroxide 1-bromobutane → butan-1-ol 9 Reduction of an aldehyde or ketone (NaBH₄ or LiAlH₄) propanone → propan-2-ol 11 Reduction of a carboxylic acid or ester (LiAlH₄) ethyl ethanoate → ethanol 12 Addition of a Grignard reagent to a carbonyl compound methanal + CH₃MgBr → ethanol 11 Fermentation of sugars by yeast glucose → ethanol + CO₂ —

Table 10.1. Methods of making alcohols.

Fermentation is the oldest of these and still produces most of the world's ethanol for drinks and fuel. Yeast enzymes convert glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide in the absence of air: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 C₂H₅OH + 2 CO₂.

docs.title: 10.3 Converting alcohols into haloalkanes and sulfonates
docs.text:
The OH group cannot leave as HO⁻, so it must be activated first.

With hydrogen halides. Concentrated HCl, HBr or HI protonate the OH, and water then leaves.

  • Tertiary alcohols react fast, even with HCl at room temperature, by an SN1 mechanism: the protonated alcohol loses water to give a tertiary carbocation, which is captured by halide.
  • Primary alcohols react by SN2: halide attacks the carbon of the protonated alcohol, displacing water. HBr and HI work well; HCl needs a zinc chloride catalyst.
  • Secondary alcohols are in between and may rearrange.

The rate difference is the basis of the Lucas test: with a solution of zinc chloride in concentrated hydrochloric acid, a tertiary alcohol gives an immediate cloudiness (the insoluble chloroalkane), a secondary alcohol does so within minutes, and a primary alcohol hardly at all at room temperature.

With thionyl chloride or phosphorus tribromide. For primary and secondary alcohols, SOCl₂ (giving chloroalkanes, with SO₂ and HCl as gaseous by-products) and PBr₃ (giving bromoalkanes) are cleaner. Both first convert the OH into a good leaving group bonded to sulfur or phosphorus, which is then displaced by halide in an SN2 step, avoiding carbocations and rearrangements.

Sulfonate esters. An alcohol reacts with 4-methylbenzenesulfonyl chloride (tosyl chloride, TsCl) in pyridine to give a tosylate, R–OTs. The C–O bond of the alcohol is not broken in this step, so the configuration of the carbon is unchanged. The tosylate ion is a very weak base (the conjugate base of a strong acid), so it is an excellent leaving group, as good as or better than bromide. Tosylates undergo SN2 and E2 reactions just like haloalkanes, which gives a two-step way to substitute an alcohol with full control of stereochemistry: tosylation (retention), then SN2 (inversion).

Caution: water is a leaving group only after protonation

Never draw HO⁻ leaving from an alcohol in neutral or basic solution. In acid, draw protonation first, then loss of H₂O. In the laboratory, alcohols are made reactive by acid, by conversion into a halide, or by conversion into a sulfonate.

docs.title: 10.4 Dehydration to alkenes
docs.text:
Heating an alcohol with concentrated sulfuric acid or phosphoric acid removes a molecule of water and forms an alkene. Cyclohexanol, warmed with concentrated phosphoric acid, gives cyclohexene, which distils out of the mixture as it forms; this is a common teaching practical.

For secondary and tertiary alcohols the mechanism is E1:

  1. The OH is protonated.
  2. Water leaves, giving a carbocation (rate-determining).
  3. A base (water, or HSO₄⁻) removes a proton from a neighbouring carbon, forming the C=C bond and regenerating the acid catalyst.

Because the reaction goes through a carbocation, the ease of dehydration is tertiary > secondary > primary, the more substituted alkene predominates (Zaitsev's rule), and rearrangements can occur. Butan-2-ol gives mainly but-2-ene. Primary alcohols dehydrate only under harsher conditions, by an E2-like pathway from the protonated alcohol.

Dehydration is the reverse of acid-catalysed hydration (Section 7.3). The position of the equilibrium is controlled by the conditions: concentrated acid and heat, with removal of the alkene by distillation, favour dehydration; dilute aqueous acid favours hydration.

Example 10.1: Predicting dehydration products

Predict the main product of heating 2-methylbutan-2-ol with concentrated H₂SO₄.

Protonation and loss of water give the tertiary cation (CH₃)₂C⁺CH₂CH₃. Loss of a proton from the CH₂ gives the trisubstituted alkene 2-methylbut-2-ene; loss from a CH₃ gives the disubstituted 2-methylbut-1-ene. By Zaitsev's rule the main product is 2-methylbut-2-ene.

docs.title: 10.5 Oxidation of alcohols
docs.text:
Oxidation of an alcohol removes the hydrogen from the O–H and a hydrogen from the carbon carrying the OH, forming a C=O bond. Whether a reaction is possible depends on whether that carbon has a hydrogen.

  • A primary alcohol (two H on the carbinol carbon) is oxidised first to an aldehyde, and the aldehyde, which is easily oxidised itself, can go on to a carboxylic acid.
  • A secondary alcohol (one H) is oxidised to a ketone, which resists further oxidation.
  • A tertiary alcohol (no H) is not oxidised under these conditions.
Figure 10.1 Oxidation of alcohols. Oxidation of alcohols with acidified potassium dichromate(VI). Propan-1-ol gives propanal, which is distilled off as it forms; under reflux the oxidation continues to propanoic acid. Propan-2-ol gives propanone. 2-Methylpropan-2-ol has no hydrogen on the carbon bearing the OH group and is not oxidised. The orange dichromate is reduced to green chromium(III).

The classic oxidising agent in teaching laboratories is acidified potassium dichromate(VI), K₂Cr₂O₇ with dilute H₂SO₄. As it oxidises the alcohol, the orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ ion is reduced to green Cr³⁺. The colour change distinguishes primary and secondary alcohols (which turn the solution green) from tertiary alcohols (which do not). To stop at the aldehyde, the primary alcohol is added to the oxidant and the aldehyde, which boils lower than the alcohol because it cannot hydrogen bond to itself, is distilled off as soon as it forms. To get the carboxylic acid, the mixture is heated under reflux with excess oxidant.

Milder, anhydrous reagents stop the oxidation of primary alcohols cleanly at the aldehyde. Pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) in dichloromethane is a traditional choice, and chromium-free methods are now preferred where possible.

Caution: chromium(VI)

Chromium(VI) compounds are toxic and carcinogenic and must be handled with gloves, in small amounts, and disposed of as hazardous waste. In modern practice they are being replaced by less hazardous oxidants, including catalytic methods that use air or hydrogen peroxide (Chapter 16).

In living cells, the oxidation of ethanol to ethanal and then to ethanoic acid is carried out by enzymes (alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase) using the coenzyme NAD⁺ as the oxidant.

docs.title: 10.6 Ethers
docs.text:
An ether has an oxygen bonded to two carbon groups, R–O–R′. The C–O–C angle is about 110°. Ethers cannot hydrogen bond to one another, so their boiling points are close to those of alkanes of similar mass (methoxymethane −24 °C). They can, however, accept hydrogen bonds from water, so small ethers are somewhat soluble in water.

Ethers are unreactive towards bases, nucleophiles, dilute acids and most oxidising and reducing agents, which makes them excellent solvents. Ethoxyethane (diethyl ether) and the cyclic ether tetrahydrofuran (oxolane, THF) are used for Grignard reactions (Chapter 11), because their lone pairs coordinate to and stabilise the magnesium.

Caution: ether hazards

Ethoxyethane is extremely flammable, with a very low flash point, and its vapour is denser than air and can travel to a distant flame. On standing in air and light, ethers slowly form explosive peroxides. Containers are dated when opened, tested for peroxides before use, never distilled to dryness, and kept away from all ignition sources.

docs.title: Making ethers: the Williamson synthesis
docs.text:
The most general method is the Williamson ether synthesis: an alkoxide ion reacts with a primary haloalkane (or tosylate) by SN2.

\[ \mathrm{CH_3CH_2O^-Na^+ + CH_3I \rightarrow CH_3CH_2OCH_3 + NaI} \]

Because it is an SN2 reaction, the haloalkane must be methyl or primary. A tertiary haloalkane with an alkoxide gives elimination instead. So to make an unsymmetrical ether, choose the combination in which the halide carries the less hindered group.

Example 10.2: Planning a Williamson synthesis

How would you make 2-methoxy-2-methylpropane, CH₃–O–C(CH₃)₃ (methyl tert-butyl ether)?

Two disconnections are possible: (a) CH₃O⁻ + (CH₃)₃CBr; (b) (CH₃)₃CO⁻ + CH₃I. Route (a) fails: methoxide with a tertiary bromide gives elimination (2-methylpropene). Route (b) works: the halide is methyl, ideal for SN2, and the bulky alkoxide is the nucleophile. Use potassium tert-butoxide and iodomethane.

Symmetrical ethers from primary alcohols can also be made by heating the alcohol with concentrated sulfuric acid at a temperature lower than that used for dehydration: one protonated alcohol molecule is attacked by another in an SN2 step. At higher temperatures elimination to the alkene takes over.

docs.title: Cleaving ethers
docs.text:
Ethers are cleaved by heating with concentrated HI or HBr. The oxygen is protonated, and the halide then attacks one of the carbons: by SN2 at a methyl or primary carbon, or by SN1 if one group is tertiary. Methoxyethane with excess HI gives iodomethane and iodoethane (the alcohol formed first is converted into a second iodoalkane).

Crown ethers, large cyclic polyethers such as 18-crown-6, have their oxygens pointing into a central cavity that binds a metal cation of the right size (K⁺ for 18-crown-6). They can carry salts such as KMnO₄ or KF into non-polar solvents.

docs.title: 10.7 Epoxides
docs.text: An epoxide (oxirane) is a cyclic ether with a three-membered ring. Like cyclopropane, it has substantial ring strain (about 110 kJ mol⁻¹), and opening the ring releases it. Epoxides therefore react with nucleophiles under conditions where ordinary ethers do not.

docs.title: Making epoxides
docs.text:
• From alkenes and peroxyacids (Section 7.6): a stereospecific syn addition of oxygen. cis-But-2-ene gives cis-2,3-dimethyloxirane.
  • From halohydrins: treating a bromohydrin with base deprotonates the OH, and the alkoxide displaces the neighbouring bromide by an intramolecular SN2 reaction, closing the ring. The O⁻ and Br must be anti-periplanar for this backside attack.
  • Industrially, oxirane (ethylene oxide) is made by oxidising ethene with oxygen over a silver catalyst.

docs.title: Ring opening
docs.text:
Epoxides are opened by nucleophiles under both basic and acidic conditions, but the two give different regiochemistry.

Basic or neutral conditions (strong nucleophile). A strong nucleophile, such as HO⁻, RO⁻, CN⁻, an amine, or a Grignard reagent, attacks the epoxide directly by an SN2 mechanism. It attacks the less hindered carbon, from the side opposite the oxygen, with inversion at that carbon. The ring oxygen becomes an alkoxide, which is protonated in a final step.

Acidic conditions (weak nucleophile). The epoxide oxygen is first protonated, which makes it a much better leaving group. The C–O bonds weaken, and positive charge builds up on the carbons, especially the more substituted one, which can stabilise it better. A weak nucleophile such as water or an alcohol then attacks the more substituted carbon, still from the back face, so the addition is anti. The mechanism lies between SN1 and SN2: it has SN1-like regiochemistry and SN2-like stereochemistry.

Figure 10.2 Opening an epoxide under basic and acidic conditions. Ring opening of 2-methyloxirane. With methoxide (basic conditions), the nucleophile attacks the less hindered CH₂ carbon by SN2, giving 1-methoxypropan-2-ol after protonation. In methanol with an acid catalyst, the protonated epoxide is attacked at the more substituted carbon, which carries more of the positive charge, giving 2-methoxypropan-1-ol.

Acid-catalysed hydrolysis of an epoxide gives a 1,2-diol with the two OH groups anti. Epoxidation of cyclohexene followed by aqueous acid gives trans-cyclohexane-1,2-diol, a useful complement to the cis diol from OsO₄ (Section 7.6).

Key idea

Strong nucleophile, basic conditions: attack at the less substituted carbon (steric control, SN2). Weak nucleophile, acid catalyst: attack at the more substituted carbon (electronic control, carbocation-like). In both cases the nucleophile enters from the face opposite the oxygen, so the stereochemistry is anti.

Epoxides are widely used. Oxirane is converted into ethane-1,2-diol (antifreeze and a monomer for polyester, Chapter 15), and epoxy resins, used as strong adhesives and coatings, are polymers formed by ring-opening reactions of epoxides with amines.

docs.title: 10.8 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Hydrogen bonding gives alcohols high boiling points and water solubility; ethers cannot hydrogen bond to themselves.
  • Alcohols are weak acids (pKa 15.5 to 18) and react with Na or NaH to give alkoxides; they are also weak bases, and protonation turns OH into a good leaving group.
  • Alcohols become haloalkanes with HX (3° by SN1, 1° by SN2), SOCl₂ or PBr₃, and tosylates with TsCl (retention).
  • Acid-catalysed dehydration (E1 for 2° and 3°) gives the more substituted alkene, with possible rearrangement.
  • Oxidation: 1° → aldehyde → carboxylic acid; 2° → ketone; 3° → no reaction. Dichromate turns from orange to green.
  • Williamson synthesis: alkoxide + methyl or primary halide (SN2). Ethers are cleaved by HI or HBr.
  • Epoxides are strained. Strong nucleophiles open them at the less substituted carbon; acid-catalysed opening occurs at the more substituted carbon; both give anti products.

docs.title: 10.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Arrange in order of increasing boiling point and explain: butan-1-ol, ethoxyethane, pentane, butane-1,4-diol. (All have molar masses between 72 and 90 g mol⁻¹.)

Answer

Ethoxyethane (35 °C) ≈ pentane (36 °C) < butan-1-ol (118 °C) < butane-1,4-diol (about 230 °C). Pentane has only dispersion forces; ethoxyethane is polar but cannot hydrogen bond to itself; butan-1-ol forms hydrogen bonds through one OH group; the diol forms hydrogen bonds through two.

Exercise 2

Give reagents to convert butan-1-ol into: (a) 1-bromobutane; (b) 1-chlorobutane; (c) butanal; (d) butanoic acid; (e) but-1-ene (as the main product, avoiding rearrangement).

Answer

(a) PBr₃ (or concentrated HBr). (b) SOCl₂. (c) PCC in dichloromethane, or acidified dichromate with the aldehyde distilled off as it forms. (d) Excess acidified potassium dichromate, heated under reflux. (e) Direct acid dehydration of a primary alcohol is slow and can give rearranged but-2-ene; a cleaner route is to make the tosylate (TsCl, pyridine) or 1-bromobutane and eliminate with a bulky base such as potassium tert-butoxide (E2), which gives but-1-ene.

Exercise 3

Write the mechanism of the acid-catalysed dehydration of cyclohexanol to cyclohexene. Why is the alkene distilled out of the reaction mixture as it forms?

Answer

(1) The OH oxygen is protonated by the acid, giving an oxonium ion. (2) Water leaves, giving the secondary cyclohexyl carbocation (rate-determining). (3) Water or the conjugate base of the acid removes a proton from a neighbouring carbon; the C–H electrons form the C=C π bond, giving cyclohexene and regenerating the acid. Dehydration is reversible (the reverse is hydration). Cyclohexene (bp 83 °C) boils lower than cyclohexanol (bp 161 °C), so distilling it out as it forms shifts the equilibrium towards the products (Le Chatelier's principle).

Exercise 4

Three unlabelled bottles contain butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol. Describe chemical tests that would identify each.

Answer

Warm a few drops of each with acidified potassium dichromate. The tertiary alcohol (2-methylpropan-2-ol) does not react: the solution stays orange. The other two turn the solution green. To tell these apart, use the Lucas reagent (ZnCl₂ in concentrated HCl) at room temperature: the secondary alcohol, butan-2-ol, turns cloudy within a few minutes, while the primary alcohol, butan-1-ol, stays clear. (Alternatively, collect the oxidation products: butan-1-ol gives an aldehyde, which gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent; butan-2-ol gives a ketone, which does not; Chapter 11.)

Exercise 5

Which combination of reagents would you use to make each ether by the Williamson synthesis? (a) 1-ethoxypropane; (b) tert-butyl phenyl ether, C₆H₅–O–C(CH₃)₃, explaining any difficulty; (c) methoxycyclohexane.

Answer

(a) Sodium ethoxide + 1-bromopropane, or sodium propoxide + bromoethane: both halides are primary, so either works.

(b) This ether cannot be made by the Williamson method. Phenoxide + 2-bromo-2-methylpropane gives elimination (2-methylpropene), because the halide is tertiary. The other combination, tert-butoxide + bromobenzene, fails because SN2 does not occur at an sp² carbon of a benzene ring. A different method (for example, acid-catalysed addition of phenol to 2-methylpropene) is needed.

(c) Sodium cyclohexoxide (from cyclohexanol + NaH) + iodomethane. The reverse, methoxide + bromocyclohexane, would give a lot of cyclohexene by E2, because the halide is secondary.

Exercise 6

Give the main product of 2,2-dimethyloxirane, (CH₃)₂C–CH₂ joined through O, with (a) sodium methoxide in methanol; (b) methanol with a trace of sulfuric acid.

Answer

(a) Methoxide attacks the less hindered CH₂ carbon by SN2: after protonation, 1-methoxy-2-methylpropan-2-ol, (CH₃)₂C(OH)CH₂OCH₃.

(b) After protonation of the epoxide oxygen, methanol attacks the more substituted (tertiary) carbon, which bears more positive charge: 2-methoxy-2-methylpropan-1-ol, (CH₃)₂C(OCH₃)CH₂OH.

Exercise 7

Describe two ways to make cyclohexane-1,2-diol from cyclohexene, one giving the cis isomer and one giving the trans isomer.

Answer

cis-Diol: syn dihydroxylation with OsO₄ (catalytic, with a co-oxidant) or cold, dilute, alkaline KMnO₄. trans-Diol: epoxidation with a peroxyacid, followed by acid-catalysed ring opening with water; water attacks from the face opposite the epoxide oxygen, giving anti addition (as a racemic mixture of the two trans enantiomers).

docs.title: 10.10 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of alcohols, ethers and epoxides

Exercise 1

Which alcohol is NOT oxidised by acidified potassium dichromate?

  1. ethanol
  2. propan-2-ol
  3. butan-1-ol
  4. 2-methylpropan-2-ol
Answer

2-methylpropan-2-ol

Exercise 2

Propan-2-ol is oxidised to

  1. propanal
  2. propanone
  3. propanoic acid
  4. propene
Answer

propanone

Exercise 3

Before the OH of an alcohol can leave in a substitution, it is usually

  1. deprotonated
  2. protonated or converted into a sulfonate
  3. oxidised
  4. reduced
Answer

protonated or converted into a sulfonate

Exercise 4

Acid-catalysed dehydration of butan-2-ol gives mainly

  1. but-1-ene
  2. but-2-ene
  3. butane
  4. butanone
Answer

but-2-ene

Exercise 5

In the Williamson ether synthesis, the haloalkane should preferably be

  1. tertiary
  2. secondary
  3. primary or methyl
  4. aromatic
Answer

primary or methyl

Exercise 6

Under basic conditions, methoxide opens 2-methyloxirane at

  1. the more substituted carbon
  2. the less substituted carbon
  3. the oxygen
  4. both carbons equally
Answer

the less substituted carbon

Exercise 7

What colour does acidified dichromate turn when it oxidises a primary alcohol?

Answer

green

docs.title: Chapter 11: Aldehydes and Ketones
docs.text:
Nucleophilic addition to the carbonyl group

The carbonyl group, C=O, is the most important functional group in organic chemistry. It appears in aldehydes and ketones, in carboxylic acids and their derivatives, in sugars and in many of the molecules of life. Its chemistry rests on one simple fact: the carbon is electron-poor and the oxygen electron-rich. Nucleophiles attack the carbon; acids and electrophiles attach to the oxygen. This chapter treats aldehydes and ketones, where the main reaction is nucleophilic addition. It also introduces the second great theme of carbonyl chemistry, the acidity of the hydrogens next to the C=O group and the reactions of enols and enolates.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  • describe the structure and polarity of the carbonyl group and the physical properties of aldehydes and ketones;
  • explain why aldehydes are more reactive than ketones;
  • write the general mechanisms of nucleophilic addition under basic and acidic conditions;
  • predict the products of addition of water, HCN, hydride reagents, Grignard reagents, alcohols and amines;
  • use acetals as protecting groups;
  • distinguish aldehydes from ketones with Tollens', Fehling's or Benedict's reagent, and recognise methyl ketones with the iodoform test;
  • explain keto–enol tautomerism and the acidity of α-hydrogens, and write the mechanism of the aldol reaction.

docs.title: 11.1 The carbonyl group
docs.text:
In an aldehyde, the carbonyl carbon carries at least one hydrogen (RCHO; in methanal, HCHO, it carries two). In a ketone, it carries two carbon groups (RCOR′). Naming was covered in Section 2.4: the suffixes are -al and -one.

The carbonyl carbon is sp² hybridised and trigonal planar, with bond angles near 120°. The C=O double bond consists of a σ bond and a π bond, and both are polarised towards oxygen. The polarity can be pictured with two resonance contributors, C=O and C⁺–O⁻ (Example 1.4). The second is minor, but it shows clearly that the carbon is electrophilic and the oxygen nucleophilic and basic.

docs.title: Physical properties
docs.text: Carbonyl compounds are polar, so their boiling points are higher than those of alkanes of similar mass, but they cannot hydrogen bond to one another, so they boil lower than alcohols. Propanal (58 g mol⁻¹) boils at 48 °C, between butane (−1 °C) and propan-1-ol (97 °C). The oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds from water, so small aldehydes and ketones are water-soluble; propanone mixes with water in all proportions and is a widely used solvent. Methanal is a gas, usually supplied as an aqueous solution (formalin), and is toxic. Many larger aldehydes and ketones have pleasant odours and are used as flavourings and in perfumes: benzaldehyde smells of almonds, and vanillin, the main flavour of vanilla, is an aromatic aldehyde.

docs.title: Making aldehydes and ketones
docs.text: The main routes are covered in earlier chapters: oxidation of primary alcohols (to aldehydes) and secondary alcohols (to ketones) (Section 10.5), ozonolysis of alkenes (Section 7.6), hydration of alkynes (Section 7.8) and Friedel–Crafts acylation of arenes (Section 8.4).

docs.title: 11.2 Nucleophilic addition: the general mechanism
docs.text:
A nucleophile adds to the carbonyl carbon. As the new bond forms, the π electrons move onto the oxygen, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate. Protonation of the oxygen then gives the addition product. The carbon changes from trigonal planar (sp²) to tetrahedral (sp³).

Figure 11.1 Nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl group. The general mechanism of nucleophilic addition to an aldehyde or ketone. The nucleophile attacks the δ+ carbon; the π electrons of C=O move onto oxygen, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide. Protonation of the alkoxide gives the neutral addition product.

There are two variants:

  • Basic conditions, strong nucleophile. A strong, usually negatively charged nucleophile (H⁻ from a hydride reagent, R⁻ from a Grignard reagent, CN⁻) attacks the neutral carbonyl directly. The alkoxide is protonated in a later step, often by adding water or dilute acid.
  • Acidic conditions, weak nucleophile. A weak nucleophile (water, an alcohol) does not attack a neutral carbonyl fast enough. An acid catalyst first protonates the carbonyl oxygen. The protonated carbonyl, whose positive charge is shared between O and C, is a much stronger electrophile, and the weak nucleophile attacks it.

If the two groups on the carbonyl carbon are different and the nucleophile is new, the addition creates a stereocentre. Attack on either face of the flat carbonyl is equally likely (unless the molecule or the reagent is chiral), so a racemic product results.

docs.title: Why aldehydes are more reactive than ketones
docs.text:
Aldehydes undergo nucleophilic addition faster and more completely than ketones, for two reasons:

  1. Steric: an aldehyde has a small hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon, so a nucleophile approaches more easily, and the tetrahedral product, with four groups crowded around one carbon, is less strained.
  2. Electronic: alkyl groups donate electrons and reduce the partial positive charge on the carbonyl carbon. A ketone has two alkyl groups, an aldehyde only one.

Methanal, with two hydrogens, is the most reactive of all.

docs.title: 11.3 Addition of oxygen, carbon and hydride nucleophiles
Water: hydrates
docs.text: In water, aldehydes and ketones are in equilibrium with their hydrates (geminal diols, two OH groups on one carbon). The reaction is catalysed by both acid and base. The position of the equilibrium reflects the reactivity of the carbonyl compound: methanal is almost entirely hydrated in water, ethanal about half, and propanone hardly at all. Hydrates usually cannot be isolated, because removing the water reverses the reaction.

docs.title: Hydrogen cyanide: cyanohydrins
docs.text:
Cyanide ion adds to aldehydes and most ketones to give cyanohydrins, with OH and CN on the same carbon. A little base is needed to generate CN⁻, the true nucleophile, from HCN; in practice the reaction is done with a cyanide salt and a controlled amount of acid. The reaction is important because it forms a new C–C bond, and the nitrile group can later be converted into a carboxylic acid (Chapter 12) or an amine (Chapter 13).

\[ \mathrm{CH_3CHO + HCN \rightarrow CH_3CH(OH)CN} \]

Caution: cyanide

Hydrogen cyanide and cyanide salts are extremely toxic. Cyanohydrin reactions are carried out only by trained chemists with specialist precautions. This reaction is described for its chemistry, not as a laboratory procedure.

docs.title: Hydride reducing agents
docs.text:
Sodium tetrahydridoborate, NaBH₄ (sodium borohydride), and lithium tetrahydridoaluminate, LiAlH₄ (lithium aluminium hydride), deliver a hydride ion (H⁻) to the carbonyl carbon. After protonation, aldehydes give primary alcohols and ketones give secondary alcohols:

\[ \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHO \xrightarrow{\ NaBH_4,\ then\ H_2O\ } CH_3CH_2CH_2OH} \] \[ \mathrm{CH_3COCH_3 \xrightarrow{\ NaBH_4,\ then\ H_2O\ } CH_3CH(OH)CH_3} \]

NaBH₄ is mild and convenient; it can be used in water or ethanol and reduces aldehydes and ketones but not esters, carboxylic acids or C=C double bonds. LiAlH₄ is far more reactive: it also reduces esters, acids and amides (Chapter 12), and it reacts violently with water, so it must be used in a dry ether solvent, with the water added cautiously afterwards. Catalytic hydrogenation (H₂ with Ni, Pd or Pt) also reduces C=O groups, but it usually reduces C=C bonds as well.

docs.title: Grignard reagents
docs.text:
A Grignard reagent, R–MgX (Section 9.6), is a source of the carbon nucleophile R⁻. It adds to carbonyl compounds to form a new carbon–carbon bond. After the addition, the magnesium alkoxide is protonated with dilute aqueous acid. The class of alcohol formed depends on the carbonyl compound:

Carbonyl compound Product after protonation Example methanal, HCHO primary alcohol, RCH₂OH CH₃MgBr + HCHO → ethanol other aldehyde, R′CHO secondary alcohol, RR′CHOH CH₃MgBr + CH₃CHO → propan-2-ol ketone, R′COR″ tertiary alcohol, RR′R″COH CH₃MgBr + CH₃COCH₃ → 2-methylpropan-2-ol carbon dioxide, CO₂ carboxylic acid, RCOOH CH₃MgBr + CO₂ → ethanoic acid

Table 11.1. Products of Grignard reagents with carbonyl compounds.

Example 11.1: Planning a Grignard synthesis

Suggest two ways to make 2-phenylbutan-2-ol, C₆H₅C(OH)(CH₃)CH₂CH₃, using a Grignard reagent.

The alcohol carbon carries three groups (phenyl, methyl, ethyl). Remove any one of them as the Grignard reagent; the rest forms the ketone.

(a) Ethylmagnesium bromide + 1-phenylethanone (C₆H₅COCH₃), then H₃O⁺.

(b) Phenylmagnesium bromide + butanone (CH₃COCH₂CH₃), then H₃O⁺.

(A third choice, methylmagnesium bromide + 1-phenylpropan-1-one, also works.) Working backwards from a target to simpler starting materials like this is called retrosynthesis.

docs.title: 11.4 Addition of alcohols: hemiacetals and acetals
docs.text:
An alcohol adds to an aldehyde or ketone under acid catalysis to give a hemiacetal, with an OH and an OR group on the same carbon. Hemiacetals are usually unstable and revert to the carbonyl compound, with one important exception: when the OH and the C=O are in the same molecule and can form a five- or six-membered ring, the cyclic hemiacetal is favoured. This is why glucose and other sugars exist mainly as rings (Chapter 15).

With excess alcohol and an acid catalyst, the hemiacetal reacts further: its OH is protonated, water leaves to give an oxygen-stabilised cation (R₂C=OR⁺), and a second alcohol molecule adds. The product, with two OR groups on one carbon, is an acetal:

\[ \mathrm{R_2C{=}O + 2\,R'OH \overset{H^+}{\rightleftharpoons} R_2C(OR')_2 + H_2O} \]

Every step is reversible. Removing water drives the reaction towards the acetal; adding water and acid hydrolyses the acetal back to the carbonyl compound. Acetals are stable to bases, nucleophiles and hydride reagents, so they are used as protecting groups: a carbonyl group is turned into an acetal (often with ethane-1,2-diol, giving a cyclic acetal) while a reaction is carried out elsewhere in the molecule, and then released by aqueous acid.

Example 11.2: Using a protecting group

How could the ester group of methyl 4-oxopentanoate, CH₃COCH₂CH₂COOCH₃, be reduced with LiAlH₄ without also reducing the ketone?

(1) Protect the ketone as a cyclic acetal with ethane-1,2-diol and an acid catalyst (removing water). (2) Reduce the ester with LiAlH₄ (the acetal is unaffected) to give the primary alcohol. (3) Remove the protecting group with aqueous acid, regenerating the ketone. The product is 5-hydroxypentan-2-one, CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₂OH.

docs.title: 11.5 Addition of nitrogen nucleophiles
docs.text:
Primary amines (RNH₂) add to aldehydes and ketones, and the addition product then loses water to give an imine (a Schiff base), containing a C=N double bond:

\[ \mathrm{R_2C{=}O + R'NH_2 \rightleftharpoons R_2C{=}NR' + H_2O} \]

The reaction is fastest at a moderately acidic pH, around 4 to 5. Some acid is needed to protonate the OH of the intermediate so that it can leave as water; too much acid protonates the amine and destroys its nucleophilicity. Imine formation is reversible and is widely used in biology: many enzymes bind carbonyl-containing substrates as imines with the NH₂ groups of lysine side chains.

Derivatives of ammonia such as hydrazine (H₂N–NH₂) and hydroxylamine (H₂N–OH) react in the same way. A classic test for aldehydes and ketones uses 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (Brady's reagent), supplied as a solution: it gives a yellow, orange or red precipitate of the 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone. Before spectroscopy, the melting point of this crystalline derivative was used to identify the original carbonyl compound.

docs.title: 11.6 Oxidation, and tests for aldehydes
docs.text:
Aldehydes have a hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon and are easily oxidised to carboxylic acids, even by mild oxidising agents. Ketones lack this hydrogen and resist oxidation except under harsh conditions that break C–C bonds. This difference is the basis of the classic tests that distinguish aldehydes from ketones:

  • Tollens' reagent is a solution of the diamminesilver(I) ion, [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺, in aqueous ammonia. Aldehydes reduce it to metallic silver, which deposits as a silver mirror on the inside of a clean test tube; the aldehyde is oxidised to a carboxylate ion.
  • Fehling's solution and Benedict's solution contain blue copper(II) complexes in alkaline solution. Aliphatic aldehydes reduce them, on warming, to a brick-red precipitate of copper(I) oxide, Cu₂O. Benedict's test has long been used to detect reducing sugars such as glucose.
  • Ketones give no reaction with any of these.

Caution: Tollens' reagent

Tollens' reagent must be freshly prepared for each test, used in small amounts, and washed away with dilute acid immediately afterwards. On standing, it can form explosive silver compounds.

docs.title: The iodoform test
docs.text: Iodine in aqueous sodium hydroxide reacts with methyl ketones (RCOCH₃) and with ethanal to give a pale yellow precipitate of triiodomethane (iodoform, CHI₃), which has a characteristic antiseptic smell. The three hydrogens of the methyl group are replaced by iodine, and the CI₃ group is then cleaved off as CHI₃, leaving a carboxylate ion. Alcohols that are oxidised under the conditions to methyl ketones or ethanal (ethanol and secondary alcohols of the form CH₃CH(OH)R) also give a positive test.

docs.title: 11.7 Enols, enolates and the aldol reaction
docs.text: The carbon next to a carbonyl group is the α-carbon, and its hydrogens are α-hydrogens. They are much more acidic than ordinary C–H bonds: the pKa of the α-hydrogens of propanone is about 19, compared with about 50 for an alkane. Removing an α-hydrogen gives an enolate ion, whose negative charge is shared by resonance between the α-carbon and the oxygen.

docs.title: Keto–enol tautomerism
docs.text:
An aldehyde or ketone with an α-hydrogen is in equilibrium with an isomer called its enol, in which the hydrogen has moved to the oxygen and the double bond has moved to between the α-carbon and the carbonyl carbon:

\[ \mathrm{CH_3COCH_3\ (keto) \rightleftharpoons CH_2{=}C(OH)CH_3\ (enol)} \]

Isomers that interconvert rapidly by the movement of a hydrogen atom and a double bond are called tautomers. The interconversion is catalysed by both acid and base. For simple ketones the keto form is overwhelmingly favoured (propanone contains only a tiny fraction of enol at equilibrium), because the C=O bond is stronger than the C=C bond. But the small amount of enol or enolate present is the reactive species in many reactions.

docs.title: The aldol reaction
docs.text:
When ethanal is treated with dilute aqueous sodium hydroxide, two molecules join together. Hydroxide removes an α-hydrogen to form an enolate. The enolate, a carbon nucleophile, adds to the carbonyl carbon of a second ethanal molecule. Protonation of the resulting alkoxide gives 3-hydroxybutanal, a compound that is both an aldehyde and an alcohol, hence the name aldol.

Figure 11.2 The aldol reaction. The base-catalysed aldol reaction of ethanal. Hydroxide removes an α-hydrogen to give a resonance-stabilised enolate ion. The nucleophilic α-carbon of the enolate attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second ethanal molecule. Protonation of the alkoxide by water gives 3-hydroxybutanal and regenerates hydroxide.

On heating, the aldol loses water (the OH and an α-hydrogen), giving an α,β-unsaturated aldehyde, but-2-enal. The overall process is an aldol condensation. It is one of the most important ways of making carbon–carbon bonds, and nature uses it too: an aldol-type reaction is a step in the breakdown of glucose in cells.

Key idea

Carbonyl compounds have two reactive sites. The carbonyl carbon is an electrophile, attacked by nucleophiles. The α-carbon, once deprotonated to an enolate, is a nucleophile. In the aldol reaction one molecule uses its α-carbon to attack the carbonyl carbon of another.

The enol and enolate are also involved in the halogenation of ketones at the α-carbon (as in the first stage of the iodoform reaction) and in the racemisation of ketones whose α-carbon is a stereocentre.

docs.title: 11.8 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • The C=O group is polar: the carbon is electrophilic and the oxygen basic. Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones for steric and electronic reasons.
  • Nucleophilic addition: the nucleophile attacks carbon, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide, which is protonated. Weak nucleophiles need acid catalysis.
  • Water gives hydrates; HCN gives cyanohydrins; NaBH₄ and LiAlH₄ give alcohols (aldehyde → 1°, ketone → 2°); Grignard reagents give alcohols with a new C–C bond (methanal → 1°, aldehyde → 2°, ketone → 3°).
  • Alcohols with acid give hemiacetals and acetals; acetals protect carbonyl groups and are removed by aqueous acid.
  • Primary amines give imines; 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine gives coloured precipitates with aldehydes and ketones.
  • Aldehydes are oxidised by Tollens' reagent (silver mirror) and Fehling's or Benedict's solution (red Cu₂O); ketones are not. Methyl ketones give iodoform.
  • α-Hydrogens are acidic (pKa about 19); enolates and enols are nucleophilic at the α-carbon. The aldol reaction joins two carbonyl compounds.

docs.title: 11.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Arrange in order of increasing reactivity towards nucleophilic addition, and explain: propanone, methanal, ethanal, 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-one.

Answer

3,3-Dimethylbutan-2-one < propanone < ethanal < methanal. Ketones are less reactive than aldehydes because two alkyl groups both hinder attack and reduce the δ+ charge on carbon. The tert-butyl group of 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-one makes it the most hindered. Methanal, with two hydrogens, is the least hindered and the most electrophilic.

Exercise 2

Give the product of each reaction: (a) butanal + NaBH₄, then H₂O; (b) cyclohexanone + CH₃MgBr, then H₃O⁺; (c) propanone + excess methanol with an acid catalyst; (d) benzaldehyde + methanamine (CH₃NH₂) at pH 5.

Answer

(a) Butan-1-ol. (b) 1-Methylcyclohexan-1-ol, a tertiary alcohol. (c) 2,2-Dimethoxypropane, an acetal (with water). (d) The imine C₆H₅CH=NCH₃ (N-benzylidenemethanamine), with water.

Exercise 3

Show how to make each alcohol from a Grignard reagent and a carbonyl compound: (a) pentan-3-ol; (b) 2-methylbutan-2-ol; (c) phenylmethanol (benzyl alcohol).

Answer

(a) Pentan-3-ol, (CH₃CH₂)₂CHOH, is a secondary alcohol: ethylmagnesium bromide + propanal, then H₃O⁺.

(b) 2-Methylbutan-2-ol, (CH₃)₂C(OH)CH₂CH₃, is tertiary: methylmagnesium bromide + butanone, or ethylmagnesium bromide + propanone, then H₃O⁺.

(c) Phenylmethanol, C₆H₅CH₂OH, is primary: phenylmagnesium bromide + methanal, then H₃O⁺.

Exercise 4

Write the mechanism of the acid-catalysed formation of the hemiacetal from ethanal and methanol.

Answer

(1) The carbonyl oxygen of ethanal is protonated by the acid, giving CH₃CH=OH⁺ (positive charge shared with the carbon). (2) A lone pair on the oxygen of methanol attacks the carbonyl carbon; the C=O π electrons move onto the protonated oxygen, which becomes an OH group. The methanol oxygen now has three bonds and a positive charge. (3) A base (another methanol molecule) removes the proton from that oxygen. Product: CH₃CH(OH)OCH₃, 1-methoxyethan-1-ol, and the acid catalyst is regenerated.

Exercise 5

Three liquids, C₃H₆O, are propanal, propanone and prop-2-en-1-ol (CH₂=CHCH₂OH). Describe simple chemical tests to identify each.

Answer

Brady's reagent (2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine) gives an orange precipitate with propanal and propanone but not with the alcohol. Of those two, propanal gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent (or a red precipitate with Fehling's solution); propanone does not, but gives a yellow precipitate of iodoform with iodine and sodium hydroxide. Prop-2-en-1-ol decolourises bromine water (C=C) and fizzes with sodium (O–H).

Exercise 6

Which of these give a positive iodoform test? (a) propanone; (b) pentan-3-one; (c) ethanol; (d) propan-2-ol; (e) methanol; (f) 1-phenylethanone.

Answer

Positive: (a) propanone (a methyl ketone), (c) ethanol (oxidised to ethanal), (d) propan-2-ol (oxidised to propanone) and (f) 1-phenylethanone (a methyl ketone, C₆H₅COCH₃). Negative: (b) pentan-3-one (no CH₃CO group) and (e) methanol.

Exercise 7

Draw the enol form of cyclohexanone. Then give the aldol product formed from two molecules of propanal with dilute NaOH, and the product formed when it is heated.

Answer

The enol of cyclohexanone is cyclohex-1-en-1-ol: the OH on C1, with a C1=C2 double bond.

Propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO, has its α-hydrogens on C2. The enolate (from C2) attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second molecule. The aldol is CH₃CH₂CH(OH)–CH(CH₃)–CHO, 3-hydroxy-2-methylpentanal. On heating it loses water to give 2-methylpent-2-enal, CH₃CH₂CH=C(CH₃)CHO.

docs.title: 11.10 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of aldehydes and ketones

Exercise 1

Nucleophiles attack the carbonyl group at

  1. the oxygen
  2. the carbon
  3. the alpha-hydrogen
  4. the C=O pi bond from the oxygen end
Answer

the carbon

Exercise 2

Reduction of butanone with NaBH₄ gives

  1. butan-1-ol
  2. butan-2-ol
  3. butanal
  4. butanoic acid
Answer

butan-2-ol

Exercise 3

A Grignard reagent reacts with a ketone (after acid work-up) to give

  1. a primary alcohol
  2. a secondary alcohol
  3. a tertiary alcohol
  4. a carboxylic acid
Answer

a tertiary alcohol

Exercise 4

Which reagent gives a silver mirror with aldehydes but not with ketones?

  1. Tollens' reagent
  2. Brady's reagent
  3. bromine water
  4. Lucas reagent
Answer

Tollens' reagent

Exercise 5

Acetals are stable to

  1. aqueous acid
  2. bases and nucleophiles
  3. water with an acid catalyst
  4. all reagents
Answer

bases and nucleophiles

Exercise 6

What is the name of the product of the aldol reaction of two molecules of ethanal?

Answer

3-hydroxybutanal

Exercise 7

The pKa of the alpha-hydrogens of propanone is about

  1. 5
  2. 10
  3. 19
  4. 50
Answer

19

docs.title: Chapter 6: Alkanes and Conformations
docs.text:
Saturated hydrocarbons, their shapes and their radical reactions

Alkanes are the simplest organic compounds: only carbon and hydrogen, joined by single bonds. They make up natural gas and most of petroleum, and they are the hydrocarbon backbone on which the functional groups of later chapters sit. Alkanes are not very reactive, but they are far from dull. Rotation about their single bonds gives them shapes, called conformations, whose energies explain much about the behaviour of larger molecules, and the chair shape of cyclohexane is one of the most important structures in chemistry and biology. This chapter covers the properties and sources of alkanes, the conformations of chains and rings, and the two reactions alkanes do undergo: combustion and radical halogenation.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  • relate the physical properties of alkanes to their size and shape;
  • draw Newman projections and explain the energy differences between staggered and eclipsed conformations;
  • describe the conformations of butane and the origin of torsional and steric strain;
  • explain ring strain in small rings and the absence of strain in the cyclohexane chair;
  • draw the chair conformation of cyclohexane with axial and equatorial bonds, and predict the preferred conformation of substituted cyclohexanes;
  • write the radical chain mechanism for the halogenation of an alkane and predict product ratios from relative reactivities.

docs.title: 6.1 Alkanes: structure, sources and properties
docs.text:
Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons: each carbon is sp³ hybridised and bonded to four other atoms by single bonds, the most hydrogen a carbon skeleton can carry. Open-chain alkanes have the formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; cycloalkanes with one ring have CₙH₂ₙ. Members of a series that differ by one CH₂ unit form a homologous series, with gradually changing physical properties and very similar chemistry.

The main source of alkanes is petroleum (crude oil) and natural gas. Natural gas is mostly methane, with some ethane, propane and butane. Crude oil is a complex mixture separated in a refinery by fractional distillation into fractions of different boiling ranges: gases (C₁ to C₄), petrol or gasoline (roughly C₅ to C₁₀), kerosene, diesel and fuel oils, and the residue used for lubricants and bitumen. Larger molecules are broken into smaller, more useful ones by cracking, which also produces the alkenes used to make polymers (Chapter 15).

docs.title: Physical properties
docs.text:
Alkanes are non-polar. The only forces between their molecules are London dispersion forces (Section 1.8), so:

  • Boiling points rise with chain length, roughly 20 to 30 °C for each extra CH₂ in the middle of the series. At room temperature, C₁ to C₄ are gases, C₅ to about C₁₇ are liquids, and larger alkanes are waxy solids.
  • Branching lowers the boiling point, because a compact, nearly spherical molecule has less surface in contact with its neighbours. Pentane boils at 36 °C, 2-methylbutane at 28 °C and 2,2-dimethylpropane at about 10 °C.
  • Alkanes are insoluble in water and less dense than water, which is why oil floats on the sea. They dissolve in other non-polar solvents and are themselves used as solvents (hexane, heptane).
Alkane Formula Boiling point (°C) State at 25 °C methane CH₄ −162 gas ethane C₂H₆ −89 gas propane C₃H₈ −42 gas butane C₄H₁₀ −1 gas pentane C₅H₁₂ 36 liquid hexane C₆H₁₄ 69 liquid octane C₈H₁₈ 126 liquid decane C₁₀H₂₂ 174 liquid

Table 6.1. Boiling points of some unbranched alkanes.

docs.title: 6.2 Conformations of ethane
docs.text:
Rotation about a C–C single bond is easy (Section 1.5). As one methyl group of ethane turns relative to the other, the molecule passes through an infinite number of shapes. These shapes, which interconvert by rotation about single bonds without breaking any bond, are conformations (or conformers).

The best way to see them is a Newman projection: look straight down the C–C bond. The front carbon is a point where three bonds meet; the back carbon is a circle, with its three bonds coming out from behind the edge.

Figure 6.1 Staggered and eclipsed ethane. Newman projections of ethane. In the staggered conformation (left) the C–H bonds on the back carbon lie exactly between those on the front carbon, 60° apart. In the eclipsed conformation (right) each back C–H bond lies behind a front C–H bond; it is drawn slightly offset so that both can be seen.

Two conformations are special:

  • In the staggered conformation the C–H bonds on the two carbons are as far apart as possible, with a dihedral angle of 60° between neighbouring bonds on the front and back carbons. This is the conformation of lowest energy.
  • In the eclipsed conformation each C–H bond on the back carbon lies directly behind one on the front, with a dihedral angle of 0°. This is the conformation of highest energy.

The eclipsed conformation is about 12 kJ mol⁻¹ higher in energy than the staggered one. The extra energy is called torsional strain. It comes mainly from the repulsion between the electron pairs of bonds that are lined up with each other, and partly from the loss of a favourable interaction between filled C–H bonding orbitals and empty antibonding orbitals that is possible only in the staggered arrangement. A barrier of 12 kJ mol⁻¹ is small compared with the thermal energy available at room temperature: ethane rotates through its conformations many millions of times each second. At any instant most molecules are close to the staggered conformation.

Key idea

Conformations are not isomers. They interconvert rapidly at room temperature and cannot be separated. But the populations of conformations, and the energy differences between them, control the shapes of molecules and often the outcome of their reactions.

docs.title: 6.3 Conformations of butane
docs.text:
Butane has a more interesting energy profile, because the groups on C2 and C3 are not all the same. Looking along the C2–C3 bond, each carbon carries one methyl group and two hydrogens. The key conformations are named by the dihedral angle between the two methyl groups:

  • Anti (180°): the methyl groups are as far apart as possible. This is the most stable conformation.
  • Gauche (60°): the methyl groups are staggered but next to each other. They are close enough to crowd each other, raising the energy by about 3.8 kJ mol⁻¹. This repulsion between groups that are forced too close together is called steric strain.
  • Eclipsed, CH₃ with H (120°): about 16 kJ mol⁻¹ above anti, from torsional strain plus some steric strain.
  • Fully eclipsed, CH₃ with CH₃ (0°): the highest point, about 19 kJ mol⁻¹ above anti, from torsional strain and severe steric strain between the methyl groups.
Figure 6.2 Conformational energy of butane. The energy of butane as a function of the dihedral angle between its two methyl groups. The minima are the anti conformation at 180° and the two gauche conformations at 60° and 300°. The maxima are eclipsed conformations; the highest, at 0°, has the two methyl groups eclipsing each other.

At room temperature about two-thirds of butane molecules are anti and one-third gauche. For longer chains, the preference for anti arrangements is why unbranched alkane chains in crystals and in the hydrocarbon tails of fats adopt the extended zigzag shape that we draw in skeletal formulas.

Example 6.1: The energy of a conformation

Using these approximate costs: H/H eclipsing 4.0 kJ mol⁻¹, CH₃/H eclipsing 6.0 kJ mol⁻¹, CH₃/CH₃ eclipsing 11 kJ mol⁻¹, and gauche CH₃/CH₃ 3.8 kJ mol⁻¹, estimate the energy of the two eclipsed conformations of butane relative to anti.

At 120°, the eclipsed pairs are CH₃/H, CH₃/H and H/H: 6.0 + 6.0 + 4.0 = 16 kJ mol⁻¹.

At 0°, the pairs are CH₃/CH₃, H/H and H/H: 11 + 4.0 + 4.0 = 19 kJ mol⁻¹.

Both agree with Figure 6.2. The same bookkeeping (adding up the cost of each interaction) is used to estimate the energies of more complicated conformations.

docs.title: 6.4 Cycloalkanes and ring strain
docs.text:
In a ring, the carbon atoms cannot rotate freely, and the C–C–C bond angles are constrained by the ring size. A flat ring with \(n\) atoms would have internal angles of 60° (cyclopropane), 90° (cyclobutane), 108° (cyclopentane) and 120° (cyclohexane). Since sp³ carbon prefers 109.5°, small rings suffer angle strain. Rings also suffer torsional strain if their C–H bonds are forced to eclipse.

The total ring strain can be measured from heats of combustion. Each CH₂ group in a strain-free chain releases about 659 kJ mol⁻¹ when burned; any extra energy released per CH₂ by a ring compound is strain energy that is released when the ring is destroyed.

Cycloalkane Heat of combustion per CH₂ (kJ mol⁻¹) Total strain energy (kJ mol⁻¹) cyclopropane 697 about 115 cyclobutane 686 about 110 cyclopentane 664 about 26 cyclohexane 659 about 0

Table 6.2. Ring strain from heats of combustion.

  • Cyclopropane must be flat, with 60° angles and all its C–H bonds eclipsed. Its C–C bonds are bent, with poor orbital overlap, and they are weak: cyclopropane opens more easily than other alkanes.
  • Cyclobutane puckers slightly (one carbon bends out of the plane), which relieves some torsional strain at the cost of a little more angle strain.
  • Cyclopentane adopts an envelope shape, with one carbon out of the plane, and has little strain.
  • Cyclohexane is essentially strain-free, because it is not flat at all.

docs.title: 6.5 The chair conformation of cyclohexane
docs.text: Cyclohexane adopts a puckered chair conformation, so called for its resemblance to a reclining chair. In the chair every C–C–C angle is close to the tetrahedral 109.5°, and every C–H bond is perfectly staggered with its neighbours. The chair therefore has neither angle strain nor torsional strain. Six-membered rings are extremely common in nature, in sugars, steroids and many drugs, partly for this reason.

docs.title: Axial and equatorial positions
docs.text:
Each carbon of the chair has two hydrogens, which point in different directions:

  • One is axial: parallel to the axis of the ring, pointing straight up or straight down. The axial positions alternate up and down around the ring.
  • The other is equatorial: pointing outwards from the ring, roughly along its "equator", slightly up on carbons whose axial bond points down and slightly down on carbons whose axial bond points up.
Figure 6.3 Axial and equatorial bonds. The chair conformation of cyclohexane. The six axial bonds (red) are vertical, alternately up and down. The six equatorial bonds (blue) point outwards; each equatorial bond is parallel to the two ring bonds that are one bond away from it.

How to draw a chair

  1. Draw two parallel lines sloping slightly downwards, offset from each other.
  2. Join their ends to make the two tips: the left tip pointing down, the right tip pointing up.
  3. Draw the axial bonds vertically: up at the "up" carbons (the right tip and every second carbon from it), down at the others.
  4. Draw each equatorial bond parallel to the ring bonds one bond away, pointing outwards.

Practise until you can draw a neat chair in ten seconds; it is worth it.

docs.title: Ring flipping
docs.text: The chair is not rigid. By rotating about its C–C bonds, it can turn into a second chair, passing through higher-energy shapes on the way (the half-chair and the twist-boat; the boat conformation, about 30 kJ mol⁻¹ above the chair, suffers eclipsing along its sides and crowding between the two "flagpole" hydrogens). This ring flip has a barrier of about 45 kJ mol⁻¹ and happens roughly a hundred thousand times a second at room temperature.
