In a ring flip, every axial position becomes equatorial and every equatorial position becomes axial, while up stays up and down stays down.

docs.title: Substituted cyclohexanes
docs.text:
In cyclohexane itself the two chairs are identical. In a substituted cyclohexane they are not. In methylcyclohexane, one chair has the methyl group axial and the other has it equatorial.

Figure 6.4 Axial and equatorial methylcyclohexane. The ring flip of methylcyclohexane. In the axial conformer the methyl group is close to the two axial hydrogens on the same side of the ring, three carbons away (red), an unfavourable 1,3-diaxial interaction. In the equatorial conformer the methyl group points away from the ring and has no such interaction, so this conformer is preferred, by about 7 kJ mol⁻¹.

An axial substituent is crowded by the two axial hydrogens on the same face of the ring, on carbons 3 and 5 relative to it. These 1,3-diaxial interactions are the same kind of steric strain as the gauche interaction in butane. For a methyl group the equatorial conformer is favoured by about 7.3 kJ mol⁻¹, enough for about 95% of methylcyclohexane molecules to have the methyl group equatorial at room temperature. Larger groups have larger preferences. A tert-butyl group is so strongly equatorial that it effectively locks the ring in one chair.

Example 6.2: The more stable conformation of a disubstituted cyclohexane

Which is more stable, cis- or trans-1,4-dimethylcyclohexane? Draw the preferred chair of each.

In the chair, C1 and C4 are carbons of opposite type: if C1 has its axial bond pointing down, C4 has its axial bond pointing up. An equatorial bond points slightly to the face opposite its carbon's axial bond, so the two equatorial bonds at C1 and C4 point to opposite faces. Hence a trans arrangement allows both groups to be equatorial, while a cis arrangement forces one group axial and one equatorial.

  • trans: one chair is diequatorial, the other diaxial. The diequatorial chair is strongly preferred.
  • cis: both chairs have one axial and one equatorial methyl; they are equal in energy.

So trans-1,4-dimethylcyclohexane is more stable, by roughly the cost of one axial methyl group (about 7 kJ mol⁻¹).

Caution: cis/trans is not axial/equatorial

Cis and trans describe whether two groups are on the same face or opposite faces of the ring; they never change. Axial and equatorial describe positions in one particular chair; they swap on ring flipping. Whether a cis compound can be diequatorial depends on the positions: for 1,2 and 1,4 substitution trans can be diequatorial, but for 1,3 substitution it is the cis isomer that can be diequatorial.

docs.title: 6.6 Reactions of alkanes
docs.text: Alkanes are sometimes called paraffins, from the Latin for "little affinity". They do not react with acids, bases, most oxidising agents or nucleophiles at room temperature, because their C–C and C–H bonds are strong and nearly non-polar, offering no site for polar attack. They have two important reactions.

docs.title: Combustion
docs.text:
Alkanes burn in excess oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water, releasing a great deal of energy:

\[ \mathrm{CH_4 + 2\,O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2\,H_2O} \qquad \Delta H^\circ \approx -890\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} \]

This is why alkanes are our main fuels. In a limited supply of oxygen, combustion is incomplete and produces carbon monoxide, a toxic gas, and soot (carbon). Combustion of fossil fuels is also the main source of the carbon dioxide that is driving climate change, a point taken up in Chapter 16.

docs.title: Radical halogenation
docs.text:
When a mixture of an alkane and chlorine or bromine is exposed to ultraviolet light or heated, a hydrogen is replaced by a halogen:

\[ \mathrm{CH_4 + Cl_2 \xrightarrow{\ h\nu\ } CH_3Cl + HCl} \]

The reaction does not occur in the dark at room temperature. It goes by a radical chain mechanism with three stages.

Initiation. Light splits a chlorine molecule homolytically (the Cl–Cl bond, 242 kJ mol⁻¹, is much weaker than C–H):

  • Cl–Cl → 2 Cl•

Propagation. Two steps repeat in a cycle. Each consumes one radical and produces another, so a single initiation can lead to thousands of product molecules:

  • Cl• + H–CH₃ → H–Cl + •CH₃
  • •CH₃ + Cl–Cl → CH₃–Cl + Cl•

Add the two propagation steps and the radicals cancel, leaving the overall equation CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl.

Termination. The chain stops when two radicals meet and combine, which is rare because radicals are present at very low concentration:

  • Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂
  • •CH₃ + Cl• → CH₃Cl
  • •CH₃ + •CH₃ → CH₃CH₃

Each step uses fish-hook arrows: in the first propagation step, one electron from the C–H bond pairs with the unpaired electron of Cl• to form H–Cl, and the other electron stays on carbon. The small amount of ethane formed by termination is evidence for the methyl radical.

Caution: mixtures of products

Radical halogenation is hard to control. The product CH₃Cl can react further to give CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄, and alkanes with different kinds of hydrogen give mixtures of isomers. It is useful industrially and for simple molecules, but rarely the method of choice in the laboratory.

docs.title: Selectivity: chlorination versus bromination
docs.text:
In propane there are six primary hydrogens (on the two CH₃ groups) and two secondary hydrogens (on the CH₂). If every hydrogen were equally reactive, chlorination would give 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane in the ratio 6 : 2. In fact it gives about 45% 1-chloropropane and 55% 2-chloropropane. Secondary hydrogens are more reactive, because breaking a secondary C–H bond gives a more stable secondary radical (Section 5.6).

At room temperature, the relative reactivity per hydrogen for chlorination is roughly tertiary : secondary : primary ≈ 5 : 4 : 1. Bromination is far more selective: the reactivity ratio for tertiary to primary hydrogens is of the order of a thousand to one or more, and bromination of propane gives about 97% 2-bromopropane.

The difference comes from the energetics of the first propagation step. Removal of a hydrogen by Cl• is exothermic, with an early transition state that resembles the reactants and is little affected by the stability of the radical being formed. Removal by Br• is endothermic, with a late transition state that resembles the alkyl radical, so the differences in radical stability are strongly felt (the Hammond postulate, Section 5.7).

Example 6.3: Predicting a product ratio

Predict the ratio of the two monochlorination products of 2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CH, using relative reactivities tertiary : primary = 5 : 1.

There are 9 primary hydrogens (three CH₃ groups) and 1 tertiary hydrogen.

  • Primary: 9 × 1 = 9 → 1-chloro-2-methylpropane.
  • Tertiary: 1 × 5 = 5 → 2-chloro-2-methylpropane.

Fraction of tertiary product = 5/14 = 36%; primary product 64%. The large number of primary hydrogens outweighs their lower reactivity. With bromine, the tertiary product would dominate almost completely.

docs.title: 6.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Alkanes (CₙH₂ₙ₊₂) are saturated, non-polar hydrocarbons from petroleum and natural gas. Boiling point rises with chain length and falls with branching.
  • Conformations interconvert by rotation about single bonds. In ethane, staggered is about 12 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable than eclipsed (torsional strain).
  • In butane: anti is most stable, gauche is 3.8 kJ mol⁻¹ higher (steric strain), and the fully eclipsed form is highest.
  • Small rings have angle and torsional strain; cyclohexane in the chair conformation is strain-free.
  • The chair has six axial and six equatorial positions; a ring flip swaps them. Substituents prefer equatorial positions to avoid 1,3-diaxial interactions.
  • Alkanes burn to CO₂ and H₂O and undergo radical halogenation by initiation, propagation and termination.
  • Reactivity of C–H bonds towards radicals is 3° > 2° > 1°; bromination is much more selective than chlorination.

docs.title: 6.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Arrange in order of increasing boiling point: hexane, 2,2-dimethylbutane, pentane, 2-methylpentane. Explain.

Answer

Pentane (36 °C) < 2,2-dimethylbutane (about 50 °C) < 2-methylpentane (about 60 °C) < hexane (69 °C). Pentane has the fewest carbons and the weakest dispersion forces. The three C₆ isomers have the same formula; the more branched and compact the molecule, the smaller its surface area and the lower its boiling point.

Exercise 2

Draw Newman projections, looking along the C–C bond, of the staggered and eclipsed conformations of chloroethane, CH₃CH₂Cl. Why is the energy difference slightly larger than in ethane?

Answer

Front carbon (C1): three H. Back carbon (C2): two H and one Cl. In the staggered conformation the Cl lies between two hydrogens of the front carbon; in the eclipsed conformation it lies behind one of them. The barrier is a little larger than in ethane (about 15 kJ mol⁻¹ rather than 12) because eclipsing an H with the larger Cl atom adds some steric strain to the torsional strain.

Exercise 3

Using Figure 6.2, sketch Newman projections of butane at dihedral angles of 0°, 60°, 120° and 180°, and label each as anti, gauche or eclipsed.

Answer

Looking along C2–C3, each carbon carries CH₃, H, H. At 180° the two CH₃ groups point in opposite directions (anti). At 60° they are staggered and adjacent (gauche). At 120° each CH₃ eclipses an H (eclipsed). At 0° the CH₃ groups eclipse each other (fully eclipsed, the highest energy).

Exercise 4

Explain why cyclopropane reacts with bromine (opening the ring to give 1,3-dibromopropane) under conditions where propane and cyclohexane do not react.

Answer

Cyclopropane has about 115 kJ mol⁻¹ of ring strain: its C–C–C angles are forced to 60° instead of 109.5°, its bonds are bent with poor overlap, and all its C–H bonds are eclipsed. Opening the ring releases this strain, so the C–C bonds of cyclopropane are weaker and more reactive than those of an unstrained alkane. Cyclohexane is essentially strain-free and behaves like an open-chain alkane.

Exercise 5

For each compound, draw both chair conformations and say which is preferred: (a) tert-butylcyclohexane; (b) cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane; (c) trans-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane.

Answer

(a) One chair has the tert-butyl group equatorial, the other axial. The axial form suffers severe 1,3-diaxial interactions; the equatorial chair is overwhelmingly preferred, and the ring is effectively locked.

(b) cis-1,2: in either chair one methyl is axial and the other equatorial. The two chairs have equal energy.

(c) trans-1,2: one chair is diequatorial, the other diaxial. The diequatorial chair is strongly preferred (there is a gauche interaction between the two adjacent equatorial methyls, but this is much less costly than two axial methyl groups).

Exercise 6

Write the initiation, two propagation steps and two termination steps for the radical monobromination of ethane.

Answer

Initiation: Br₂ → 2 Br• (light or heat).

Propagation: Br• + CH₃CH₃ → HBr + CH₃CH₂•; then CH₃CH₂• + Br₂ → CH₃CH₂Br + Br•.

Termination (any two): Br• + Br• → Br₂; CH₃CH₂• + Br• → CH₃CH₂Br; 2 CH₃CH₂• → CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ (butane).

Exercise 7

Butane is chlorinated in light. Using the relative reactivity per hydrogen secondary : primary = 4 : 1, predict the percentages of 1-chlorobutane and 2-chlorobutane. Is 2-chlorobutane formed as a single enantiomer?

Answer

Butane has 6 primary H (two CH₃) and 4 secondary H (two CH₂). Primary: 6 × 1 = 6. Secondary: 4 × 4 = 16. 1-Chlorobutane = 6/22 = 27%; 2-chlorobutane = 16/22 = 73%. (Experimentally about 30 : 70.)

2-Chlorobutane has a stereocentre at C2. The intermediate secondary radical is planar, and chlorine can attack either face equally, so 2-chlorobutane is formed as a racemic mixture.

docs.title: 6.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of alkanes and conformations

Exercise 1

In the most stable conformation of butane, the two methyl groups are

  1. eclipsed
  2. gauche
  3. anti
  4. axial
Answer

anti

Exercise 2

The energy difference between eclipsed and staggered ethane is mainly due to

  1. angle strain
  2. torsional strain
  3. hydrogen bonding
  4. ring strain
Answer

torsional strain

Exercise 3

Which cycloalkane is essentially free of ring strain?

  1. cyclopropane
  2. cyclobutane
  3. cyclopentane
  4. cyclohexane
Answer

cyclohexane

Exercise 4

When a cyclohexane chair flips, an axial substituent becomes

  1. equatorial
  2. axial on the other face
  3. a cis substituent
  4. a boat
Answer

equatorial

Exercise 5

How many axial hydrogens does a cyclohexane chair have?

Answer

6 / six

Exercise 6

In the propagation step Cl• + CH₄ →, the products are

  1. CH₃Cl + H•
  2. HCl + •CH₃
  3. CH₃• + Cl₂
  4. CH₂Cl₂ + H₂
Answer

HCl + •CH₃

Exercise 7

Bromination of 2-methylpropane gives mainly

  1. 1-bromo-2-methylpropane
  2. 2-bromo-2-methylpropane
  3. a 9 to 1 mixture of the two
  4. no reaction
Answer

2-bromo-2-methylpropane

Bromination is highly selective for the tertiary C-H bond, which gives the most stable radical.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Alkenes and Alkynes
docs.text:
Addition reactions of carbon–carbon multiple bonds

The π bond of an alkene is a store of loosely held electrons sitting above and below the plane of the molecule. Electron-seeking reagents attack it, and the typical result is addition: the π bond disappears and two new σ bonds form, one to each carbon. A handful of addition reactions turns an alkene into an alkane, a haloalkane, an alcohol, a diol, an epoxide or a pair of carbonyl compounds, which makes alkenes among the most versatile starting materials in synthesis. This chapter explains the stability of alkenes, the mechanism of electrophilic addition and the rules that predict where the new groups go, and then extends the same ideas to alkynes.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  • relate the stability of alkenes to their substitution pattern and geometry;
  • write the mechanism of electrophilic addition of HX and explain Markovnikov's rule in terms of carbocation stability;
  • predict products when carbocation rearrangements can occur;
  • describe the addition of halogens through a bromonium ion and explain anti addition;
  • give the reagents and products, including regiochemistry and stereochemistry, for hydration, hydroboration–oxidation, hydrogenation, epoxidation, dihydroxylation and ozonolysis;
  • describe the acidity of terminal alkynes and the main addition reactions of alkynes;
  • use the bromine-water test for unsaturation.

docs.title: 7.1 Structure and stability of alkenes
docs.text:
An alkene has a C=C double bond made of one σ bond and one π bond (Section 1.5). The two carbons of the double bond and the four atoms attached to them all lie in one plane, with bond angles of about 120°. Because the π bond prevents rotation, alkenes with two different groups on each carbon exist as E/Z isomers (Section 3.2).

Not all alkenes are equally stable. A convenient measure is the heat of hydrogenation, the energy released when H₂ adds to the double bond to give an alkane. For the three butenes, which all give butane:

Alkene Structure Heat of hydrogenation (kJ mol⁻¹) but-1-ene CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃ −126 (Z)-but-2-ene cis-CH₃CH=CHCH₃ −119 (E)-but-2-ene trans-CH₃CH=CHCH₃ −115

Table 7.1. Heats of hydrogenation of the butenes. Less heat released means a more stable alkene.

Two rules follow:

  1. More substituted alkenes are more stable. An alkene with more alkyl groups on the double-bond carbons is lower in energy: tetrasubstituted > trisubstituted > disubstituted > monosubstituted > ethene. Alkyl groups donate electron density to the sp² carbons, partly by hyperconjugation.
  2. Trans (E) alkenes are more stable than cis (Z), because in the cis isomer the two groups on the same side crowd each other.

These rules matter when a reaction can make more than one alkene, as in the eliminations of Chapter 9: the more stable alkene is usually the main product.

docs.title: 7.2 Electrophilic addition of hydrogen halides
docs.text:
Alkenes react with hydrogen halides (HCl, HBr, HI) to give haloalkanes. With ethene there is only one possible product:

\[ \mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2 + HBr \rightarrow CH_3CH_2Br} \]

docs.title: The mechanism
docs.text:
The reaction takes place in two steps.

  1. The π bond attacks the proton. The alkene is the nucleophile and H–Br the electrophile. The π electrons form a new C–H bond to one carbon, and the H–Br bonding pair leaves with bromine as Br⁻. The other carbon of the former double bond is left with only three bonds: a carbocation. This step is slow and rate-determining.
  2. Bromide attacks the carbocation. The bromide ion, a nucleophile, gives a lone pair to the empty p orbital of the cation, forming the C–Br bond.

The overall process is called electrophilic addition, after the first step, in which the alkene is attacked by an electrophile.

docs.title: Markovnikov's rule
docs.text:
With an unsymmetrical alkene such as propene, two products are possible: 1-bromopropane and 2-bromopropane. In practice the product is almost entirely 2-bromopropane. In the nineteenth century the Russian chemist Vladimir Markovnikov summarised many such results in a rule: when HX adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the hydrogen goes to the carbon that already has more hydrogens.

The mechanism explains why. The product is decided in the first step, when the proton adds. If the proton adds to C1 (the CH₂ end), the positive charge is left on C2, giving a secondary carbocation. If it adds to C2, the charge is left on C1, giving a primary carbocation. The secondary cation is much more stable (Section 5.6), and by the Hammond postulate the transition state leading to it is lower in energy, so that path is much faster.

Figure 7.1 Markovnikov addition of HBr to propene. The mechanism of the addition of HBr to propene. The π electrons attack the proton of H–Br, adding H to C1 and leaving a secondary carbocation at C2. Bromide then attacks the positive carbon, giving 2-bromopropane. The alternative, adding H to C2, would produce a far less stable primary carbocation and is not observed.

Key idea

The modern form of Markovnikov's rule: an electrophile adds to an alkene so as to form the more stable carbocation. This version works for any electrophile, not only H⁺, and explains every case the original rule describes.

A reaction that can give two constitutional isomers but gives mainly one is called regioselective. Electrophilic addition of HX is strongly regioselective.

Example 7.1: Predicting Markovnikov products

Predict the main product of (a) 2-methylpropene + HCl; (b) 1-methylcyclohexene + HBr.

(a) (CH₃)₂C=CH₂. Adding H⁺ to the CH₂ carbon gives the tertiary cation (CH₃)₃C⁺; adding it to the other carbon would give a primary cation. Chloride then captures the tertiary cation: 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CCl.

(b) The double bond joins C1 (which carries the methyl) and C2 (which carries a hydrogen). Adding H⁺ to C2 gives a tertiary cation at C1. Bromide adds there: 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane.

docs.title: Carbocation rearrangements
docs.text: Because the reaction passes through a carbocation, the cation can rearrange before the halide arrives, if a hydride or alkyl shift would make it more stable. Adding HCl to 3-methylbut-1-ene, CH₂=CH–CH(CH₃)₂, first gives a secondary cation at C2. A hydrogen on the neighbouring C3, with its pair of electrons, then shifts to C2, putting the positive charge on C3, which is tertiary. Chloride captures both cations, but the rearranged product, 2-chloro-2-methylbutane, is the major one, alongside some 2-chloro-3-methylbutane. Rearrangements like this are evidence that a carbocation intermediate is really formed.

docs.title: The peroxide effect
docs.text: Hydrogen bromide (but not HCl or HI) adds to alkenes the "wrong" way, anti-Markovnikov, when peroxides (R–O–O–R) are present. Peroxides start a radical chain: a bromine atom adds to the alkene first, at the end that gives the more stable carbon radical, and the resulting radical then takes a hydrogen atom from HBr. So propene with HBr and a peroxide gives 1-bromopropane. The orientation is still decided by forming the more stable intermediate; it is simply that the first species to add is Br•, not H⁺.

docs.title: 7.3 Addition of water: hydration
docs.text:
Water itself does not add to alkenes, because it is not acidic enough to protonate the π bond. With an acid catalyst (dilute sulfuric or phosphoric acid), alkenes add water to give alcohols. The mechanism is the same as for HX, with water as the nucleophile:

  1. The alkene is protonated to the more stable carbocation.
  2. Water attacks the carbocation, giving an oxonium ion, R–OH₂⁺.
  3. Water removes a proton from the oxonium ion, giving the alcohol and regenerating H₃O⁺, the catalyst.

The regiochemistry is Markovnikov: propene gives propan-2-ol. Industrially, ethanol is made by the direct hydration of ethene with steam over a phosphoric acid catalyst at high temperature and pressure. Because a carbocation is involved, rearrangements can occur, and the reaction is reversible: the reverse reaction, acid-catalysed dehydration of an alcohol, is a way of making alkenes (Chapter 10).

docs.title: 7.4 Addition of halogens
docs.text:
Bromine and chlorine add rapidly to alkenes at room temperature, without light, to give 1,2-dihalides (vicinal dihalides):

\[ \mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2 + Br_2 \rightarrow BrCH_2CH_2Br} \]

docs.title: The test for unsaturation
docs.text: Bromine water (or a solution of bromine in an inert solvent) is orange-brown. When it is shaken with an alkene, the colour disappears as the bromine adds. Alkanes do not decolourise bromine water in the dark. This is the classic laboratory test for a C=C double bond. (Bromine is toxic and corrosive, and the test is done in small quantities in a fume cupboard.)

docs.title: The mechanism: a bromonium ion
docs.text:
Br₂ has no permanent dipole, but as it approaches the electron-rich π bond the Br–Br bond becomes polarised; the nearer bromine becomes δ+ and acts as the electrophile. The π electrons attack it and the Br–Br bond breaks, with the far bromine leaving as Br⁻. The intermediate is not an open carbocation but a three-membered ring, the bromonium ion, in which the bromine bridges both carbons and carries the positive charge (a lone pair on bromine forms the second C–Br bond).

The bromonium ion blocks one face of the molecule. The bromide ion must therefore attack from the opposite face, opening the ring. The two bromines end up on opposite faces of the original double bond: anti addition.

Figure 7.2 Anti addition of bromine. The addition of bromine through a bromonium ion. The π bond attacks one bromine of Br₂, forming a cyclic bromonium ion in which bromine bridges both carbons. Bromide then attacks one carbon from the side away from the bridge, opening the ring. The two bromine atoms end up on opposite sides: anti addition.

The stereochemistry is easiest to see with a ring. Cyclohexene and bromine give only trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane (as a racemic mixture); no cis isomer is formed. A reaction in which the stereochemistry of the product is determined by the mechanism, so that a particular stereoisomer of the reactant gives a particular stereoisomer of the product, is called stereospecific.

docs.title: Halohydrins
docs.text: When bromine is added to an alkene in water, the solvent competes with bromide to open the bromonium ion. Water is present in vast excess, so the main product is a bromohydrin, with OH on one carbon and Br on the next, added anti. Water attacks the carbon of the bromonium ion that can better carry positive charge, which is the more substituted carbon. Propene therefore gives 1-bromopropan-2-ol, with OH on the central carbon: the electrophile (Br) has gone to the end with more hydrogens, as Markovnikov's rule predicts.

docs.title: 7.5 Hydroboration–oxidation: anti-Markovnikov alcohols
docs.text:
Sometimes we want the OH on the less substituted carbon. Hydroboration–oxidation achieves this in two steps.

  1. Hydroboration. Borane, BH₃ (used as a complex with a solvent such as tetrahydrofuran, THF), adds across the double bond. Boron, which has an empty p orbital, is the electrophile; it bonds to the less substituted carbon, while a hydrogen from boron moves to the other carbon. The B–H bond adds in one step through a four-centre transition state, so H and B add to the same face (syn addition), and no carbocation is formed, so there are no rearrangements.
  2. Oxidation. Alkaline hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂, NaOH) replaces the boron with an OH group, with retention of configuration.

The net result is the anti-Markovnikov, syn addition of H and OH. Propene gives propan-1-ol; 1-methylcyclohexene gives trans-2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol, in which the H and OH that were added are cis to each other, so the methyl and OH end up trans.

Boron goes to the less substituted carbon for two reasons: it is a large group and that carbon is less crowded, and in the transition state a partial positive charge builds up on the more substituted carbon, which can stabilise it better.

docs.title: Catalytic hydrogenation
docs.text:
Alkenes add hydrogen in the presence of a finely divided metal catalyst, such as platinum, palladium or nickel, to give alkanes:

\[ \mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CH_2 + H_2 \xrightarrow{\ Pt\ } CH_3CH_2CH_3} \]

Both hydrogen and the alkene are adsorbed on the metal surface, and the two hydrogens are delivered from the surface to the same face of the alkene (syn addition). Hydrogenation is used in the food industry to harden vegetable oils into spreads. Partial hydrogenation can isomerise some of the remaining cis double bonds to trans, giving "trans fats", whose links to heart disease have led many countries to restrict them.

docs.title: Epoxidation
docs.text: A peroxycarboxylic acid (a peroxyacid, RCO₃H, such as 3-chloroperoxybenzoic acid, mCPBA) transfers an oxygen atom to an alkene in a single step, giving an epoxide, a three-membered cyclic ether (Chapter 10). The oxygen adds to one face, so the reaction is a stereospecific syn addition: a cis alkene gives a cis epoxide.

docs.title: Dihydroxylation
docs.text:
Two OH groups can be added to the same face (syn dihydroxylation) with osmium tetroxide (OsO₄, usually in catalytic amounts with a second oxidant to regenerate it) or with cold, dilute, alkaline potassium manganate(VII) (KMnO₄). Both pass through a cyclic intermediate in which the metal is bonded to two oxygens that are delivered to one face. Cyclohexene gives cis-cyclohexane-1,2-diol. The colour change of KMnO₄, from purple to a brown precipitate of manganese(IV) oxide, is another test for unsaturation. Anti dihydroxylation is achieved in two steps, by epoxidation followed by ring opening with water and acid (Chapter 10).

Caution: hazardous reagents

Osmium tetroxide is volatile and very toxic, ozone is a toxic gas, and peroxyacids are strong oxidants. Reactions with them are carried out by trained chemists with full precautions, on small scale. In teaching laboratories, the milder tests (bromine water, dilute KMnO₄) are used under supervision with appropriate protection.

docs.title: Ozonolysis
docs.text:
Ozone (O₃) cleaves the C=C double bond completely. The alkene is treated with ozone at low temperature, and the resulting ozonide is then worked up with a reducing agent such as zinc and water, or dimethyl sulfide. Each carbon of the old double bond becomes a C=O group:

\[ \mathrm{(CH_3)_2C{=}CHCH_3 \xrightarrow[\ 2.\ Zn,\ H_2O\ ]{1.\ O_3} (CH_3)_2C{=}O + CH_3CHO} \]

Ozonolysis of 2-methylbut-2-ene gives propanone and ethanal. Working backwards from the carbonyl products tells you where the double bond was, which made ozonolysis an important tool for finding structures before spectroscopy (Chapter 14). Hot, acidified KMnO₄ also cleaves double bonds, but it oxidises further: a CH= carbon becomes a carboxylic acid, and a =CH₂ carbon becomes carbon dioxide.

docs.text:
