BH₃, THF; 2. H₂O₂, NaOH propan-1-ol anti-Markovnikov syn Br₂ 1,2-dibromopropane — anti Br₂, H₂O 1-bromopropan-2-ol Br to less substituted C anti H₂, Pt or Pd propane — syn RCO₃H (peroxyacid) 2-methyloxirane (an epoxide) — syn OsO₄ or cold KMnO₄ propane-1,2-diol — syn 1. O₃; 2. Zn, H₂O ethanal + methanal — —

Table 7.2. The main addition reactions of alkenes, illustrated with propene.

docs.title: 7.7 Conjugated dienes
docs.text:
A molecule with two double bonds separated by one single bond, such as buta-1,3-diene, CH₂=CH–CH=CH₂, is a conjugated diene. Its four p orbitals overlap continuously, so its π electrons are delocalised over all four carbons, which gives extra stability. With one equivalent of HBr, buta-1,3-diene gives two products. Protonation at C1 gives an allylic carbocation, whose charge is shared between C2 and C4 by resonance. Bromide can attack either carbon, giving 3-bromobut-1-ene (1,2-addition) or 1-bromobut-2-ene (1,4-addition). At low temperature the 1,2-product, formed faster, predominates (kinetic control); at higher temperature, when the reaction is reversible, the more stable 1,4-product, with the more substituted double bond, predominates (thermodynamic control).

Conjugated dienes also take part in the Diels–Alder reaction, in which a diene and an alkene combine in a single cyclic step to form a six-membered ring. It is the best-known example of a pericyclic reaction and a powerful way of making rings.

docs.title: 7.8 Alkynes
docs.text: Alkynes contain a C≡C triple bond: one σ bond and two π bonds. Each carbon of the triple bond is sp hybridised and the C–C≡C–C unit is linear. Ethyne (acetylene), the simplest alkyne, burns in oxygen with a very hot flame used for welding and cutting metal.

docs.title: Acidity of terminal alkynes
docs.text:
A hydrogen on a triple-bond carbon is unusually acidic for a hydrocarbon (pKa about 25), because the lone pair of the resulting acetylide (alkynide) ion sits in an sp orbital with 50% s character (Section 4.4). Sodium amide deprotonates terminal alkynes completely:

\[ \mathrm{HC{\equiv}CH + NaNH_2 \rightarrow HC{\equiv}C^- Na^+ + NH_3} \]

Acetylide ions are good nucleophiles. They react with primary haloalkanes by nucleophilic substitution (Chapter 9) to form a new carbon–carbon bond, a way of lengthening a carbon chain:

\[ \mathrm{HC{\equiv}C^- + CH_3CH_2Br \rightarrow HC{\equiv}CCH_2CH_3 + Br^-} \]

docs.title: Addition reactions of alkynes
docs.text:
Alkynes undergo most of the addition reactions of alkenes, and can add two equivalents of reagent.

  • Hydrogenation. With H₂ and platinum or palladium, alkynes add two molecules of hydrogen to give alkanes. With a deliberately weakened catalyst, Lindlar's catalyst (palladium on calcium carbonate treated with a lead salt and quinoline), the reaction stops at the alkene, and the two hydrogens add syn, giving the cis (Z) alkene. Reduction with sodium in liquid ammonia gives the trans (E) alkene instead.
  • Hydrogen halides add with Markovnikov orientation. One equivalent gives a haloalkene; a second gives a geminal dihalide, with both halogens on the same carbon: propyne + 2 HBr → 2,2-dibromopropane.
  • Halogens add once to give a dihaloalkene and again to give a tetrahalide.
  • Hydration. With aqueous acid and a mercury(II) salt as catalyst, water adds with Markovnikov orientation. The first product is an enol, with OH on a double-bond carbon. Enols rapidly rearrange to the isomeric carbonyl compound (keto–enol tautomerism, Chapter 11). Propyne gives propanone. Because mercury compounds are highly toxic, other catalysts are now preferred where possible.

Example 7.2: Making a cis or trans alkene from an alkyne

How would you make (Z)-hex-3-ene and (E)-hex-3-ene from hex-3-yne, CH₃CH₂C≡CCH₂CH₃?

(Z)-hex-3-ene: H₂ with Lindlar's catalyst. The two hydrogens add to the same face of the triple bond, giving the cis alkene, and the poisoned catalyst does not reduce the alkene further.

(E)-hex-3-ene: sodium in liquid ammonia. The hydrogens are delivered in separate steps through radical and anion intermediates that adopt the less crowded trans arrangement.

docs.title: 7.9 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • More substituted alkenes and trans alkenes are more stable.
  • Electrophilic addition of HX: the π bond attacks H⁺ to give the more stable carbocation, which is captured by X⁻. This is Markovnikov's rule. Rearrangements can occur.
  • HBr with peroxides adds anti-Markovnikov by a radical mechanism.
  • Acid-catalysed hydration gives Markovnikov alcohols; hydroboration–oxidation gives anti-Markovnikov alcohols by syn addition without rearrangement.
  • Halogens add anti through a cyclic halonium ion; in water, halohydrins form, with OH on the more substituted carbon. Bromine water is decolourised by alkenes.
  • Hydrogenation, epoxidation and dihydroxylation with OsO₄ or cold KMnO₄ are syn additions. Ozonolysis cleaves C=C into two C=O groups.
  • Terminal alkynes are weakly acidic (pKa 25); acetylides alkylate primary haloalkanes.
  • Alkynes add H₂ (Lindlar gives cis alkenes, Na/NH₃ gives trans), HX and X₂ (twice), and water (giving ketones via enols).

docs.title: 7.10 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Rank in order of increasing stability: (E)-pent-2-ene, pent-1-ene, 2-methylbut-2-ene, (Z)-pent-2-ene.

Answer

Pent-1-ene (monosubstituted) < (Z)-pent-2-ene (disubstituted, cis) < (E)-pent-2-ene (disubstituted, trans) < 2-methylbut-2-ene (trisubstituted).

Exercise 2

Give the major product, with a mechanism, for the reaction of 2-methylbut-2-ene with HBr.

Answer

(CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃. The π bond attacks H⁺ of HBr. Adding H to the CH carbon (C3) leaves a tertiary cation at C2; adding it to C2 would leave a secondary cation at C3. The tertiary cation forms, and Br⁻ attacks it. Product: 2-bromo-2-methylbutane, (CH₃)₂CBrCH₂CH₃.

Exercise 3

3,3-Dimethylbut-1-ene, CH₂=CH–C(CH₃)₃, reacts with HCl to give mainly 2-chloro-2,3-dimethylbutane. Explain with a mechanism.

Answer

Protonation of C1 gives a secondary cation at C2: CH₃–C⁺H–C(CH₃)₃. A methyl group on the neighbouring quaternary C3 moves, with its bonding pair, to C2 (a methyl shift). This places the positive charge on C3, which now carries two methyls and the CH(CH₃) group: a tertiary cation, (CH₃)₂C⁺–CH(CH₃)₂. Chloride captures it to give (CH₃)₂CCl–CH(CH₃)₂, 2-chloro-2,3-dimethylbutane. The rearranged skeleton is evidence for the carbocation.

Exercise 4

Give the product of each reaction of 1-methylcyclohexene, including stereochemistry where relevant: (a) H₂O, H₂SO₄; (b) 1. BH₃, THF; 2. H₂O₂, NaOH; (c) Br₂; (d) H₂, Pd; (e) 1. O₃; 2. Zn, H₂O.

Answer

(a) 1-Methylcyclohexan-1-ol (Markovnikov; OH on the tertiary carbon).

(b) trans-2-Methylcyclohexan-1-ol (anti-Markovnikov; H and OH added syn, so the OH and the methyl end up trans), as a racemic mixture.

(c) trans-1,2-Dibromo-1-methylcyclohexane (anti addition), racemic.

(d) Methylcyclohexane.

(e) The ring opens to a single chain with a ketone at one end and an aldehyde at the other: 6-oxoheptanal, CH₃CO(CH₂)₄CHO.

Exercise 5

An alkene C₆H₁₂ gives only propanone on ozonolysis (followed by Zn, H₂O). What is its structure?

Answer

Each half of the double bond becomes (CH₃)₂C=O, so both carbons of the double bond carry two methyl groups: (CH₃)₂C=C(CH₃)₂, 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene. Check: C₆H₁₂, DBE 1.

Exercise 6

Propene is treated separately with (a) Br₂ in CH₂Cl₂ and (b) Br₂ in water. Give the products and explain the difference.

Answer

Both reactions form the same bromonium ion. (a) In CH₂Cl₂ the only nucleophile is Br⁻, giving 1,2-dibromopropane. (b) In water, the solvent (present in huge excess) opens the bromonium ion at the more substituted carbon, which carries more of the positive charge, giving after loss of a proton 1-bromopropan-2-ol.

Exercise 7

Show how to make pent-2-yne from propyne and any other reagents, and then convert it into (Z)-pent-2-ene.

Answer

Deprotonate propyne with NaNH₂: CH₃C≡CH → CH₃C≡C⁻ Na⁺. Alkylate with bromoethane (a primary haloalkane): CH₃C≡C⁻ + CH₃CH₂Br → CH₃C≡CCH₂CH₃ (pent-2-yne) + Br⁻. Then reduce with H₂ and Lindlar's catalyst to give (Z)-pent-2-ene by syn addition.

docs.title: 7.11 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of alkenes and alkynes

Exercise 1

Which alkene is the most stable?

  1. pent-1-ene
  2. (Z)-pent-2-ene
  3. (E)-pent-2-ene
  4. 2-methylbut-2-ene
Answer

2-methylbut-2-ene

It is trisubstituted; the more alkyl groups on the double-bond carbons, the more stable the alkene.

Exercise 2

HBr adds to propene (no peroxides) to give mainly

  1. 1-bromopropane
  2. 2-bromopropane
  3. 1,2-dibromopropane
  4. propan-2-ol
Answer

2-bromopropane

Exercise 3

Which reagent sequence converts propene into propan-1-ol?

  1. H₂O, H₂SO₄
  2. 1. BH₃, THF; 2. H₂O₂, NaOH
  3. 1. O₃; 2. Zn, H₂O
  4. Br₂, H₂O
Answer

1. BH₃, THF; 2. H₂O₂, NaOH

Exercise 4

Bromine adds to cyclohexene to give

  1. cis-1,2-dibromocyclohexane
  2. trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane
  3. bromocyclohexane
  4. 1,1-dibromocyclohexane
Answer

trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane

Exercise 5

Which reaction is a syn addition?

  1. Br₂ addition
  2. hydrogenation with Pt
  3. bromohydrin formation
  4. HBr addition
Answer

hydrogenation with Pt

Exercise 6

Name the alkene formed when but-2-yne is reduced with H₂ and Lindlar's catalyst.

Answer

(Z)-but-2-ene / Z-but-2-ene / cis-but-2-ene / cis but-2-ene

Exercise 7

A positive test with bromine water shows

  1. an alcohol
  2. a carbon-carbon double or triple bond
  3. a carboxylic acid
  4. an alkane
Answer

a carbon-carbon double or triple bond

docs.title: Chapter 9: Alkyl Halides: Substitution and Elimination
docs.text:
SN2, SN1, E2 and E1, and how to choose between them

A carbon bonded to a halogen is electron-poor, and the halogen can leave as a stable halide ion. This makes haloalkanes (alkyl halides) the textbook case of an electrophile, and their reactions are the model for a vast range of organic chemistry. A nucleophile can replace the halogen (substitution), or a base can remove a neighbouring hydrogen so that the halogen leaves and a double bond forms (elimination). Each process can happen in one step or two. Learning which of the four resulting mechanisms (SN2, SN1, E2, E1) operates in a given case, and why, is one of the central skills of a first course.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  • describe the structure and properties of haloalkanes and why the C–X carbon is electrophilic;
  • write the SN2 mechanism, its rate law and its stereochemistry (inversion), and explain the effects of substrate, nucleophile, leaving group and solvent;
  • write the SN1 mechanism, its rate law and its stereochemistry (racemisation), and explain why tertiary substrates react this way;
  • write the E2 mechanism, explain the anti-periplanar requirement and predict Zaitsev and Hofmann products;
  • describe the E1 mechanism and its competition with SN1;
  • predict the main mechanism and product for a given haloalkane, reagent and solvent.

docs.title: 9.1 Haloalkanes
docs.text:
Haloalkanes contain a halogen atom (F, Cl, Br or I) bonded to an sp³ carbon. They are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary according to the carbon that carries the halogen (Section 2.1). Halogens bonded to sp² carbons, as in chlorobenzene or chloroethene, behave very differently and do not undergo the reactions of this chapter under normal conditions.

The C–X bond is polar, with carbon δ+. Going down the group, the bond becomes longer and weaker:

Bond Length (pm) Bond energy (kJ mol⁻¹) C–F 139 about 485 C–Cl 178 about 340 C–Br 193 about 285 C–I 214 about 215

Table 9.1. Carbon–halogen bonds in halomethanes (approximate values).

The weaker the bond, and the more stable the halide ion, the better the halogen leaves. Iodoalkanes react fastest, then bromoalkanes and chloroalkanes; fluoroalkanes hardly react at all.

Haloalkanes are made from alkenes (Chapter 7), from alcohols (Chapter 10) and by radical halogenation of alkanes (Chapter 6). They are useful solvents and synthetic intermediates. Some have caused environmental harm: chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), once used as refrigerants and aerosol propellants, release chlorine atoms in the stratosphere that destroy ozone, and their production has been phased out under the Montreal Protocol of 1987.

Example 9.1: A practical test for haloalkanes

When a haloalkane is warmed with aqueous ethanolic silver nitrate, water slowly substitutes the halogen, and the halide ion released precipitates as a silver halide: AgCl (white), AgBr (cream) or AgI (yellow). Precipitates appear fastest for iodoalkanes and slowest for chloroalkanes, showing the order of C–X bond strength. Tertiary haloalkanes react faster than primary ones, for reasons explained in Section 9.3.

docs.title: 9.2 The SN2 reaction
docs.text:
Hydroxide ion reacts with bromomethane to give methanol:

\[ \mathrm{HO^- + CH_3Br \rightarrow CH_3OH + Br^-} \]

Experiment shows that the rate is proportional to the concentrations of both reactants:

\[ \text{rate} = k[\mathrm{CH_3Br}][\mathrm{HO^-}] \]

Both species must therefore be involved in the rate-determining step. The mechanism is a single, concerted step called SN2: Substitution, Nucleophilic, bimolecular (two species in the rate-determining step).

docs.title: The mechanism
docs.text:
The nucleophile approaches the carbon from the side directly opposite the leaving group (backside attack). As the new Nu–C bond forms, the C–X bond breaks. In the transition state the carbon is partly bonded to both, with the three other groups lying flat in a plane, like an umbrella caught halfway in a gust of wind. As the leaving group departs, the three groups flip over to the other side.

Figure 9.1 The SN2 mechanism and inversion of configuration. The SN2 reaction of hydroxide with (R)-2-bromobutane. Hydroxide attacks from the back, opposite the bromine. In the transition state the carbon is partly bonded to both oxygen and bromine, and the other three groups lie in a plane. The product is (S)-butan-2-ol: the configuration has been inverted, like an umbrella turning inside out.

The result is inversion of configuration (the Walden inversion): if the substrate is a single enantiomer, the product is a single enantiomer with the opposite spatial arrangement. In Figure 9.1, (R)-2-bromobutane gives (S)-butan-2-ol. (Here the letter changes from R to S because OH takes over bromine's place at the top of the priority order, so the inverted geometry receives the opposite label. If a nucleophile changed the order of priorities, the letter could stay the same even though the geometry is inverted: the real test is the geometry, not the letter.)

docs.title: What controls the rate of SN2?
docs.text:
1. The substrate. Backside attack is blocked by bulky groups around the carbon. The rate falls steeply with substitution:

\[ \mathrm{CH_3X > primary > secondary \gg tertiary\ (no\ SN2)} \]

Tertiary haloalkanes do not react by SN2 at all, because the three alkyl groups shield the back of the carbon. Even branching one carbon further away slows the reaction: 1-bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentyl bromide), although primary, reacts extremely slowly.

2. The nucleophile. Stronger nucleophiles react faster. Negatively charged nucleophiles are stronger than their neutral conjugate acids (HO⁻ > H₂O, CH₃O⁻ > CH₃OH). Useful SN2 nucleophiles include HO⁻, RO⁻, CN⁻, I⁻, N₃⁻, RS⁻, NH₃, amines and acetylide ions, each giving a different family of product.

3. The leaving group. The best leaving groups are weak bases, the conjugate bases of strong acids: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ >> F⁻. Hydroxide (from water, pKa 15.7) is a very poor leaving group, which is why alcohols do not undergo SN2 directly. They must first be converted into a better leaving group, by protonation (–OH₂⁺ leaves as water) or by conversion into a sulfonate ester such as a tosylate (Chapter 10).

4. The solvent. SN2 reactions with anionic nucleophiles are fastest in polar aprotic solvents, such as propanone, dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) and N,N-dimethylmethanamide (DMF). These dissolve ionic reagents by solvating the cation, but leave the anion relatively free and reactive. Polar protic solvents (water, alcohols) surround anions with hydrogen bonds, which stabilises them and makes them less reactive. In protic solvents, small anions such as F⁻ are held most strongly, so nucleophilicity runs I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻.

Key idea

SN2: one step, rate depends on substrate and nucleophile, backside attack, inversion of configuration. Favoured by methyl and primary substrates, strong nucleophiles, good leaving groups and polar aprotic solvents.

Example 9.2: Products of SN2 reactions

Give the products of 1-bromobutane with (a) NaCN in DMSO; (b) NaI in propanone; (c) CH₃CH₂ONa in ethanol (a substitution product only).

(a) CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CN, pentanenitrile: a new C–C bond, lengthening the chain by one carbon. (b) 1-iodobutane. In propanone, NaI is soluble but NaBr is not; NaBr precipitates and drives the reaction forward (the Finkelstein reaction). (c) CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OCH₂CH₃, 1-ethoxybutane, an ether (the Williamson ether synthesis, Chapter 10).

docs.title: 9.3 The SN1 reaction
docs.text:
2-Bromo-2-methylpropane, a tertiary haloalkane, reacts with water quickly even though water is a poor nucleophile, and the rate does not depend on the concentration of the nucleophile:

\[ \text{rate} = k[\mathrm{(CH_3)_3CBr}] \]

Only the haloalkane is involved in the rate-determining step. The mechanism, SN1 (unimolecular), has two main steps:

  1. Ionisation (slow). The C–Br bond breaks heterolytically, giving a carbocation and a bromide ion.
  2. Nucleophilic attack (fast). The nucleophile (here water) attacks the carbocation. When the nucleophile is neutral, a final fast proton transfer gives the neutral product.

You have already met this sequence as the example of Figure 5.2.

docs.title: Stereochemistry: racemisation
docs.text:
The carbocation is planar (sp²), with an empty p orbital on each face. The nucleophile can attack from either face with nearly equal probability. If the carbon was a stereocentre, both configurations of the product form: a single enantiomer of substrate gives a racemic (or nearly racemic) product. In practice a slight excess of the inverted product is often found, because the departing halide ion briefly shields the face it left.

Figure 9.2 The SN1 mechanism and racemisation. The SN1 mechanism. The C–Br bond ionises slowly to give a planar carbocation with an empty p orbital. The nucleophile can attack either face of the cation, giving the two enantiomers of the product in equal amounts.

docs.title: What controls the rate of SN1?
docs.text:
1. The substrate. The rate depends on how easily the carbocation forms, which follows carbocation stability (Section 5.6):

\[ \mathrm{tertiary > secondary \gg primary,\ methyl\ (no\ SN1)} \]

Allylic and benzylic halides also react readily by SN1, because their carbocations are stabilised by resonance.

2. The leaving group. As for SN2: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻.

3. The solvent. Polar protic solvents (water, alcohols, methanoic acid) strongly favour SN1. They stabilise both the carbocation and the leaving anion by solvation, and so lower the energy of the transition state of the ionisation step. A reaction in which the solvent is also the nucleophile is called solvolysis.

4. The nucleophile does not affect the rate, because it is not involved in the rate-determining step. Weak, neutral nucleophiles (water, alcohols) are typical of SN1 conditions.

Because a carbocation is formed, rearrangements can occur in SN1 reactions, just as in additions to alkenes.

Feature SN2 SN1 Steps one (concerted) two (via carbocation) Rate law k[RX][Nu] k[RX] Substrate methyl > 1° > 2°; not 3° 3° > 2°; not 1° or methyl (except allylic, benzylic) Nucleophile strong, often anionic weak, often neutral (solvent) Solvent polar aprotic best polar protic Stereochemistry inversion racemisation Rearrangements no possible

Table 9.2. A comparison of SN2 and SN1.

docs.title: 9.4 The E2 reaction
docs.text:
When 2-bromopropane is heated with a strong base such as sodium ethoxide in ethanol, the main product is propene, not an ether. The base has removed a proton from the carbon next to the C–Br carbon (the β-carbon), and HBr has been lost: an elimination. The rate depends on both the haloalkane and the base:

\[ \text{rate} = k[\mathrm{RX}][\mathrm{B^-}] \]

This is the E2 mechanism (Elimination, bimolecular). It happens in one concerted step, with three arrows:

  1. the base takes a β-hydrogen;
  2. the C–H bonding pair moves in to form the C=C π bond;
  3. the C–X bond breaks, and the halide leaves with its electron pair.

docs.title: The anti-periplanar requirement
docs.text:
For the C–H bonding electrons to flow smoothly into the forming π bond and push out the leaving group, the H and the leaving group must lie in the same plane and on opposite sides of the C–C bond, with a dihedral angle of 180°. This arrangement is called anti-periplanar. It corresponds to the staggered, anti conformation of Section 6.3.

Figure 9.3 The E2 mechanism. The E2 mechanism. The base removes a hydrogen that is anti-periplanar to the bromine. The C–H bonding pair forms the π bond as the bromide leaves, all in a single step.

The anti-periplanar requirement makes E2 reactions stereospecific. In cyclohexanes it means that both the H and the leaving group must be axial (one up, one down), because only then are they anti-periplanar. A cyclohexyl halide whose halogen is held equatorial (for example by a tert-butyl group elsewhere on the ring) eliminates very slowly.

docs.title: Regiochemistry: Zaitsev and Hofmann
docs.text:
When a haloalkane has more than one kind of β-hydrogen, different alkenes can form. With small, strong bases (HO⁻, CH₃O⁻, CH₃CH₂O⁻), the more substituted, more stable alkene usually predominates. This is Zaitsev's rule (also spelled Saytzeff). 2-Bromobutane with ethoxide gives mainly but-2-ene (with the trans isomer in excess) and less but-1-ene.

With a bulky base, such as potassium tert-butoxide, (CH₃)₃CO⁻ K⁺, the less hindered hydrogens on the end carbon are removed more easily, and the less substituted alkene predominates. This is called the Hofmann product. 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane with tert-butoxide gives mainly 2-methylbut-1-ene, whereas with ethoxide it gives mainly 2-methylbut-2-ene.

Example 9.3: Predicting E2 products

Predict the main product of 2-bromo-2-methylbutane, (CH₃)₂CBrCH₂CH₃, with (a) NaOCH₂CH₃ in ethanol, heated; (b) KOC(CH₃)₃ in 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

The β-carbons are the two methyl groups (six equivalent H) and the CH₂ (two H).

(a) A small base gives the Zaitsev product: removing H from CH₂ gives the trisubstituted alkene 2-methylbut-2-ene, (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃.

(b) A bulky base removes the more accessible methyl hydrogens, giving the disubstituted Hofmann product 2-methylbut-1-ene, CH₂=C(CH₃)CH₂CH₃.

docs.title: 9.5 The E1 reaction
docs.text:
Tertiary and secondary haloalkanes in polar protic solvents can also eliminate through a carbocation. In the E1 mechanism (unimolecular), the first step is the same slow ionisation as in SN1. Then, instead of being attacked by a nucleophile, the carbocation loses a proton from a neighbouring carbon to a weak base (often the solvent), forming the alkene. The rate law is rate = k[RX].

E1 and SN1 share their first step and always compete. Heating favours elimination, because elimination produces more molecules than substitution and so has a more favourable entropy change. E1 reactions follow Zaitsev's rule, giving mainly the more stable alkene, and can involve rearrangements. They are not stereospecific, because the carbocation can lose any suitable β-hydrogen.

The acid-catalysed dehydration of alcohols (Chapter 10) is a typical E1 reaction.

docs.title: 9.6 Substitution or elimination? Putting it together
docs.text:
Most nucleophiles are also bases, so substitution and elimination usually compete. The outcome depends mainly on four things: the structure of the substrate, the strength and size of the nucleophile or base, the solvent and the temperature. The following guide predicts the main pathway in nearly all cases met in a first course.

flowchart TD
    A[Haloalkane] --> M[Methyl or primary]
    A --> S[Secondary]
    A --> T[Tertiary]
    M --> M1[Strong unhindered nucleophile: SN2]
    M --> M2[Strong bulky base, e.g. tert-butoxide: E2]
    S --> S1[Strong base, e.g. HO- or EtO-, heat: mainly E2]
    S --> S2[Good nucleophile, weak base, e.g. I-, CN-, N3-, polar aprotic solvent: SN2]
    S --> S3[Weak nucleophile in protic solvent: slow SN1 and E1]
    T --> T1[Strong base: E2]
    T --> T2[Weak nucleophile or base, protic solvent: SN1, with E1 on heating]
Figure 9.4 Choosing between SN1, SN2, E1 and E2. Start from the class of the haloalkane, then consider the reagent.

A few rules of thumb summarise the diagram:

  • Primary haloalkanes almost always undergo SN2, unless the base is bulky.
  • Tertiary haloalkanes never undergo SN2. With a strong base they give E2; with a weak base in a protic solvent they give SN1 (and E1 when heated).
  • Secondary haloalkanes are the borderline case. Strong bases give mainly E2; good nucleophiles that are weak bases give SN2; weak nucleophiles in protic solvents give slow SN1/E1.
  • Higher temperature favours elimination over substitution.

Caution: strength as a nucleophile versus strength as a base

Iodide, cyanide, azide and thiolate ions are good nucleophiles but relatively weak bases, so they favour substitution. tert-Butoxide is a strong base but a poor nucleophile (it is too bulky to reach carbon), so it favours elimination. Hydroxide and alkoxides are both strong nucleophiles and strong bases, so the substrate decides.

Example 9.4: Predict the mechanism and the product

(a) Bromoethane + NaOH in water. (b) 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane + water, at room temperature. (c) 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane + NaOCH₃ in methanol. (d) 2-Bromopropane + NaCN in DMSO.

(a) Primary substrate, strong unhindered nucleophile: SN2, ethanol.

(b) Tertiary substrate, weak nucleophile, protic solvent: SN1, 2-methylpropan-2-ol (with a little 2-methylpropene by E1).

(c) Tertiary substrate, strong base: E2, 2-methylpropene.

(d) Secondary substrate, good nucleophile that is a weak base, polar aprotic solvent: SN2, 2-methylpropanenitrile, (CH₃)₂CHCN, with inversion if the carbon were a stereocentre.

docs.title: Organometallic compounds
docs.text: Haloalkanes react with magnesium metal in dry ether to form Grignard reagents, R–MgX. The carbon bonded to magnesium is strongly δ−, and the reagent behaves as a source of the carbanion R⁻: a very strong base and a powerful carbon nucleophile. Grignard reagents are destroyed by water and any other acidic O–H or N–H group, so they must be made and used with dry solvents and apparatus. Their main use is to add to carbonyl compounds to make new carbon–carbon bonds, described in Chapter 11.

docs.title: 9.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • The C–X carbon is electrophilic; leaving-group ability is I > Br > Cl >> F.
  • SN2: one step, rate = k[RX][Nu], backside attack with inversion; methyl > 1° > 2°, never 3°; favoured by strong nucleophiles and polar aprotic solvents.
  • SN1: two steps via a planar carbocation, rate = k[RX], racemisation and possible rearrangement; 3° > 2°; favoured by polar protic solvents and weak nucleophiles.
  • E2: one step, rate = k[RX][B], H and X anti-periplanar (diaxial in cyclohexanes); small bases give the Zaitsev (more substituted) alkene, bulky bases the Hofmann (less substituted) alkene.
  • E1: via a carbocation, competes with SN1, favoured by heat; Zaitsev product.
  • To predict the outcome, consider the substrate class, the reagent's nucleophilicity, basicity and size, the solvent and the temperature.

docs.title: 9.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Rank in order of decreasing SN2 rate with sodium iodide in propanone: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, 1-bromobutane, 2-bromobutane, bromomethane. Explain.

Answer

Bromomethane > 1-bromobutane > 2-bromobutane > 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (essentially no SN2). SN2 requires backside attack, and each additional alkyl group on the reacting carbon increases steric hindrance in the crowded five-coordinate transition state.

Exercise 2

(S)-2-Iodooctane reacts with sodium azide (NaN₃) in DMF. Give the product with its configuration, and the rate law. What happens to the rate if the azide concentration is doubled?

Answer

SN2 with inversion gives (R)-2-azidooctane. (The azide group takes the place of iodine at the top of the priority order, so the inverted geometry is labelled R.) Rate = k[RI][N₃⁻]; doubling the azide concentration doubles the rate.

Exercise 3

The reaction of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane with water in propanone–water mixtures goes faster as the proportion of water increases. Explain using the mechanism.

Answer

The reaction is SN1. The rate-determining step is ionisation to a carbocation and bromide ion. Water, a polar protic solvent, stabilises the developing charges in the transition state by solvation (hydrogen bonds to the leaving bromide, dipole interactions with the cation). More water means better stabilisation of the transition state, a lower activation energy and a faster reaction.

Exercise 4

Optically active (R)-3-bromo-3-methylhexane is dissolved in aqueous ethanol. Over time the optical rotation falls almost to zero. Explain.

Answer

The tertiary bromide undergoes SN1 solvolysis. The planar carbocation is attacked by water (or ethanol) from either face with nearly equal probability, so the product alcohol (or ether) is formed as a nearly racemic mixture. The rotation therefore falls to almost zero.

Exercise 5

Give the main product(s) of 2-bromobutane with sodium ethoxide in ethanol, heated, and explain the regiochemistry and the stereochemistry.

Answer

E2 elimination. Removing a hydrogen from C3 gives but-2-ene, a disubstituted alkene; removing one from C1 gives but-1-ene, monosubstituted. The small base gives mainly the more stable Zaitsev product, but-2-ene, and of its two isomers mainly (E)-but-2-ene, the more stable trans isomer, formed through the less crowded anti-periplanar conformation. But-1-ene is the minor product, and some substitution (2-ethoxybutane) also forms.

Exercise 6

Why does cis-1-bromo-4-tert-butylcyclohexane undergo E2 with ethoxide much faster than the trans isomer?

Answer

The tert-butyl group locks the ring with itself equatorial. In the cis isomer the bromine is therefore axial, and there are axial hydrogens on the neighbouring carbons anti-periplanar to it, so E2 is easy. In the trans isomer the bromine is forced equatorial, where no β-hydrogen is anti-periplanar to it; E2 would require a ring flip to a conformation with an axial tert-butyl group, which is extremely unfavourable. So the trans isomer eliminates very slowly.

Exercise 7

Predict the main mechanism and product: (a) 1-bromopropane + KOC(CH₃)₃; (b) 1-bromopropane + NaSCH₃ in DMF; (c) bromocyclohexane + NaOH in ethanol, heated; (d) 2-chloro-2-methylbutane in methanol, warm.

Answer

(a) Bulky strong base with a primary halide: E2, propene. (b) Good nucleophile, weak base, aprotic solvent: SN2, CH₃CH₂CH₂SCH₃ (1-(methylsulfanyl)propane). (c) Secondary halide, strong base, heat: mainly E2, cyclohexene. (d) Tertiary halide, weak nucleophile, protic solvent: SN1 giving 2-methoxy-2-methylbutane, together with E1 products (mainly 2-methylbut-2-ene).

docs.title: 9.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of substitution and elimination

Exercise 1

The rate law rate = k[RX][Nu] indicates which mechanism?

  1. SN1
  2. SN2
  3. E1
  4. both SN1 and E1
Answer

SN2

Exercise 2

An SN2 reaction at a stereocentre gives

  1. retention of configuration
  2. inversion of configuration
  3. racemisation
  4. no change in the molecule
Answer

inversion of configuration

Exercise 3

Which substrate reacts fastest by SN1?

  1. bromomethane
  2. 1-bromobutane
  3. 2-bromobutane
  4. 2-bromo-2-methylpropane
Answer

2-bromo-2-methylpropane

Exercise 4

Which is the best leaving group?

  1. F⁻
  2. Cl⁻
  3. Br⁻
  4. I⁻
Answer

I⁻

Exercise 5

In an E2 reaction the H and the leaving group must be

  1. syn-periplanar
  2. anti-periplanar
  3. both equatorial
  4. on the same carbon
Answer

anti-periplanar

Exercise 6

2-Bromo-2-methylbutane with potassium tert-butoxide gives mainly

  1. 2-methylbut-2-ene
  2. 2-methylbut-1-ene
  3. 2-methylbutan-2-ol
  4. 2-tert-butoxy-2-methylbutane
Answer

2-methylbut-1-ene

The bulky base removes the more accessible hydrogens of a methyl group, giving the Hofmann product.

Exercise 7

Which solvent is polar aprotic?

  1. water
  2. ethanol
  3. dimethyl sulfoxide
  4. methanoic acid
Answer

dimethyl sulfoxide

docs.title: Chapter 13: Amines
docs.text:
Organic bases and nitrogen nucleophiles

Amines are organic derivatives of ammonia in which one or more hydrogens have been replaced by carbon groups. They are the main organic bases, and they are everywhere in biology and medicine: amino acids, the bases of DNA, neurotransmitters such as dopamine and serotonin, and a large share of all drugs contain amine nitrogen. The lone pair on nitrogen explains almost everything about amines: it makes them bases, it makes them nucleophiles, and how available it is decides how strongly they do both. This chapter covers the structure, properties and basicity of amines, how they are made, and their main reactions.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  • classify amines and name simple examples;
  • describe the shape of amines and explain why most amines with a nitrogen stereocentre cannot be resolved;
  • explain the physical properties of amines in terms of hydrogen bonding;
  • compare the basicity of alkylamines, aniline, pyridine and amides using pKa values of conjugate acids, and explain the differences;
  • use the basicity of amines to separate them from neutral compounds;
  • give methods of making amines, including reduction of nitriles, amides and nitro compounds, and reductive amination;
  • predict the products of alkylation and acylation of amines, and describe the formation of diazonium salts and azo dyes.

docs.title: 13.1 Structure and classification
docs.text:
Amines are classified by the number of carbon groups bonded to the nitrogen (Section 2.1): primary (RNH₂), secondary (R₂NH) and tertiary (R₃N). A nitrogen with four carbon groups carries a positive charge and is a quaternary ammonium ion, R₄N⁺. Amines in which the nitrogen is part of a ring, such as pyrrolidine and piperidine, are common in natural products; when the ring is aromatic, as in pyridine, the compound is an aromatic heterocycle (Section 8.2). An amine with nitrogen bonded directly to a benzene ring is an arylamine, the simplest being aniline (phenylamine), C₆H₅NH₂.

Figure 13.1 Classes of amines. The classes of amines. In primary, secondary and tertiary amines the nitrogen is pyramidal, with a lone pair occupying the fourth position of a tetrahedron. In a quaternary ammonium ion the nitrogen has four carbon groups and a positive charge.

The nitrogen of an amine is sp³ hybridised. Its three bonds and its lone pair point roughly to the corners of a tetrahedron, so the molecule is trigonal pyramidal, with C–N–C angles close to 108°.

docs.title: Nitrogen inversion
docs.text: A tertiary amine with three different groups on nitrogen, such as N-ethyl-N-methylpropan-1-amine, has four different "groups" around nitrogen if the lone pair is counted, and it is chiral. Yet such amines cannot be separated into enantiomers. The reason is nitrogen inversion: the pyramid turns inside out like an umbrella in the wind, passing through a planar transition state, with a barrier of only about 25 kJ mol⁻¹. At room temperature this happens many millions of times a second, so the two enantiomers interconvert far too fast to be isolated. Quaternary ammonium ions, which have no lone pair, cannot invert, and those with four different groups can be resolved.

docs.title: 13.2 Physical properties
docs.text:
Primary and secondary amines can form hydrogen bonds to one another (N–H···N), but these are weaker than O–H···O hydrogen bonds because nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen. Amines therefore boil higher than alkanes of similar mass but lower than alcohols. Propan-1-amine boils at 48 °C, between butane (−1 °C) and propan-1-ol (97 °C). Tertiary amines have no N–H bond and boil lower still: trimethylamine boils at about 3 °C.

All amines can accept hydrogen bonds from water through the nitrogen lone pair, so small amines are very soluble in water. Low-molecular-mass amines have sharp, fishy smells; the odour of decaying fish comes partly from trimethylamine, and the aptly named putrescine (butane-1,4-diamine) and cadaverine (pentane-1,5-diamine) are formed when proteins decay.

docs.title: 13.3 Basicity
docs.text:
The nitrogen lone pair can take a proton, so amines are bases:

\[ \mathrm{RNH_2 + H_2O \rightleftharpoons RNH_3^+ + OH^-} \]

As in Section 4.5, the strength of an amine as a base is expressed by the pKa of its conjugate acid, the ammonium ion (pKaH). The higher the pKaH, the stronger the base.

Amine Conjugate acid pKa of conjugate acid ammonia, NH₃ NH₄⁺ 9.25 methanamine, CH₃NH₂ CH₃NH₃⁺ 10.6 N-methylmethanamine, (CH₃)₂NH (CH₃)₂NH₂⁺ 10.7 N,N-dimethylmethanamine, (CH₃)₃N (CH₃)₃NH⁺ 9.8 pyridine, C₅H₅N C₅H₅NH⁺ 5.2 aniline, C₆H₅NH₂ C₆H₅NH₃⁺ 4.6 4-nitroaniline O₂NC₆H₄NH₃⁺ 1.0 ethanamide, CH₃CONH₂ (protonated on O) about −0.5

Table 13.1. Basicity of amines and related compounds.

docs.title: Alkylamines
docs.text: Simple alkylamines are slightly stronger bases than ammonia, because alkyl groups donate electron density to the nitrogen and stabilise the positive charge of the ammonium ion. In water, however, tertiary amines are not the strongest: their ammonium ions, R₃NH⁺, have only one N–H to hydrogen bond to water and are less well solvated than R₂NH₂⁺ and RNH₃⁺. The balance between the inductive effect and solvation gives the observed order in water: secondary ≳ primary > tertiary > ammonia.

docs.title: Arylamines
docs.text:
Aniline is about a million times weaker as a base than an alkylamine of similar size (pKaH 4.6 against 10.6 for cyclohexanamine). Its nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring by resonance, so it is less available to take a proton; and protonating it would destroy this stabilising resonance, which costs energy. The nitrogen of aniline is also attached to an sp² carbon, which is more electronegative than an sp³ carbon.

Figure 13.2 Why aniline is a weak base. Resonance in aniline. A lone pair on nitrogen moves into the ring, and the ring π electrons are pushed along, placing negative charge at the ortho and para carbons. The delocalisation stabilises the free amine and makes the lone pair less available, so aniline is a much weaker base than cyclohexanamine.

Substituents on the ring change the basicity of arylamines as you would expect. Electron-withdrawing groups, especially those para or ortho to the amino group that can withdraw electrons by resonance (such as –NO₂), weaken the base further: 4-nitroaniline (pKaH 1.0) is about four thousand times weaker than aniline. Electron-donating groups such as –OCH₃ make arylamines slightly more basic.

docs.title: Other nitrogen compounds
docs.text:
In pyridine the lone pair occupies an sp² orbital (33% s character), which holds it closer to the nucleus than an sp³ orbital does, so pyridine is a weaker base than an alkylamine (pKaH 5.2). In pyrrole the lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet, and pyrrole is hardly basic. Amides are not basic at all under ordinary conditions, because the lone pair is delocalised onto the carbonyl oxygen (Section 12.6).

Key idea

The basicity of a nitrogen compound depends on how available its lone pair is. A lone pair that is delocalised (anilines, amides, pyrrole) or held in an orbital with more s character (pyridine, nitriles) is less basic. Alkyl groups make the lone pair slightly more available.

docs.title: Ammonium salts and extraction
docs.text:
Amines react with acids to give ammonium salts: CH₃NH₂ + HCl → CH₃NH₃⁺Cl⁻. These are ionic, crystalline, odourless and much more soluble in water than the free amines. Many amine drugs are sold as their hydrochloride salts for this reason. Adding a strong base (NaOH) to an ammonium salt releases the free amine.

The same chemistry allows an amine to be separated from neutral compounds by acid–base extraction: shaking an ether solution of the mixture with dilute hydrochloric acid moves the amine into the aqueous layer as its salt; making that layer basic with sodium hydroxide releases the amine, which can then be extracted back into fresh ether. Combined with the extraction of acids by sodium hydrogencarbonate (Section 4.6), this lets acids, bases and neutral compounds be separated from one mixture.

docs.title: Alkylation of ammonia and amines
docs.text:
Ammonia and amines are nucleophiles and react with haloalkanes by SN2. The difficulty is that the product amine is also a nucleophile, often a better one than the starting material, so it reacts further:

\[ \mathrm{NH_3 \xrightarrow{RX} RNH_2 \xrightarrow{RX} R_2NH \xrightarrow{RX} R_3N \xrightarrow{RX} R_4N^+X^-} \]

A mixture of products results. A large excess of ammonia favours the primary amine, and an excess of haloalkane drives the reaction to the quaternary ammonium salt, but direct alkylation is rarely a clean way of making primary or secondary amines.

docs.title: Reduction methods
docs.text:
Cleaner methods make the C–N bond first in a compound that cannot over-react, and then reduce it:

  • Nitriles (from haloalkanes and cyanide) are reduced by LiAlH₄ or by H₂ and a catalyst to primary amines, RCH₂NH₂, with one more carbon than the haloalkane (Section 12.7).
  • Amides (from acyl chlorides and amines) are reduced by LiAlH₄ to amines of any class: RCONHR′ → RCH₂NHR′ (Section 12.6).
  • Nitro compounds, especially nitroarenes from the nitration of benzene (Section 8.4), are reduced to primary amines with tin (or iron) and hydrochloric acid, followed by base, or by catalytic hydrogenation. This is the standard route to aniline and its derivatives: C₆H₅NO₂ → C₆H₅NH₂.

docs.title: Reductive amination
docs.text:
An aldehyde or ketone reacts with ammonia or an amine to give an imine (Section 11.5), which can be reduced to an amine in the same pot by hydrogen and a catalyst or by a selective hydride reagent (such as sodium cyanotrihydridoborate, NaBH₃CN, which reduces the imine faster than the carbonyl compound). Propanone and ammonia give propan-2-amine; propanone and methanamine give N-methylpropan-2-amine. Reductive amination is one of the most widely used ways of making amines, in the laboratory and in living cells, where amino acids are made from keto acids in a related way.

Example 13.1: Choosing a route to an amine

Suggest a synthesis of (a) pentan-1-amine from 1-bromobutane; (b) N-ethylcyclohexanamine from cyclohexanone.

(a) The amine has one more carbon than the bromide, so go through the nitrile: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Br + NaCN (SN2) → CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CN; then LiAlH₄, then water → CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂.

(b) Reductive amination: cyclohexanone + ethanamine forms the imine, which is reduced (H₂ with a nickel catalyst, or NaBH₃CN) to C₆H₁₁NHCH₂CH₃.

docs.title: Acylation: making amides
docs.text:
Primary and secondary amines react rapidly with acyl chlorides and acid anhydrides to give amides (Section 12.4). A second equivalent of the amine, or another base such as pyridine, takes up the acid produced:

\[ \mathrm{CH_3COCl + 2\,CH_3NH_2 \rightarrow CH_3CONHCH_3 + CH_3NH_3^+Cl^-} \]

The product amide is not nucleophilic (its lone pair is delocalised), so, unlike alkylation, acylation stops cleanly after one step. Tertiary amines have no N–H and cannot form stable amides.

Acylation is also used to moderate the reactivity of aniline in electrophilic aromatic substitution (Section 8.5). The amide group –NHCOCH₃ is a milder activator than –NH₂, so ethanoylating the nitrogen first allows a single, controlled substitution on the ring. Hydrolysis of the amide afterwards gives back the amino group. Paracetamol is itself an amide of this kind, N-(4-hydroxyphenyl)ethanamide.

docs.title: Amines as bases in elimination
docs.text: Bulky tertiary amines are useful non-nucleophilic bases. When a quaternary ammonium hydroxide is heated, it undergoes an E2 elimination (the Hofmann elimination), and because the leaving group, a neutral amine, is large, the less substituted alkene (the Hofmann product of Section 9.4) is formed.

docs.title: Diazonium salts and azo dyes
docs.text:
Primary arylamines react with nitrous acid, HNO₂ (made in the reaction mixture from sodium nitrite and dilute hydrochloric acid), at 0 to 5 °C to give arenediazonium salts, Ar–N₂⁺ Cl⁻. For example, aniline gives benzenediazonium chloride.

Arenediazonium ions are reactive but, at low temperature in solution, stable enough to be used straight away. Their nitrogen leaves readily as N₂ gas, an exceptionally good leaving group, so the N₂⁺ group can be replaced by many other groups (OH on warming with water, Cl, Br or CN with copper(I) salts, I with potassium iodide), giving access to substituted benzenes that cannot be made by direct electrophilic substitution.

Diazonium ions are also weak electrophiles. They attack strongly activated aromatic rings, such as phenoxide ions and arylamines, usually at the para position, in an electrophilic substitution called azo coupling. The products contain an –N=N– (azo) group linking two aromatic rings. The extended conjugated system absorbs visible light, so azo compounds are intensely coloured. They are an important class of synthetic dyes, and some are acid–base indicators: methyl orange is an azo dye.

Caution: diazonium salts

Diazonium salts are made only in cold solution and used immediately. In the dry, solid state many are shock-sensitive and can decompose violently. They are never isolated or stored in teaching laboratories.

docs.title: Amines in biology and medicine
docs.text: Many important biological molecules are amines. Adrenaline (epinephrine), dopamine and serotonin are neurotransmitters; histamine is involved in allergic responses; the amino acids that make up proteins all contain amino groups (Chapter 15). Plant alkaloids, nitrogen-containing bases such as caffeine, nicotine, quinine and morphine, have strong effects on the body, and many medicines are based on their structures. Because most of these molecules are bases, their charge, and therefore their solubility and ability to cross cell membranes, depends on pH, a central consideration in the design of drugs.

docs.title: 13.6 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Amines are primary, secondary or tertiary according to the number of carbon groups on N; R₄N⁺ is a quaternary ammonium ion.
  • Amines are pyramidal and invert rapidly at nitrogen, so chiral amines cannot usually be resolved.
  • N–H···N hydrogen bonds are weaker than O–H···O, so amines boil lower than alcohols; small amines are water-soluble.
  • Alkylamines are moderately strong bases (pKaH about 10 to 11). Aniline (4.6), pyridine (5.2) and especially amides are much weaker, because their lone pairs are delocalised or in orbitals with more s character.
  • Amines form water-soluble ammonium salts with acids, used in extraction and in formulating drugs.
  • Amines are made by reducing nitriles, amides and nitro compounds and by reductive amination; direct alkylation gives mixtures.
  • Amines are acylated to amides cleanly. Primary arylamines give diazonium salts with nitrous acid at 0 to 5 °C, which couple with phenols and arylamines to give azo dyes.

docs.title: 13.7 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Classify each as a primary, secondary or tertiary amine or a quaternary ammonium salt, and name it: (a) CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂; (b) (CH₃CH₂)₂NH; (c) (CH₃)₃CNH₂; (d) (CH₃)₄N⁺ I⁻; (e) C₆H₅N(CH₃)₂.

Answer

(a) Primary: propan-1-amine. (b) Secondary: N-ethylethanamine (diethylamine). (c) Primary (one carbon group on N, even though that carbon is tertiary): 2-methylpropan-2-amine. (d) Quaternary ammonium salt: tetramethylammonium iodide. (e) Tertiary: N,N-dimethylaniline.

Exercise 2

Explain why ethanamine (bp 17 °C) boils higher than propane (bp −42 °C) but lower than ethanol (bp 78 °C).

Answer

Ethanamine molecules form N–H···N hydrogen bonds, which propane cannot form; propane has only dispersion forces. Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so the N–H bond is less polar and N–H···N hydrogen bonds are weaker than the O–H···O hydrogen bonds of ethanol. So ethanamine lies between the two.

Exercise 3

Arrange in order of increasing basicity and explain: aniline, ethanamide, cyclohexanamine, 4-nitroaniline, ammonia.

Answer

Ethanamide (about −0.5) < 4-nitroaniline (1.0) < aniline (4.6) < ammonia (9.25) < cyclohexanamine (10.6). The amide lone pair is delocalised onto the carbonyl oxygen. In aniline it is delocalised into the ring, and in 4-nitroaniline further still onto the nitro group. Ammonia's lone pair is localised. Cyclohexanamine has a localised lone pair and an electron-donating alkyl group.

Exercise 4

A mixture of benzoic acid, aniline and naphthalene is dissolved in ethoxyethane. Describe how to separate all three by extraction.

Answer

(1) Shake with aqueous NaHCO₃: benzoic acid is converted into sodium benzoate and moves into the aqueous layer. Separate; acidify the aqueous layer to recover benzoic acid. (2) Shake the ether layer with dilute HCl: aniline is protonated to anilinium chloride and moves into the aqueous layer. Separate; make this aqueous layer basic with NaOH to release aniline, and extract it into fresh ether. (3) Naphthalene, a neutral compound, remains in the original ether layer; evaporate the solvent to recover it.

Exercise 5

Why does reaction of ammonia with bromoethane give a mixture of products, while reaction of ammonia with ethanoyl chloride gives only ethanamide?

Answer

Ethanamine, the first product of alkylation, is itself a nucleophile, slightly stronger than ammonia, so it competes for the bromoethane and is alkylated further to diethylamine, triethylamine and the tetraethylammonium salt. Ethanamide, the product of acylation, has its nitrogen lone pair delocalised onto the carbonyl oxygen, so it is not nucleophilic and does not react further.

Exercise 6

Give a synthesis of 4-methylaniline from methylbenzene, and of N-propylaniline from aniline without using alkylation.

Answer

4-Methylaniline: nitrate methylbenzene (conc. HNO₃, conc. H₂SO₄, controlled temperature), separate the para isomer from the ortho, then reduce the nitro group with tin and HCl (then NaOH) or H₂ and a catalyst.

N-Propylaniline: acylate aniline with propanoyl chloride to give N-phenylpropanamide, then reduce the amide with LiAlH₄. (Reductive amination of propanal with aniline is an alternative.)

Exercise 7

What is formed when aniline is treated with NaNO₂ and dilute HCl at 0 to 5 °C, and the product is then added to an alkaline solution of phenol? Why must the first step be kept cold?

Answer

The first step gives benzenediazonium chloride. In alkaline solution phenol is present as phenoxide, a strongly activated ring; the diazonium ion attacks it at the para position (azo coupling), giving 4-(phenyldiazenyl)phenol, an orange-yellow azo dye. The diazonium salt must be kept cold because it decomposes on warming, losing N₂ (and in water forming phenol); solid diazonium salts can decompose explosively.

docs.title: 13.8 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of amines

Exercise 1

  1. primary amine
  2. secondary amine
  3. tertiary amine
  4. quaternary ammonium ion
Answer

Exercise 2

  2. ethanamide

Exercise 3

  2. its lone pair is delocalised into the ring
  3. it cannot form hydrogen bonds

Exercise 4

  2. nitrogen inversion

Exercise 5

  1. Sn and HCl, then NaOH
  2. NaBH₄

  4. Br₂ and FeBr₃

Exercise 6

  2. propan-2-amine
  3. propanamide
  4. propanenitrile

Exercise 7

What functional group links the two rings of an azo dye?

Answer

docs.title: Chapter 8: Aromatic Compounds and Electrophilic Substitution
docs.text:
Benzene, aromaticity and the reactions that keep the ring intact

Benzene, C₆H₆, has three formal double bonds, yet it does not decolourise bromine water and it resists the addition reactions that alkenes undergo so readily. Instead, under forcing conditions, it swaps one of its hydrogens for another group and keeps its ring of six π electrons. This special stability, called aromaticity, makes benzene rings among the most common structural units in dyes, plastics, medicines and natural products. This chapter explains the structure of benzene, the rule that predicts which rings are aromatic, the mechanism of electrophilic aromatic substitution, and how groups already on the ring control the rate and position of further substitution.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  • describe the structure of benzene and explain its resonance energy;
  • apply Hückel's rule to decide whether a ring is aromatic, including simple heterocycles and ions;
  • write the general mechanism of electrophilic aromatic substitution and show how each electrophile is generated;
  • give the reagents and products for halogenation, nitration, sulfonation and Friedel–Crafts alkylation and acylation, and the limitations of each;
  • classify substituents as activating or deactivating and as ortho/para- or meta-directing, and explain why;
  • plan the order of steps in the synthesis of a disubstituted benzene.

docs.title: 8.1 The structure of benzene
docs.text:
In 1865 August Kekulé proposed that benzene is a ring of six carbons with alternating single and double bonds. But his structure posed a puzzle. If the bonds alternated, 1,2-dibromobenzene should exist as two isomers, one with a single bond between the brominated carbons and one with a double bond. Only one is known. Kekulé suggested that the two arrangements interconverted rapidly. We now know the truth is subtler.

Modern measurements show that benzene is a regular, planar hexagon. All six C–C bonds have the same length, 139 pm, between the length of a C–C single bond (154 pm) and a C=C double bond (134 pm). All the bond angles are 120°, and every carbon is sp² hybridised. Each carbon has one p orbital perpendicular to the ring, and the six p orbitals overlap all the way round to form a continuous ring of π electron density above and below the plane.

In resonance language (Section 1.7), benzene is a hybrid of two equivalent Kekulé contributors. Neither exists on its own; the six π electrons are spread evenly over all six carbons. The hybrid is often drawn as a hexagon with a circle inside, though for following electrons in mechanisms you must use a Kekulé structure.

Figure 8.1 The structure of benzene. Benzene as two equivalent Kekulé resonance contributors and as the delocalised hybrid. The circle represents six π electrons shared equally by all six carbons. All six bonds have the same length, intermediate between single and double bonds.

docs.title: Resonance energy
docs.text:
How much does delocalisation stabilise benzene? Heats of hydrogenation provide the answer. Cyclohexene, with one double bond, releases about 120 kJ mol⁻¹ when hydrogenated to cyclohexane. A hypothetical "cyclohexatriene" with three isolated double bonds would be expected to release about three times as much, 360 kJ mol⁻¹. Benzene actually releases only about 208 kJ mol⁻¹. It is about 150 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable than expected. This extra stability is the resonance energy (or aromatic stabilisation energy) of benzene.

The resonance energy explains benzene's chemistry. Addition to the ring would destroy the delocalised system and lose this stabilisation. Substitution, in which a hydrogen is replaced and the ring of six π electrons is restored, keeps it. Benzene therefore undergoes substitution rather than addition.

docs.title: 8.2 Aromaticity and Hückel's rule
docs.text:
Benzene is the parent of a large family of aromatic compounds. A compound is aromatic if it meets all four of these conditions:

  1. It is cyclic.
  2. It is planar (or nearly so).
  3. It is fully conjugated: every atom of the ring has a p orbital that is part of the π system.
  4. It has 4n + 2 π electrons, where n is a whole number (0, 1, 2 ...): that is, 2, 6, 10, 14 ... π electrons. This is Hückel's rule.

A cyclic, planar, fully conjugated ring with 4n π electrons (4, 8 ...) is antiaromatic and is especially unstable. Cyclobutadiene, with four π electrons, is so unstable that it can be studied only at very low temperatures. Cyclooctatetraene, with eight, avoids antiaromaticity by bending into a tub shape; it is not planar and behaves as an ordinary polyene.

Figure 8.2 Aromatic and antiaromatic rings. Applying Hückel's rule. Benzene, pyridine, pyrrole, furan and the cyclopentadienyl anion each have six π electrons in a planar, fully conjugated ring and are aromatic. Cyclobutadiene, with four π electrons, is antiaromatic.

docs.title: Counting π electrons in heterocycles and ions
docs.text:
Rings containing atoms other than carbon (heterocycles) and charged rings can be aromatic too. The skill is to count which electrons belong to the π system.

  • Pyridine, C₅H₅N: a benzene ring with one CH replaced by N. The nitrogen contributes one electron to the π system, through its p orbital, just like each CH. Its lone pair sits in an sp² orbital in the plane of the ring, pointing outwards, and is not part of the π system. Six π electrons: aromatic. Because its lone pair is free, pyridine is a base (pKa of its conjugate acid 5.2).
  • Pyrrole, C₄H₄NH: a five-membered ring with two C=C bonds (four π electrons) and an N–H. The nitrogen is sp² hybridised and its lone pair occupies the p orbital, completing a sextet. Six π electrons: aromatic. Because the lone pair is part of the aromatic system, pyrrole is hardly basic at all: protonating the nitrogen would destroy the aromaticity.
  • Furan, C₄H₄O: like pyrrole, with oxygen contributing one of its two lone pairs to the π system. Aromatic.
  • The cyclopentadienyl anion, C₅H₅⁻: removing a proton from the CH₂ of cyclopenta-1,3-diene leaves a lone pair in a p orbital, giving six π electrons over five carbons. The anion is aromatic, which is why cyclopentadiene is unusually acidic for a hydrocarbon (pKa about 16).

Fused rings can be aromatic as well. Naphthalene (two fused benzene rings, ten π electrons) and many larger polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons follow the same pattern.

Example 8.1: Is it aromatic?

Decide whether each species is aromatic: (a) the cycloheptatrienyl (tropylium) cation, C₇H₇⁺; (b) cyclopentadiene, C₅H₆.

(a) A seven-membered ring with three C=C bonds and one carbocation carbon, which is sp² with an empty p orbital. Every ring atom has a p orbital, so the ring is fully conjugated; it is planar; and it has six π electrons (three π bonds). Six is 4n + 2 with n = 1: aromatic. The tropylium cation is unusually stable for a carbocation.

(b) Cyclopentadiene has a CH₂ group, an sp³ carbon with no p orbital. The ring is not fully conjugated: not aromatic.

docs.title: 8.3 Electrophilic aromatic substitution: the general mechanism
docs.text:
The π electrons of benzene make it a nucleophile, but a much weaker one than an alkene, because reaction costs aromatic stabilisation. Benzene therefore reacts only with strong electrophiles, usually generated with the help of a catalyst. The reaction is electrophilic aromatic substitution (EAS), and it always follows the same two-step mechanism.

  1. Attack on the electrophile (slow). A pair of π electrons from the ring forms a bond to the electrophile, E⁺. The carbon that is attacked becomes sp³, carrying both H and E, and the ring is left with a positive charge. The cation, called an arenium ion (or σ complex, or Wheland intermediate), is not aromatic, but it is stabilised by resonance: the charge is shared by the three carbons ortho and para to the site of attack. This step is rate-determining because it breaks the aromatic system.
  2. Loss of a proton (fast). A base removes the proton from the sp³ carbon. The C–H bonding pair moves back into the ring, restoring the aromatic sextet.

The net result is the replacement of H by E.

Figure 8.3 Mechanism of electrophilic aromatic substitution. The mechanism of electrophilic aromatic substitution, shown for nitration. The ring's π electrons attack the nitronium ion, NO₂⁺, forming an arenium ion whose positive charge is delocalised over three carbons. A base (hydrogensulfate ion) then removes the proton from the sp³ carbon, and the aromatic ring is restored, giving nitrobenzene.

Key idea

Every electrophilic aromatic substitution has the same two steps: the ring attacks E⁺ to give an arenium ion, then loses H⁺. What differs from one reaction to the next is only how the electrophile is made. Learn the mechanism once and the five reactions below follow.

docs.title: Halogenation
docs.text:
Benzene does not react with bromine alone. A Lewis acid catalyst, such as iron(III) bromide (often formed in the flask from iron filings and bromine) or aluminium chloride, polarises the Br–Br bond by accepting a lone pair from one bromine. The other bromine becomes strongly electrophilic:

\[ \mathrm{Br_2 + FeBr_3 \rightarrow Br^{\delta+}\!-\!Br\!-\!FeBr_3^{\delta-}} \]

The ring attacks the outer bromine, and FeBr₄⁻ is released, which later takes back the proton to give HBr and regenerate the catalyst. The product is bromobenzene. Chlorination with Cl₂ and AlCl₃ or FeCl₃ works the same way.

docs.title: Nitration
docs.text:
A mixture of concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids nitrates benzene. Sulfuric acid, the stronger acid, protonates nitric acid, which then loses water to give the nitronium ion, NO₂⁺, a powerful electrophile:

\[ \mathrm{HNO_3 + 2\,H_2SO_4 \rightleftharpoons NO_2^+ + H_3O^+ + 2\,HSO_4^-} \]

The product is nitrobenzene. Nitration is important mainly because the nitro group can be reduced to an amino group (with tin and hydrochloric acid, or hydrogen and a catalyst), giving aniline and its derivatives, the starting point for many dyes and drugs (Chapter 13). Nitration is strongly exothermic and must be controlled carefully; teaching practicals use small quantities of a deactivated substrate under supervision, with the temperature kept low.

docs.title: Sulfonation
docs.text: Benzene reacts with fuming sulfuric acid (sulfuric acid containing dissolved SO₃). The electrophile is sulfur trioxide, or its protonated form, HSO₃⁺. The product is benzenesulfonic acid, C₆H₅SO₃H, a strong acid. Unlike the other substitutions, sulfonation is reversible: heating a sulfonic acid in dilute aqueous acid removes the SO₃H group. Sulfonic acids are used to make detergents and sulfonamide drugs.

docs.title: Friedel–Crafts alkylation
docs.text:
A haloalkane and aluminium chloride alkylate benzene. AlCl₃ takes the halide from the haloalkane, generating a carbocation (or a polarised complex that behaves like one), which is the electrophile:

\[ \mathrm{C_6H_6 + (CH_3)_3CCl \xrightarrow{\ AlCl_3\ } C_6H_5C(CH_3)_3 + HCl} \]

This reaction makes a new carbon–carbon bond, but it has three serious limitations:

  1. Rearrangement. The carbocation can rearrange before it reacts. Benzene and 1-chloropropane give mainly isopropylbenzene (cumene), not propylbenzene, because the primary cation rearranges to the secondary one by a hydride shift.
  2. Polyalkylation. An alkyl group activates the ring (Section 8.5), so the product is more reactive than benzene and reacts again, giving mixtures of di- and trialkylbenzenes.
  3. Deactivated rings do not react. Rings carrying strongly electron-withdrawing groups such as –NO₂ are too unreactive. Rings carrying –NH₂ fail too, because the amine's lone pair binds to the AlCl₃ catalyst.

docs.title: Friedel–Crafts acylation
docs.text:
An acyl chloride (RCOCl) and AlCl₃ generate an acylium ion, R–C≡O⁺, which is stabilised by resonance (R–C⁺=O ↔ R–C≡O⁺) and does not rearrange. The product is an aryl ketone:

\[ \mathrm{C_6H_6 + CH_3COCl \xrightarrow{\ AlCl_3\ } C_6H_5COCH_3 + HCl} \]

The ketone group withdraws electrons and deactivates the ring, so the reaction stops cleanly after one substitution. Acylation therefore avoids both main problems of alkylation. If an alkyl chain is wanted, the ketone can afterwards be reduced to CH₂ (for example by the Clemmensen reduction with zinc amalgam and hydrochloric acid). Making propylbenzene without rearrangement is done in this way: acylate with propanoyl chloride, then reduce.

Reaction Reagents Electrophile Product from benzene Bromination Br₂, FeBr₃ Br⁺ (as Br–Br–FeBr₃) bromobenzene Chlorination Cl₂, AlCl₃ or FeCl₃ Cl⁺ (as Cl–Cl–AlCl₃) chlorobenzene Nitration conc. HNO₃, conc. H₂SO₄ NO₂⁺ nitrobenzene Sulfonation fuming H₂SO₄ (SO₃) SO₃ or HSO₃⁺ benzenesulfonic acid Friedel–Crafts alkylation R–Cl, AlCl₃ R⁺ alkylbenzene (may rearrange) Friedel–Crafts acylation RCOCl, AlCl₃ RC≡O⁺ aryl ketone

Table 8.1. Electrophilic aromatic substitution reactions of benzene.

docs.title: 8.5 Substituent effects: reactivity and orientation
docs.text: When the ring already carries a substituent, two questions arise. Does the substituent make the ring react faster or slower than benzene? And where does the new group go: ortho, meta or para? The answers come from the arenium ion.

docs.title: Activating and deactivating groups
docs.text:
A substituent that donates electrons to the ring makes it more nucleophilic and stabilises the positively charged arenium ion. It activates the ring: methylbenzene (toluene) nitrates about 25 times faster than benzene, and phenol and aniline react extremely fast. A substituent that withdraws electrons makes the ring less nucleophilic and destabilises the arenium ion. It deactivates the ring: nitrobenzene reacts many orders of magnitude more slowly than benzene.

Groups donate or withdraw electrons in two ways:

  • by the inductive effect, through the σ bond, according to electronegativity;
  • by resonance, through the π system. A group with a lone pair on the atom attached to the ring (–OH, –OR, –NH₂, –halogen) can donate that pair into the ring. A group with a π bond to an electronegative atom (–NO₂, –C=O, –C≡N, –SO₃H) withdraws π electrons from the ring.

When the two effects conflict, resonance usually wins, with the important exception of the halogens.

docs.title: Orientation: ortho/para versus meta
docs.text:
Consider attack at the three positions of methoxybenzene (anisole). For ortho or para attack, one of the three resonance contributors of the arenium ion places the positive charge on the ring carbon that carries the OCH₃ group. The oxygen lone pair can then form a C=O⁺ π bond, giving a fourth contributor in which every atom has an octet. That extra contributor makes the ortho and para arenium ions much more stable. For meta attack the positive charge never reaches the carbon bearing the OCH₃ group, so no such contributor is possible.

Figure 8.4 Why OCH₃ directs ortho and para. Attack by an electrophile para to a methoxy group. The positive charge of the arenium ion appears at three carbons, one of which is the carbon bonded to oxygen. A lone pair on oxygen then forms a fourth contributor, an oxonium ion in which every atom has a full octet. This extra stabilisation makes ortho and para attack much faster than meta attack.

The same reasoning, applied to each kind of group, gives three classes:

  1. Activating, ortho/para-directing. Groups that donate electrons: –NH₂, –NHR, –NR₂, –OH, –OR, –NHCOR (strongly or moderately, by resonance), and alkyl groups (weakly, by induction and hyperconjugation). Each stabilises the ortho and para arenium ions most.
  2. Deactivating, ortho/para-directing. The halogens. Their strong inductive withdrawal makes the ring less reactive overall, but their lone pairs can still stabilise the ortho and para arenium ions by resonance. Chlorobenzene reacts more slowly than benzene but gives mainly ortho and para products.
  3. Deactivating, meta-directing. Groups whose atom attached to the ring is δ+ or carries a positive charge: –NO₂, –CN, –SO₃H, –CHO, –COR, –COOH, –COOR, –CF₃, –NR₃⁺. For ortho or para attack, one contributor puts the positive charge right next to this electron-poor group, which is especially bad. Meta attack avoids that contributor, so meta is the least disfavoured position.
Class Groups Effect on rate Directs to strongly activating –NH₂, –NHR, –NR₂, –OH, –O⁻ much faster ortho, para moderately activating –OR, –NHCOR faster ortho, para weakly activating –R (alkyl), –C₆H₅ slightly faster ortho, para weakly deactivating –F, –Cl, –Br, –I slower ortho, para strongly deactivating –NO₂, –CN, –SO₃H, –CHO, –COR, –COOH, –COOR, –CF₃, –NR₃⁺ much slower meta

Table 8.2. Effects of substituents on electrophilic aromatic substitution.

Key idea

A quick rule: if the atom attached to the ring has a lone pair (or is an alkyl carbon), the group directs ortho/para. If it is δ+, bonded to a more electronegative atom by a multiple bond, or positively charged, the group directs meta. All meta directors deactivate; all activators direct ortho/para; the halogens are the exception that deactivate yet direct ortho/para.

Of the two ortho/para products, the para isomer often predominates, especially for bulky groups, because the ortho positions are more crowded. Nitration of toluene gives roughly 60% ortho, 40% para and only a few per cent meta; nitration of tert-butylbenzene gives mainly para.

Caution: very reactive rings

Phenol and aniline are so strongly activated that they react with bromine water at room temperature, without a catalyst, and are brominated at every free ortho and para position: phenol gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol as a white precipitate. To get a single substitution on aniline, the amino group is first converted into an amide (–NHCOCH₃), a milder activator, and changed back afterwards.

docs.title: 8.6 Planning a synthesis
docs.text:
Because substituents direct further substitution, the order of reactions matters.

Example 8.2: Ordering the steps

Make (a) 1-bromo-3-nitrobenzene and (b) 1-bromo-4-nitrobenzene from benzene.

(a) The two groups are meta to each other. The nitro group is a meta director; bromine is an ortho/para director. So nitrate first (HNO₃, H₂SO₄), then brominate (Br₂, FeBr₃): the nitro group sends the bromine to the meta position. The deactivated ring brominates slowly, but it does react.

(b) The groups are para. Brominate first, then nitrate: bromine directs the incoming nitro group ortho and para. The para isomer is separated from the ortho by crystallisation (the para isomer, being more symmetrical, has a higher melting point and lower solubility).

Example 8.3: Where does the third group go?

Predict the main product of nitrating 4-methylphenol (p-cresol).

Both groups are ortho/para directors, and the para position of each is occupied by the other. The OH group is a much stronger activator than CH₃, so it controls the orientation: the nitro group enters ortho to OH. Product: 4-methyl-2-nitrophenol. When groups disagree, the stronger activator wins.

docs.title: Reactions of side chains
docs.text:
Groups attached to the ring can also be changed. The carbon directly attached to a benzene ring is the benzylic position. Benzylic C–H bonds are weak, because breaking them gives a resonance-stabilised benzylic radical. Consequently:

  • Oxidation. Hot, alkaline potassium manganate(VII) oxidises any alkyl side chain with at least one benzylic hydrogen all the way to –COOH, whatever its length. Methylbenzene gives benzoic acid. This changes an ortho/para-directing alkyl group into a meta-directing carboxyl group, which can be useful in synthesis.
  • Radical bromination occurs selectively at the benzylic position, for example with N-bromosuccinimide (NBS) and light.
  • Reduction of a nitro group gives an amino group, turning a strong meta director and deactivator into a strong ortho/para director and activator.

docs.title: 8.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Benzene is a planar regular hexagon with six equal C–C bonds (139 pm) and six delocalised π electrons; its resonance energy is about 150 kJ mol⁻¹.
  • Hückel's rule: a cyclic, planar, fully conjugated ring with 4n + 2 π electrons is aromatic; with 4n it is antiaromatic.
  • In pyridine the N lone pair is outside the π system (basic); in pyrrole it is part of it (not basic).
  • EAS: the ring attacks E⁺ to give a resonance-stabilised arenium ion (slow), which loses H⁺ (fast).
  • Electrophiles: Br⁺/Cl⁺ from X₂ and a Lewis acid; NO₂⁺ from HNO₃/H₂SO₄; SO₃ from fuming H₂SO₄; R⁺ and RCO⁺ from RCl or RCOCl with AlCl₃.
  • Friedel–Crafts alkylation suffers rearrangement and polyalkylation; acylation does not.
  • Electron donors activate and direct ortho/para; electron-withdrawing groups deactivate and direct meta; halogens deactivate but direct ortho/para.
  • Plan syntheses so that each group is introduced when the existing groups direct it to the right place.

docs.title: 8.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Use heats of hydrogenation to explain why benzene is said to have a resonance energy of about 150 kJ mol⁻¹. Why does this make benzene prefer substitution to addition?

Answer

Cyclohexene releases about 120 kJ mol⁻¹ on hydrogenation; three isolated double bonds would release about 360 kJ mol⁻¹. Benzene releases only about 208 kJ mol⁻¹, so it is about 150 kJ mol⁻¹ lower in energy than a ring with three isolated double bonds. Addition would destroy the aromatic π system and lose this stabilisation, while substitution restores it in the final step, so substitution is thermodynamically and kinetically preferred.

Exercise 2

Which are aromatic? (a) cyclopropenyl cation, C₃H₃⁺; (b) cyclooctatetraene; (c) thiophene, C₄H₄S; (d) cyclohepta-1,3,5-triene, C₇H₈.

Answer

(a) Aromatic: planar, fully conjugated (the cationic carbon has an empty p orbital) and two π electrons (n = 0). (b) Not aromatic: eight π electrons would make it antiaromatic if planar, so it adopts a non-planar tub shape and behaves as a polyene. (c) Aromatic: like furan, sulfur contributes one lone pair, giving six π electrons. (d) Not aromatic: the CH₂ carbon is sp³, so the ring is not fully conjugated.

Exercise 3

Write the mechanism of the bromination of benzene with Br₂ and FeBr₃, showing how the catalyst is regenerated.

Answer

(1) A lone pair of Br₂ coordinates to FeBr₃, giving Br–Br⁺–FeBr₃⁻ and making the outer bromine electrophilic. (2) The π electrons of the ring attack the outer bromine; the Br–Br bond breaks, releasing FeBr₄⁻, and an arenium ion forms with the charge delocalised over the ortho and para carbons. (3) FeBr₄⁻ acts as a base: a bromide removes the proton from the sp³ carbon, the C–H bonding pair restores the aromatic ring, and HBr and FeBr₃ are formed. The catalyst is regenerated.

Exercise 4

Benzene reacts with 1-chlorobutane and AlCl₃. Predict the main product and explain. How could butylbenzene itself be made?

Answer

The primary carbocation (or its complex with AlCl₃) rearranges by a hydride shift to the more stable secondary cation, CH₃CH₂C⁺HCH₃. The main product is therefore (butan-2-yl)benzene, sec-butylbenzene, together with some polyalkylated material. To make butylbenzene, use Friedel–Crafts acylation with butanoyl chloride and AlCl₃ (no rearrangement), giving 1-phenylbutan-1-one, then reduce the C=O to CH₂.

Exercise 5

Predict the main mononitration product(s) of: (a) methoxybenzene; (b) benzoic acid; (c) chlorobenzene; (d) nitrobenzene. Say whether each reacts faster or slower than benzene.

Answer

(a) 2- and 4-nitromethoxybenzene (ortho and para), mainly para; faster. (b) 3-nitrobenzoic acid (meta); slower. (c) 1-chloro-2-nitro- and 1-chloro-4-nitrobenzene (ortho and para); slower. (d) 1,3-dinitrobenzene (meta); much slower, needing more forcing conditions.

Exercise 6

Explain, by drawing the arenium ions, why the nitro group directs incoming electrophiles to the meta position.

Answer

For ortho or para attack, one of the three contributors of the arenium ion places the positive charge on the ring carbon bonded to the nitro group. The nitrogen of the nitro group already carries a formal positive charge, so this contributor puts two positive charges on adjacent atoms and is very unfavourable; the ortho and para arenium ions are strongly destabilised. In meta attack, the positive charge is placed only on carbons not bonded to the nitro group, so this bad contributor never arises. All three ions are destabilised relative to benzene (hence deactivation), but the meta ion least, so meta substitution is fastest.

Exercise 7

Starting from benzene, give a sequence of reactions to make 3-nitrobenzoic acid. Would the order of steps matter?

Answer

Friedel–Crafts alkylation with chloromethane and AlCl₃ gives methylbenzene. Oxidation with hot alkaline KMnO₄ (then acidification) gives benzoic acid. Nitration then puts the nitro group meta to the meta-directing COOH group: 3-nitrobenzoic acid. The order matters: nitrating methylbenzene first would put the nitro group ortho or para to the methyl, and Friedel–Crafts alkylation of nitrobenzene fails because the ring is too deactivated.

docs.title: 8.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of aromatic chemistry

  3. 2n
  4. any even number

Exercise 2

Exercise 3

  2. NO₂⁺

Exercise 4

Which group is deactivating but ortho/para-directing?

  1. -OH
  2. -CH₃
  3. -Cl
  4. -NO₂

Exercise 5

Friedel-Crafts acylation is preferred over alkylation because acylation

  2. does not suffer rearrangement or polysubstitution
  3. needs no catalyst

Exercise 6

Exercise 7

Match each reagent pair to the group it introduces into benzene.

ABBr₂, FeBr₃-COCH₃conc. HNO₃, conc. H₂SO₄-SO₃HCH₃COCl, AlCl₃-Brfuming H₂SO₄-NO₂ Answer

docs.title: Chapter 12: Carboxylic Acids and Their Derivatives
docs.text:
Acidity and nucleophilic acyl substitution

Vinegar owes its sourness to ethanoic acid, the sting of an ant to methanoic acid, and the smell of rancid butter to butanoic acid. Carboxylic acids and the compounds derived from them, acyl chlorides, anhydrides, esters, amides and nitriles, form one of the largest and most useful families in organic chemistry. Esters give fruits their scents and fats their structure; amides hold proteins together; polyesters and polyamides are among our most important materials. The members of the family are linked by one reaction type, nucleophilic acyl substitution, in which one group on the carbonyl carbon is replaced by another. This chapter explains the acidity of carboxylic acids, the mechanism of acyl substitution, and the reactivity order that tells you which derivative can be turned into which.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  • explain the physical properties and acidity of carboxylic acids, and the effect of substituents on acidity;
  • list ways of making carboxylic acids;
  • write the addition–elimination mechanism of nucleophilic acyl substitution and explain how it differs from nucleophilic addition to aldehydes and ketones;
  • rank the acid derivatives by reactivity and use the order to plan interconversions;
  • write the mechanism of Fischer esterification and of ester hydrolysis in acid and in base;
  • predict the products of reactions of acyl chlorides, anhydrides, esters, amides and nitriles with water, alcohols, amines, hydride reagents and Grignard reagents.

docs.title: 12.1 Carboxylic acids: structure and properties
docs.text:
