The carboxyl group, –COOH, combines a carbonyl group and a hydroxyl group on the same carbon. The carbon is sp² and the group is planar. Naming was covered in Section 2.4: the acid is named from the alkane with -oic acid, counting the COOH carbon as C1.

Carboxylic acids are strongly hydrogen bonded. In the pure liquid and in non-polar solvents they form dimers, pairs of molecules held together by two hydrogen bonds. As a result they have high boiling points: ethanoic acid (60 g mol⁻¹) boils at 118 °C, higher than propan-1-ol (97 °C). The first four acids mix with water completely; solubility then falls with chain length, and the long-chain fatty acids such as hexadecanoic acid (palmitic acid) are insoluble.

docs.title: Acidity
docs.text:
Carboxylic acids are weak acids, with pKa values typically between 4 and 5, but they are much stronger than alcohols (pKa 16) or phenols (pKa 10). The reason is the resonance stabilisation of the carboxylate ion, in which the negative charge is shared equally between two oxygen atoms (Figure 1.4, Section 4.4).

Acid Formula pKa methanoic acid HCOOH 3.75 ethanoic acid CH₃COOH 4.76 propanoic acid CH₃CH₂COOH 4.87 chloroethanoic acid ClCH₂COOH 2.86 trichloroethanoic acid Cl₃CCOOH 0.65 benzoic acid C₆H₅COOH 4.20

Table 12.1. Acidities of some carboxylic acids. Electron-withdrawing groups near the carboxyl group increase acidity by the inductive effect.

Carboxylic acids react with strong bases (NaOH) and even with weak bases such as sodium hydrogencarbonate, giving water-soluble carboxylate salts:

\[ \mathrm{CH_3COOH + NaHCO_3 \rightarrow CH_3COO^-Na^+ + H_2O + CO_2} \]

The fizzing of carbon dioxide with sodium hydrogencarbonate is a simple test for a carboxylic acid; phenols and alcohols are too weakly acidic to give it. Sodium and potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids are soaps (Section 12.5).

docs.title: Making carboxylic acids
docs.text:
• Oxidation of primary alcohols or aldehydes (Section 10.5), or of alkyl side chains on a benzene ring with hot KMnO₄ (Section 8.6).
  • Carboxylation of Grignard reagents: RMgX + CO₂, then H₃O⁺, gives RCOOH, adding one carbon to the chain (Table 11.1).
  • Hydrolysis of nitriles: R–C≡N heated with aqueous acid or base gives RCOOH (Section 12.7). Since nitriles are made from haloalkanes and cyanide by SN2, this is another way to add one carbon.
  • Hydrolysis of esters, amides and other derivatives (Sections 12.5 and 12.6).

docs.title: 12.2 Nucleophilic acyl substitution
docs.text:
An acyl group is R–C=O. Carboxylic acid derivatives all have the form R–CO–L, where L is a group attached to the acyl carbon through an electronegative atom: Cl (acyl chloride), OCOR (anhydride), OR′ (ester), NH₂ (amide) or OH (the acid itself).

When a nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon of an aldehyde or ketone, the tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate has no good leaving group, so it is simply protonated: the result is addition. When the carbonyl carbon carries a group L that can leave, the tetrahedral intermediate collapses instead: the oxygen lone pair re-forms the C=O bond and L is expelled. The overall result is substitution of L by the nucleophile. The mechanism has two steps, addition then elimination:

Figure 12.1 The addition–elimination mechanism. Nucleophilic acyl substitution. In the first step the nucleophile adds to the carbonyl carbon and the π electrons move onto oxygen, giving a tetrahedral intermediate. In the second step the oxygen lone pair re-forms the C=O π bond and the leaving group L departs with its electron pair. The net result is the replacement of L by Nu.

Caution: not an SN2 reaction

Acyl substitution does not occur by a one-step backside attack like SN2. The sp² carbonyl carbon is first attacked to form a tetrahedral intermediate, and only then does the leaving group leave. Always draw the tetrahedral intermediate.

docs.title: The reactivity order
docs.text:
How readily a derivative undergoes acyl substitution depends on two related factors:

  1. The leaving group. The weaker the base L⁻, the better it leaves. Cl⁻ (conjugate base of HCl, pKa −7) is an excellent leaving group; NH₂⁻ (conjugate base of NH₃, pKa 38) is a very poor one.
  2. Resonance donation by L. A lone pair on L can be shared with the carbonyl group (L–C=O ↔ L⁺=C–O⁻). This makes the carbonyl carbon less electrophilic and the derivative more stable. Nitrogen donates strongly (amides are very stable), oxygen less so, and chlorine, whose 3p lone pairs overlap poorly with carbon's 2p orbital, hardly at all.

Both factors give the same order:

\[ \text{acyl chloride} > \text{acid anhydride} > \text{ester} \approx \text{carboxylic acid} > \text{amide} > \text{carboxylate ion} \] Figure 12.2 Reactivity order of acid derivatives. The reactivity of carboxylic acid derivatives towards nucleophilic acyl substitution, with each leaving group and the pKa of its conjugate acid. Acyl chlorides are the most reactive and amides the least. A more reactive derivative can be converted into a less reactive one by acyl substitution.

Key idea

You can travel down the reactivity ladder by acyl substitution, but not up. An acyl chloride can be converted into an anhydride, an ester or an amide; an ester into an amide; but an amide cannot be turned directly into an ester or an acyl chloride. To go up, first hydrolyse to the carboxylic acid, then activate it (for example with SOCl₂).

docs.title: 12.3 Reactions of carboxylic acids
docs.text:
Conversion into acyl chlorides. Thionyl chloride, SOCl₂, converts a carboxylic acid into the acyl chloride, with sulfur dioxide and hydrogen chloride as gaseous by-products:

\[ \mathrm{CH_3COOH + SOCl_2 \rightarrow CH_3COCl + SO_2 + HCl} \]

This is the usual way to climb the reactivity ladder.

Fischer esterification. A carboxylic acid and an alcohol, heated with a little concentrated sulfuric acid as catalyst, give an ester and water:

\[ \mathrm{CH_3COOH + CH_3CH_2OH \overset{H^+}{\rightleftharpoons} CH_3COOCH_2CH_3 + H_2O} \]

The mechanism is acid-catalysed acyl substitution:

  1. The carbonyl oxygen of the acid is protonated, making the carbonyl carbon more electrophilic.
  2. The alcohol oxygen attacks the carbonyl carbon, giving a tetrahedral intermediate.
  3. A proton moves from the newly attached oxygen to one of the OH groups.
  4. Water leaves, and the C=O bond re-forms (still protonated).
  5. Loss of a proton gives the ester and regenerates the catalyst.

Every step is reversible, and the equilibrium constant is close to 1 for many simple acids and alcohols. To get a good yield, one reactant (usually the cheaper alcohol) is used in excess, or water is removed as it forms (Le Chatelier's principle). Experiments with alcohol labelled with oxygen-18 show that the label ends up in the ester, not in the water, confirming that the C–O bond of the acid, not of the alcohol, is broken.

Reduction. LiAlH₄ reduces carboxylic acids to primary alcohols: CH₃COOH → CH₃CH₂OH. NaBH₄ is not strong enough.

Amide formation. Heating an acid with an amine first gives an ammonium carboxylate salt (an acid–base reaction), which loses water only on strong heating. In practice amides are made from more reactive derivatives, or by using a "coupling reagent" that activates the acid, the method used to join amino acids into peptides.

docs.title: 12.4 Acyl chlorides and acid anhydrides
docs.text:
Acyl chlorides (acid chlorides) are the most reactive derivatives. They react vigorously at room temperature with water, alcohols and amines, releasing hydrogen chloride (they fume in moist air):

  • with water: CH₃COCl + H₂O → CH₃COOH + HCl
  • with an alcohol: CH₃COCl + CH₃CH₂OH → CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ + HCl
  • with ammonia or an amine (two equivalents, one to neutralise the HCl): CH₃COCl + 2 NH₃ → CH₃CONH₂ + NH₄Cl

They also acylate benzene in the Friedel–Crafts reaction (Section 8.4). Because these reactions are fast and irreversible, acyl chlorides give much better yields of esters than Fischer esterification, but they are corrosive and lachrymatory and must be handled in a fume cupboard.

Acid anhydrides, (RCO)₂O, react in the same ways, more gently, releasing a carboxylic acid instead of HCl. Ethanoic anhydride is used industrially and in teaching laboratories to make aspirin (2-acetoxybenzoic acid) by acylating the OH group of 2-hydroxybenzoic acid (salicylic acid), with a little acid as catalyst:

\[ \mathrm{HOC_6H_4COOH + (CH_3CO)_2O \rightarrow CH_3COOC_6H_4COOH + CH_3COOH} \]

Anhydrides are preferred to acyl chlorides on a large scale because they are cheaper, less corrosive and do not release HCl.

docs.title: 12.5 Esters
docs.text:
Esters are common in nature and industry. Many have pleasant, fruity smells and are used as flavourings: ethyl ethanoate is a fruity-smelling solvent used in some nail-polish removers, and 3-methylbutyl ethanoate smells of bananas. Fats and oils are esters of glycerol (Chapter 15). Polyesters are important fibres and plastics.

Esters cannot hydrogen bond to one another, so they boil lower than acids of similar mass, close to the corresponding ketones.

docs.title: Hydrolysis
docs.text:
Esters are hydrolysed back to the acid and alcohol in two ways.

Acid-catalysed hydrolysis is the exact reverse of Fischer esterification, with the same intermediates. A large excess of water drives the equilibrium towards the acid and alcohol. It is reversible.

Base-promoted hydrolysis (saponification). Heating an ester with aqueous sodium hydroxide gives the carboxylate salt and the alcohol:

\[ \mathrm{CH_3COOCH_2CH_3 + NaOH \rightarrow CH_3COO^-Na^+ + CH_3CH_2OH} \]

The mechanism is acyl substitution: hydroxide adds to the carbonyl carbon, the tetrahedral intermediate expels the alkoxide ion, and the alkoxide immediately takes a proton from the carboxylic acid just formed. This last step, an acid–base reaction with a very large equilibrium constant, makes saponification irreversible, and it consumes a full equivalent of hydroxide, which is why base "promotes" rather than catalyses the reaction. Acidifying the mixture afterwards gives the free carboxylic acid.

The name comes from soap-making: boiling fats with sodium hydroxide hydrolyses their ester groups, giving glycerol and the sodium salts of fatty acids, which are soaps. A soap molecule has a long, non-polar hydrocarbon tail and an ionic carboxylate head. In water, soap molecules gather into micelles, spheres with the tails inside and the heads facing the water, which can hold droplets of grease in their oily core and carry them away.

docs.title: Other reactions of esters
docs.text:
• With amines: esters react with ammonia or amines to give amides (moving down the ladder).
  • Transesterification: an ester heated with a different alcohol and an acid or base catalyst exchanges its alkoxy group. Biodiesel is made by transesterifying vegetable oils with methanol.
  • Reduction: LiAlH₄ reduces an ester to two alcohols: RCOOR′ → RCH₂OH + R′OH.
  • Grignard reagents add twice: the first equivalent substitutes the OR′ group to give a ketone, which is more reactive than the ester and immediately adds a second equivalent. The product, after acid work-up, is a tertiary alcohol with two identical groups from the Grignard reagent: CH₃COOCH₃ + 2 CH₃MgBr → (CH₃)₃COH.

docs.title: 12.6 Amides
docs.text:
Amides are the least reactive of the neutral derivatives. The nitrogen lone pair is strongly delocalised onto the carbonyl oxygen, which has three consequences:

  1. The C–N bond has partial double-bond character, so rotation about it is restricted and the amide group (O=C–N with its attached atoms) is planar.
  2. The nitrogen is not basic (Section 4.5): its lone pair is not available to accept a proton.
  3. The carbonyl carbon is only weakly electrophilic, so amides are hard to hydrolyse.

These properties make the amide link, called the peptide bond in proteins, an ideal stable connector for the molecules of life (Chapter 15). The planarity of each peptide bond shapes the folding of proteins.

Amides are hydrolysed only by prolonged heating with strong aqueous acid (giving the carboxylic acid and an ammonium salt) or strong base (giving the carboxylate and the amine or ammonia). Primary amides (RCONH₂) form strong hydrogen bonds and are usually solids; ethanamide melts at about 80 °C.

Reduction of an amide with LiAlH₄ converts the C=O group into CH₂, giving an amine: CH₃CONH₂ → CH₃CH₂NH₂. This is a useful way of making amines (Chapter 13).

docs.title: 12.7 Nitriles
docs.text:
Nitriles, R–C≡N, contain a carbon at the same oxidation level as a carboxylic acid, and they are usually grouped with the acid derivatives. The C≡N carbon is electrophilic, like a carbonyl carbon. Nitriles are made by SN2 reaction of cyanide ion with primary or secondary haloalkanes (Section 9.2) or from amides by dehydration.

  • Hydrolysis with hot aqueous acid or base gives first an amide and then the carboxylic acid (or its salt): CH₃CH₂CN → CH₃CH₂COOH.
  • Reduction with LiAlH₄ (or with hydrogen and a catalyst) gives a primary amine with one more carbon than the haloalkane used to make the nitrile: CH₃CH₂CN → CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂.

Example 12.1: Adding one carbon

Show two ways of making butanoic acid from 1-bromopropane.

(a) Via a nitrile: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + NaCN (SN2, in DMSO) → CH₃CH₂CH₂CN; then hot aqueous acid → CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH.

(b) Via a Grignard reagent: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + Mg (dry ether) → CH₃CH₂CH₂MgBr; then CO₂, then H₃O⁺ → CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH.

Route (b) is preferred when the halide is tertiary (SN2 would fail); route (a) when the molecule contains groups that would destroy a Grignard reagent (such as OH or C=O).

Example 12.2: Choosing a derivative

Plan the synthesis of N-ethylethanamide, CH₃CONHCH₂CH₃, from ethanoic acid.

Amides lie at the bottom of the ladder, so they can be made from any more reactive derivative. Convert ethanoic acid into ethanoyl chloride with SOCl₂, then add two equivalents of ethanamine (one forms the amide, the other takes up the HCl as ethylammonium chloride): CH₃COCl + 2 CH₃CH₂NH₂ → CH₃CONHCH₂CH₃ + CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺Cl⁻.

docs.title: 12.8 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Carboxylic acids form hydrogen-bonded dimers and are weak acids (pKa 4 to 5) because the carboxylate ion is resonance-stabilised; electron-withdrawing groups increase acidity. They release CO₂ from NaHCO₃.
  • Acids are made by oxidation, carboxylation of Grignard reagents and hydrolysis of nitriles and other derivatives.
  • Acid derivatives react by nucleophilic acyl substitution: addition to give a tetrahedral intermediate, then elimination of the leaving group.
  • Reactivity: acyl chloride > anhydride > ester ≈ acid > amide. Conversions run downhill.
  • Fischer esterification is acid-catalysed and reversible; saponification (base hydrolysis of esters) is irreversible and makes soap from fats.
  • LiAlH₄ reduces acids and esters to primary alcohols, amides to amines and nitriles to primary amines. Grignard reagents add twice to esters, giving tertiary alcohols.
  • Amides are planar, non-basic and hard to hydrolyse: ideal for peptide bonds.

docs.title: 12.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Explain why ethanoic acid (bp 118 °C) boils higher than propan-1-ol (bp 97 °C), although their molar masses are equal.

Answer

Ethanoic acid molecules form cyclic dimers held by two strong hydrogen bonds, and in the liquid they hydrogen bond extensively through both the C=O and the O–H groups. The carboxyl group is also more polar than an alcohol group. More energy is needed to separate the molecules, so the boiling point is higher.

Exercise 2

Arrange in order of increasing acidity, and explain: ethanoic acid, 2,2-dichloroethanoic acid, ethanol, 2-chloroethanoic acid, phenol.

Answer

Ethanol (16) < phenol (10) < ethanoic acid (4.76) < 2-chloroethanoic acid (2.86) < 2,2-dichloroethanoic acid (1.29). Phenoxide is stabilised by resonance into the ring; carboxylate by resonance over two oxygens; each chlorine adds an inductive withdrawal that stabilises the carboxylate further.

Exercise 3

Write the mechanism for the saponification of methyl ethanoate with sodium hydroxide, and explain why the reaction goes to completion.

Answer

(1) Hydroxide attacks the carbonyl carbon; the π electrons move onto oxygen, giving a tetrahedral intermediate. (2) The oxygen lone pair re-forms the C=O bond and methoxide is expelled, giving ethanoic acid. (3) Methoxide (or hydroxide) removes the acidic proton from ethanoic acid, giving ethanoate and methanol. Step 3 is an acid–base reaction with an equilibrium constant of about 10¹¹ (pKa 4.8 against about 15.5), so it pulls the whole sequence to completion; the carboxylate ion is far too unreactive to be attacked by methanol.

Exercise 4

Give the products when ethanoyl chloride reacts with: (a) water; (b) propan-1-ol; (c) excess dimethylamine, (CH₃)₂NH; (d) benzene with AlCl₃.

Answer

(a) Ethanoic acid + HCl. (b) Propyl ethanoate + HCl. (c) N,N-dimethylethanamide, CH₃CON(CH₃)₂, + dimethylammonium chloride. (d) 1-Phenylethanone (acetophenone), C₆H₅COCH₃, + HCl.

Exercise 5

How would you make (a) ethyl benzoate from benzoic acid by two different routes; (b) 2-phenylpropan-2-ol from ethyl benzoate?

Answer

(a) Route 1: Fischer esterification with excess ethanol and a catalytic amount of concentrated H₂SO₄, heated under reflux. Route 2: convert benzoic acid into benzoyl chloride with SOCl₂, then react with ethanol (with a base such as pyridine to take up HCl); this route is not an equilibrium and gives a higher yield.

(b) Add two equivalents of methylmagnesium bromide, then acid work-up. The first equivalent converts the ester into 1-phenylethanone, which adds the second methyl group, giving (CH₃)₂C(OH)C₆H₅.

Exercise 6

Give the products of LiAlH₄ reduction (followed by water) of: (a) methyl propanoate; (b) N-methylethanamide; (c) butanenitrile; (d) propanoic acid.

Answer

(a) Propan-1-ol and methanol. (b) N-Ethylmethanamine, CH₃CH₂NHCH₃ (the C=O becomes CH₂). (c) Butan-1-amine, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂. (d) Propan-1-ol.

Exercise 7

Explain why amides are much less basic than amines and why the C–N bond of an amide does not rotate freely at room temperature.

Answer

In an amide the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised onto the carbonyl oxygen by resonance (O=C–NH₂ ↔ ⁻O–C=NH₂⁺). The lone pair is therefore much less available to bond to a proton, so amides are very weak bases (the pKa of a protonated amide is about −0.5, compared with about 10.6 for a protonated amine; amides are in fact protonated on oxygen). The same resonance gives the C–N bond partial double-bond character, so rotating about it would destroy the overlap of the nitrogen p orbital with the C=O π system; this costs enough energy to make rotation slow at room temperature.

docs.title: 12.10 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of carboxylic acids and derivatives

Exercise 1

Which derivative is the most reactive towards nucleophilic acyl substitution?

  1. amide
  2. ester
  3. acid anhydride
  4. acyl chloride
Answer

acyl chloride

Exercise 2

Which reagent converts a carboxylic acid into an acyl chloride?

  1. SOCl₂
  2. HCl
  3. NaCl
  4. Cl₂ with light
Answer

SOCl₂

Exercise 3

Saponification is the hydrolysis of an ester by

  1. dilute acid
  2. aqueous sodium hydroxide
  3. water alone
  4. LiAlH₄
Answer

aqueous sodium hydroxide

Exercise 4

Name the ester formed from ethanoic acid and methanol.

Answer

methyl ethanoate / methyl acetate

Exercise 5

Which observation shows that a compound is a carboxylic acid rather than a phenol?

  1. it dissolves in NaOH
  2. it fizzes with NaHCO₃
  3. it decolourises bromine water
  4. it gives a silver mirror
Answer

it fizzes with NaHCO₃

Exercise 6

Reduction of an amide with LiAlH₄ gives

  1. an alcohol
  2. an amine
  3. a carboxylic acid
  4. a nitrile
Answer

an amine

Exercise 7

The mechanism of nucleophilic acyl substitution is best described as

  1. a one-step SN2
  2. addition then elimination
  3. elimination then addition
  4. a radical chain
Answer

addition then elimination

docs.title: Chapter 2: Functional Groups and Nomenclature
docs.text:
Recognising families of compounds and naming them systematically

There are many millions of organic compounds, but they fall into a modest number of families. Every member of a family carries the same functional group, a small arrangement of atoms that reacts in the same way wherever it appears. Ethanol, a cholesterol molecule and a sugar all contain O–H groups attached to carbon, and all three show some of the typical reactions of alcohols. This chapter introduces the functional groups you will meet throughout the book and the IUPAC system for naming compounds, so that a name always leads to one structure and a structure to one name.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  • recognise the main functional groups in a structure and name the family each belongs to;
  • classify carbon atoms, alcohols, haloalkanes and amines as primary, secondary or tertiary;
  • name alkanes, cycloalkanes, alkenes and alkynes by the IUPAC rules;
  • name compounds that carry one principal functional group, using suffixes and prefixes correctly;
  • name simple benzene derivatives, including common names still in use;
  • draw a structure from its systematic name;
  • calculate the degree of unsaturation from a molecular formula.

docs.title: 2.1 Functional groups
docs.text:
A molecule can be thought of as a hydrocarbon framework, written R in general formulas, carrying one or more functional groups. The framework is fairly inert: C–C and C–H bonds are strong and nearly non-polar. The functional groups contain polar bonds, lone pairs or π bonds, and they are where reactions happen.

Figure 2.1 The main functional groups. The common functional groups. R and R′ stand for carbon frameworks, which may be the same or different. The carbonyl group, C=O, is shared by aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters and amides, which differ in what else is attached to the carbonyl carbon. Family Functional group General formula Example Name of example Alkane none (only C–C, C–H) R–H CH₃CH₃ ethane Alkene C=C R₂C=CR₂ CH₂=CH₂ ethene Alkyne C≡C RC≡CR HC≡CH ethyne Arene benzene ring Ar–H C₆H₆ benzene Haloalkane C–X (X = F, Cl, Br, I) R–X CH₃CH₂Br bromoethane Alcohol C–OH R–OH CH₃CH₂OH ethanol Ether C–O–C R–O–R′ CH₃OCH₂CH₃ methoxyethane Amine C–N R–NH₂, R₂NH, R₃N CH₃NH₂ methanamine Aldehyde –CHO RCHO CH₃CHO ethanal Ketone C–CO–C RCOR′ CH₃COCH₃ propanone Carboxylic acid –COOH RCOOH CH₃COOH ethanoic acid Ester –COO–C RCOOR′ CH₃COOCH₃ methyl ethanoate Amide –CONH₂ RCONH₂ CH₃CONH₂ ethanamide Acyl chloride –COCl RCOCl CH₃COCl ethanoyl chloride Nitrile –C≡N RCN CH₃CN ethanenitrile

Table 2.1. Functional groups, with one example of each.

Caution: an ester is not a ketone plus an ether

The atoms of a functional group act together. In an ester, the oxygen next to the C=O shares its lone pairs with the carbonyl group by resonance, and the ester reacts differently from both a ketone and an ether. Always identify the largest recognisable group: C=O with OH on the same carbon is a carboxylic acid, not a ketone and an alcohol.

docs.title: Primary, secondary and tertiary
docs.text:
A carbon atom is classified by how many other carbon atoms it is bonded to: primary (1°) if one, secondary (2°) if two, tertiary (3°) if three and quaternary (4°) if four.

  • Alcohols and haloalkanes take the class of the carbon that carries the OH or the halogen. Propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH, is a primary alcohol; propan-2-ol, (CH₃)₂CHOH, is secondary; 2-methylpropan-2-ol, (CH₃)₃COH, is tertiary.
  • Amines are classified differently, by how many carbon groups are attached to the nitrogen: RNH₂ is a primary amine, R₂NH secondary and R₃N tertiary. So (CH₃)₃C–NH₂ is a primary amine even though it is attached to a tertiary carbon.

These classes matter because they decide how a compound reacts. Tertiary alcohols resist oxidation (Chapter 10), and tertiary haloalkanes react by different mechanisms from primary ones (Chapter 9).

docs.title: 2.2 Naming alkanes
docs.text: IUPAC (the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry) names are built from three parts: a prefix (substituents), a parent (the main chain or ring) and a suffix (the principal functional group). For alkanes the suffix is simply -ane.

docs.title: The parent chains
docs.text:
Carbons Name Carbons Name 1 methane 6 hexane 2 ethane 7 heptane 3 propane 8 octane 4 butane 9 nonane 5 pentane 10 decane

Table 2.2. The first ten unbranched alkanes. The stems meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent- and so on are used in every family.

Alkanes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. A group formed by removing one hydrogen from an alkane is an alkyl group: methyl (CH₃–), ethyl (CH₃CH₂–), propyl (CH₃CH₂CH₂–) and so on. Four branched alkyl groups have common names that are still accepted:

  • isopropyl (propan-2-yl), (CH₃)₂CH–;
  • isobutyl (2-methylpropyl), (CH₃)₂CHCH₂–;
  • sec-butyl (butan-2-yl), CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)–;
  • tert-butyl (2-methylpropan-2-yl), (CH₃)₃C–, often written t-Bu.

docs.title: The rules for a branched alkane
docs.text:
1. Find the longest continuous chain of carbons. It is the parent. The chain need not be straight on paper; follow it round corners. If two chains are equally long, choose the one with more substituents.
  2. Number the chain from the end that gives the substituents the lowest locants (position numbers). Compare the sets of locants term by term and choose the set that is lower at the first point of difference: 2,3,5 beats 2,4,4.
  3. Name each substituent with its locant. If the same group appears more than once, use the multiplying prefixes di-, tri-, tetra- and give every locant: 2,2-dimethyl, not 2-dimethyl.
  4. List the substituents in alphabetical order, ignoring the multiplying prefixes (di-, tri-) and the italic prefixes sec- and tert-. So ethyl comes before dimethyl, because e precedes m.
  5. Write the name as one word, with commas between numbers and hyphens between numbers and letters.
Figure 2.2 Naming a branched alkane. Naming 4-ethyl-2-methylhexane. The longest chain, highlighted, has six carbons. Numbering from the left gives the branches locants 2 and 4; numbering from the right would give 3 and 5, so the left-hand numbering is used. The substituents are listed alphabetically.

Example 2.1: Naming an alkane from its condensed formula

Name (CH₃)₂CHCH₂C(CH₃)₃.

Write it out: a CH carbon carrying two CH₃ groups, then CH₂, then a carbon carrying three CH₃ groups. The longest chain runs CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–C(CH₃)₂–CH₃, five carbons: pentane. The branches are one methyl on one carbon and two methyls on another. Numbering from the right end gives 2,2,4; from the left, 2,4,4. At the first point of difference, 2 = 2, and at the second, 2 < 4, so the right-hand numbering wins.

Name: 2,2,4-trimethylpentane. (This compound is the reference fuel that defines an octane rating of 100.)

docs.title: Cycloalkanes
docs.text: A ring of carbons takes the prefix cyclo-: cyclopropane, cyclobutane, cyclopentane, cyclohexane. A ring with one substituent needs no locant (methylcyclohexane). With two or more substituents, number round the ring to give the lowest locants, starting at a substituted carbon and, when there is a choice, giving the lower number to the group that comes first in the alphabet: 1-ethyl-3-methylcyclohexane.

docs.title: 2.3 Alkenes and alkynes
docs.text:
The suffix for a C=C double bond is -ene and for a C≡C triple bond -yne. The locant of the multiple bond is the lower of the two carbon numbers it joins, and it is placed just before the suffix:

  • CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃ is but-1-ene; CH₃CH=CHCH₃ is but-2-ene.
  • HC≡CCH₂CH₃ is but-1-yne.
  • CH₂=CH–CH=CH₂ is buta-1,3-diene (an "a" is added to the stem to make the name easier to say).

Number the chain from the end nearer the multiple bond, even if this gives a substituent a higher number: CH₂=CHCH(CH₃)CH₃ is 3-methylbut-1-ene, not 2-methylbut-3-ene. In rings, the carbons of the double bond are C1 and C2: 3-methylcyclohexene has the methyl on the carbon next to one end of the double bond.

Note: choosing the parent chain of an alkene

Most school and first-year textbooks choose as parent the longest chain that contains the multiple bond. The 2013 IUPAC recommendations instead choose the longest chain first and consider unsaturation only to break ties. For nearly all the molecules in this book the two methods give the same name; where you are examined, follow the convention your course uses.

Alkenes can also show cis–trans (E/Z) isomerism, which is added to the front of the name, as in (E)-but-2-ene. That is the subject of Chapter 3.

docs.title: 2.4 Compounds with a principal functional group
docs.text:
When a molecule contains a functional group such as an alcohol or a ketone, the name changes in three ways:

  1. The parent chain is the longest chain that contains the carbon carrying the principal group (or, for acids, aldehydes, amides and nitriles, the chain that includes that group's own carbon).
  2. The suffix shows the principal group, and the final -e of the alkane name is dropped before a vowel: propane becomes propan-1-ol, propanal, propanone.
  3. The chain is numbered to give the principal group the lowest locant, then multiple bonds, then the other substituents.

When a molecule has more than one functional group, only one, the principal group, is named as a suffix. The others are named as prefixes. The order of priority, from highest, is:

Priority Family Suffix Prefix (when not principal) 1 carboxylic acid -oic acid carboxy- 2 ester -oate alkoxycarbonyl- 3 acyl chloride -oyl chloride chlorocarbonyl- 4 amide -amide carbamoyl- 5 nitrile -nitrile cyano- 6 aldehyde -al oxo- (or formyl-) 7 ketone -one oxo- 8 alcohol -ol hydroxy- 9 amine -amine amino- — ether, haloalkane (no suffix) alkoxy-, fluoro-, chloro-, bromo-, iodo-

Table 2.3. Priority of functional groups for naming, with their suffixes and prefixes. Alkenes and alkynes use the endings -ene and -yne together with any suffix.

docs.title: Alcohols
docs.text: Replace the -e of the alkane with -ol and give the position: ethanol, propan-2-ol, butan-2-ol. Two OH groups make a diol, and here the -e is kept: ethane-1,2-diol (the antifreeze ethylene glycol). In propane-1,2,3-triol (glycerol) each carbon carries an OH group.

docs.title: Ethers
docs.text: Simple ethers are named as alkoxyalkanes: the smaller group becomes the alkoxy prefix. CH₃OCH₂CH₃ is methoxyethane, and CH₃CH₂OCH₂CH₃ is ethoxyethane (the "ether" of old anaesthetics, also called diethyl ether).

docs.title: Amines
docs.text: Primary amines take the suffix -amine: CH₃CH₂NH₂ is ethanamine, and (CH₃)₂CHNH₂ is propan-2-amine. In secondary and tertiary amines the largest group is the parent and the others are prefixes with the locant N, to show that they are on the nitrogen: CH₃NHCH₂CH₃ is N-methylethanamine, and (CH₃)₃N is N,N-dimethylmethanamine (trimethylamine).

docs.title: Aldehydes and ketones
docs.text: The aldehyde group, –CHO, is always at the end of a chain, so its carbon is C1 and no locant is needed: CH₃CHO is ethanal, and (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CHO is 3-methylbutanal. Ketones take the suffix -one with a locant where needed: CH₃COCH₃ is propanone (acetone), CH₃COCH₂CH₃ butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₃ pentan-2-one and CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃ pentan-3-one.

docs.title: Carboxylic acids and their derivatives
docs.text:
The carbon of the COOH group is C1 of the chain: CH₃COOH is ethanoic acid (acetic acid), CH₃CH₂COOH propanoic acid, and (CH₃)₂CHCOOH 2-methylpropanoic acid. The derivatives are named from the acid:

  • Esters, RCOOR′, are named in two words: the alkyl group R′ on oxygen first, then the acid part with -oic acid changed to -oate. CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ is ethyl ethanoate (ethyl acetate); CH₃CH₂COOCH₃ is methyl propanoate. A common slip is to reverse the parts: look for the carbon attached to the C=O; that part is the "-oate".
  • Acyl chlorides change -oic acid to -oyl chloride: CH₃COCl is ethanoyl chloride.
  • Amides change -oic acid to -amide: CH₃CONH₂ is ethanamide, and CH₃CONHCH₃ is N-methylethanamide.
  • Nitriles add -nitrile to the alkane name, counting the nitrile carbon: CH₃CN is ethanenitrile and CH₃CH₂CN propanenitrile.
  • Acid anhydrides, (RCO)₂O, replace acid with anhydride: (CH₃CO)₂O is ethanoic anhydride.
Figure 2.3 Names of three molecules. Three names built by the rules. In 4-methylpentan-2-ol the chain is numbered to give the OH group the lowest locant. In 3-methylbut-1-ene the numbering starts at the end nearer the double bond. In 3-methylcyclohexan-1-ol the carbon carrying the OH group is C1.

Example 2.2: A molecule with two functional groups

Name CH₃COCH₂CH(OH)CH₃.

Both a ketone and an alcohol are present. The ketone has the higher priority (Table 2.3), so it is the suffix -one and the OH becomes the prefix hydroxy-. The chain has five carbons. Numbering from the left gives the C=O locant 2; from the right, 4. So number from the left: the OH is on C4.

Name: 4-hydroxypentan-2-one.

Example 2.3: From name to structure

Draw 3-chloro-2-methylbutanoic acid.

The parent is butanoic acid, four carbons with C1 as the COOH carbon: HOOC–C2–C3–C4. Put a methyl on C2 and a chlorine on C3, then fill in hydrogens so that each carbon has four bonds: HOOC–CH(CH₃)–CHCl–CH₃.

docs.title: 2.5 Benzene derivatives
docs.text:
Compounds that contain a benzene ring are named as substituted benzenes: chlorobenzene, nitrobenzene, ethylbenzene. Several have common names that IUPAC accepts and that you will meet constantly:

Structure Common name Systematic name C₆H₅–CH₃ toluene methylbenzene C₆H₅–OH phenol phenol (benzenol) C₆H₅–NH₂ aniline aniline (benzenamine) C₆H₅–COOH benzoic acid benzoic acid (benzenecarboxylic acid) C₆H₅–CHO benzaldehyde benzaldehyde (benzenecarbaldehyde)

Table 2.4. Common benzene derivatives. In each, C₆H₅– is a benzene ring that has lost one hydrogen.

With two substituents, their positions are given by numbers (1,2-, 1,3-, 1,4-) or by the older prefixes ortho- (o-, 1,2), meta- (m-, 1,3) and para- (p-, 1,4). So 1,4-dimethylbenzene is p-xylene, and 2-nitrophenol is o-nitrophenol. When the ring carries a group with a common name, that carbon is C1: 3-bromotoluene has the bromine meta to the methyl.

As a substituent, C₆H₅– is the phenyl group (often written Ph), and C₆H₅CH₂– is the benzyl group. A general aromatic group is written Ar.

docs.title: 2.6 Molecular formula and degree of unsaturation
docs.text:
Before you have a structure, the molecular formula already tells you something. An acyclic alkane has the formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. Each ring or π bond removes two hydrogens. The number of rings plus π bonds is the degree of unsaturation (also called the double-bond equivalent, DBE):

\[ \text{DBE} = \frac{2C + 2 + N - H - X}{2} \]

where \(C\), \(H\), \(N\) and \(X\) are the numbers of carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen and halogen atoms. Oxygen and sulfur do not appear: adding them does not change the number of hydrogens needed.

Example 2.4: Using the degree of unsaturation

Benzene, C₆H₆. DBE = (12 + 2 − 6)/2 = 4: one ring and three π bonds.

C₄H₈O. DBE = (8 + 2 − 8)/2 = 1. The molecule has one ring or one π bond. Possible structures include butanal and butanone (a C=O), but-3-en-1-ol (a C=C) and oxolane, the five-membered cyclic ether (a ring).

C₃H₆Cl₂. DBE = (6 + 2 − 6 − 2)/2 = 0. No rings and no π bonds: a dichloropropane.

Key idea

A DBE of 4 or more in a compound with six or more carbons often signals a benzene ring. This is a useful first guess when you meet an unknown compound in spectroscopy (Chapter 14).

docs.title: 2.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • A functional group is the reactive part of a molecule; compounds with the same group form a family with similar chemistry.
  • Carbons are 1°, 2°, 3° or 4° according to the number of carbons attached. Alcohols and haloalkanes take the class of the carbon carrying the group; amines are classed by the number of carbons on nitrogen.
  • An IUPAC name is prefix (substituents, alphabetical) + parent (longest chain or ring) + suffix (principal group).
  • Number the chain to give the lowest locants: first to the principal group, then to multiple bonds, then to substituents.
  • Priority for the suffix: acid > ester > acyl chloride > amide > nitrile > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine.
  • Esters are named "alkyl alkanoate", with the group on oxygen first.
  • Disubstituted benzenes use 1,2-/1,3-/1,4- or ortho/meta/para.
  • DBE = (2C + 2 + N − H − X)/2 gives the number of rings plus π bonds.

docs.title: 2.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Identify every functional group in the following molecule, written in condensed form: HOCH₂CH₂COOCH₂CH=CH₂.

Answer

An alcohol (the HOCH₂ group at the left), an ester (–COO– linking the two halves) and an alkene (CH=CH₂ at the right). The ester has the highest priority: the compound is prop-2-en-1-yl 3-hydroxypropanoate (allyl 3-hydroxypropanoate).

Exercise 2

Classify as primary, secondary or tertiary: (a) butan-2-ol; (b) 2-bromo-2-methylpropane; (c) N-methylethanamine; (d) 1-chlorobutane.

Answer

(a) Secondary alcohol: the OH carbon is bonded to two other carbons. (b) Tertiary haloalkane: the carbon carrying Br is bonded to three carbons. (c) Secondary amine: the nitrogen carries two carbon groups (methyl and ethyl). (d) Primary haloalkane.

Exercise 3

Name: (a) CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃; (b) CH₃CH₂C(CH₃)₂CH₂CH(CH₂CH₃)CH₃.

Answer

(a) Longest chain: five carbons, with methyls on C2 and C3 (numbering from the left gives 2,3; from the right, 3,4). Name: 2,3-dimethylpentane.

(b) Find the longest chain carefully. Starting at the left CH₃, the chain runs CH₃CH₂–C–CH₂–CH–, and the CH carries both an ethyl group and a methyl. Continuing into the ethyl group gives a longer chain: CH₃CH₂–C(CH₃)₂–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–CH₂CH₃, seven carbons, heptane. Substituents: two methyls on one carbon and one methyl on another. Numbering from the left gives 3,3,5; from the right, 3,5,5. So 3,3,5-trimethylheptane.

Exercise 4

Draw structures for: (a) pent-2-yne; (b) 2-methylbutan-2-ol; (c) 3-methylbutanal; (d) propyl ethanoate; (e) N,N-dimethylethanamide.

Answer

(a) CH₃C≡CCH₂CH₃. (b) CH₃C(OH)(CH₃)CH₂CH₃, a tertiary alcohol. (c) (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CHO. (d) CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₃: the ethanoate part is CH₃CO–, the propyl group is on oxygen. (e) CH₃CON(CH₃)₂: both methyls are on the nitrogen of ethanamide.

Exercise 5

Each name below breaks a rule. Say which rule, and give the correct name: (a) 2-ethylpropane; (b) 2-methylbut-3-ene; (c) 1,5-dimethylcyclohexane.

Answer

(a) The parent is not the longest chain. CH₃–CH(CH₂CH₃)–CH₃ contains a chain of four carbons (through the ethyl group) with a methyl on C2. Correct name: 2-methylbutane.

(b) The chain is numbered from the wrong end. The structure is CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH=CH₂; the double bond must have the lowest locant, so C1 is the CH₂= carbon. Correct name: 3-methylbut-1-ene.

(c) The locants are not the lowest possible. Starting at one methyl and going the short way round the ring, the other is at position 3. Correct name: 1,3-dimethylcyclohexane.

Exercise 6

Name: (a) the benzene ring with Cl and NO₂ on adjacent carbons; (b) 4-methylphenol written with o/m/p; (c) C₆H₅CH₂OH.

Answer

(a) 1-chloro-2-nitrobenzene (o-chloronitrobenzene); the substituents are numbered alphabetically, chloro before nitro. (b) p-methylphenol (p-cresol). (c) Phenylmethanol, usually called benzyl alcohol.

Exercise 7

Calculate the degree of unsaturation of (a) C₅H₈; (b) C₇H₇Br; (c) C₄H₉N; (d) C₈H₁₀. Suggest one possible structure for each.

Answer

(a) (10 + 2 − 8)/2 = 2: for example penta-1,3-diene, pent-1-yne or cyclopentene. (b) (14 + 2 − 7 − 1)/2 = 4: for example 4-bromotoluene (a benzene ring). (c) (8 + 2 + 1 − 9)/2 = 1: for example pyrrolidine (a ring) or but-3-en-1-amine. (d) (16 + 2 − 10)/2 = 4: for example ethylbenzene or one of the dimethylbenzenes.

docs.title: 2.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your naming skills

Exercise 1

Which family does CH₃CH₂COOCH₃ belong to?

  1. ketone
  2. ether
  3. ester
  4. carboxylic acid
Answer

ester

Exercise 2

Give the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO.

Answer

butanal

Exercise 3

Give the IUPAC name of CH₃COCH₂CH₃.

Answer

butanone / butan-2-one

Exercise 4

Which group has the highest priority as the suffix of a name?

  1. alcohol
  2. ketone
  3. aldehyde
  4. carboxylic acid
Answer

carboxylic acid

Exercise 5

(CH₃)₃COH is

  1. a primary alcohol
  2. a secondary alcohol
  3. a tertiary alcohol
  4. an ether
Answer

a tertiary alcohol

Exercise 6

What is the degree of unsaturation of C₆H₁₂?

Answer

1 / one

(12 + 2 - 12)/2 = 1: one ring (cyclohexane) or one double bond (a hexene).

Exercise 7

Match each common name to its systematic name.

ABacetonemethylbenzeneacetic acidethyl ethanoatetoluenepropanoneethyl acetateethanoic acid Answer

acetone — propanone; acetic acid — ethanoic acid; toluene — methylbenzene; ethyl acetate — ethyl ethanoate

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Standard books and sources for going further

docs.title: General textbooks
docs.text:
These comprehensive textbooks cover the whole of this book in more depth, with many more examples and problems. Any recent edition is suitable.

  • J. Clayden, N. Greeves and S. Warren, Organic Chemistry, Oxford University Press. Builds the subject from mechanisms and is especially strong on why reactions happen.
  • P. Y. Bruice, Organic Chemistry, Pearson.
  • J. McMurry, Organic Chemistry, Cengage Learning.
  • K. P. C. Vollhardt and N. E. Schore, Organic Chemistry: Structure and Function, W. H. Freeman.
  • L. G. Wade and J. W. Simek, Organic Chemistry, Pearson.
  • D. R. Klein, Organic Chemistry, Wiley.

docs.title: Mechanisms and stereochemistry
docs.text:
• P. Sykes, A Guidebook to Mechanism in Organic Chemistry, Longman. A classic, compact account of reaction mechanisms.
  • E. L. Eliel and S. H. Wilen, Stereochemistry of Organic Compounds, Wiley. The standard advanced reference on stereochemistry and conformational analysis.

docs.title: Spectroscopy
docs.text:
• D. L. Pavia, G. M. Lampman, G. S. Kriz and J. R. Vyvyan, Introduction to Spectroscopy, Cengage Learning. A clear introduction to IR, NMR, UV and mass spectrometry with many worked problems.
  • D. H. Williams and I. Fleming, Spectroscopic Methods in Organic Chemistry, McGraw-Hill (later editions Springer). Concise, with extensive tables of data.

docs.title: Nomenclature
docs.text: • International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry, Nomenclature of Organic Chemistry: IUPAC Recommendations and Preferred Names 2013, Royal Society of Chemistry, 2014. The official rules for naming organic compounds.

docs.title: Practical work and safety
docs.text:
• B. S. Furniss, A. J. Hannaford, P. W. G. Smith and A. R. Tatchell, Vogel's Textbook of Practical Organic Chemistry, 5th edition, Longman, 1989. The classic laboratory reference for techniques and preparations.
  • United Nations, Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals (GHS). The international basis of chemical hazard labels and safety data sheets.

docs.title: Green chemistry
docs.text: • P. T. Anastas and J. C. Warner, Green Chemistry: Theory and Practice, Oxford University Press, 1998. The book that set out the twelve principles.

docs.title: Biomolecules
docs.text: • J. M. Berg, J. L. Tymoczko and L. Stryer, Biochemistry, W. H. Freeman. For the structures and roles of carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids in much greater depth.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Key terms used in this book

docs.title: A–C
docs.text: Acetal A compound with two OR groups on the same carbon, formed from an aldehyde or ketone and two molecules of alcohol with an acid catalyst. Used to protect carbonyl groups (Chapter 11). Activation energy The energy difference between the reactants and the transition state of a reaction step; the barrier that must be crossed for the reaction to occur. Acyl group The group R–C=O. Acyl chlorides, anhydrides, esters and amides are acyl compounds. Addition reaction A reaction in which two reactants combine to form a single product, as when HBr adds to an alkene. Alkoxide The conjugate base of an alcohol, RO⁻; a strong base and good nucleophile. Anomer One of the two stereoisomers of a cyclic sugar that differ only in the configuration at the anomeric carbon (C1 of an aldose); α and β. Anti addition Addition of two groups to opposite faces of a double bond, as in the addition of bromine to an alkene. Anti-periplanar An arrangement in which two groups on adjacent carbons lie in the same plane on opposite sides of the C–C bond (dihedral angle 180°). Required in E2 eliminations. Arenium ion The resonance-stabilised carbocation formed when an electrophile adds to a benzene ring; the intermediate of electrophilic aromatic substitution. Also called a σ complex. Aromatic Describes a cyclic, planar, fully conjugated system with 4n + 2 π electrons, which has special stability (Hückel's rule). Atom economy The molar mass of the desired product as a percentage of the total molar mass of all reactants in the balanced equation. Axial In the chair conformation of cyclohexane, a bond parallel to the axis of the ring, pointing straight up or down. Base peak The most intense peak in a mass spectrum, assigned a relative abundance of 100. Bromonium ion A cyclic ion with a positively charged bromine bridging two carbons; the intermediate in the addition of bromine to alkenes. Carbanion A species with a negatively charged carbon that has three bonds and a lone pair. Carbocation A species with a positively charged carbon that has three bonds and an empty p orbital; stability increases from methyl to tertiary. Chemical shift The position of an NMR signal, δ, in parts per million relative to tetramethylsilane. Chiral Not superimposable on its mirror image. Condensation polymer A polymer formed from monomers with two functional groups each, with loss of a small molecule (usually water) at each link; polyesters and polyamides. Conformation One of the shapes a molecule can adopt by rotation about single bonds. Conformations interconvert rapidly and are not isomers. Conjugate acid and base A pair of species that differ by one proton; when an acid loses a proton it becomes its conjugate base. Constitutional isomers Isomers that differ in the order in which their atoms are connected. Curly arrow An arrow showing the movement of a pair of electrons from a lone pair or bond (the tail) to an atom or new bond position (the head). A fish-hook arrow shows one electron.

docs.title: D–H
docs.text: Degree of unsaturation The number of rings plus π bonds in a molecule, calculated from the molecular formula as (2C + 2 + N − H − X)/2. Also called double-bond equivalent. Diastereomers Stereoisomers that are not mirror images of each other. E/Z Descriptors for the configuration of a double bond: Z when the higher-priority groups (by the CIP rules) are on the same side, E when they are on opposite sides. E1 and E2 Elimination mechanisms: E1 is unimolecular, through a carbocation; E2 is bimolecular and concerted, with the H and leaving group anti-periplanar. Electronegativity The tendency of an atom in a molecule to attract the electrons of a bond. Electrophile A species that accepts a pair of electrons to form a new bond; a Lewis acid. Elimination reaction A reaction in which atoms or groups are removed from adjacent carbons to form a multiple bond. Enantiomers Stereoisomers that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other. Enol A tautomer of a carbonyl compound with an OH group on a carbon of a C=C double bond. Enolate ion The resonance-stabilised anion formed by removing an α-hydrogen from a carbonyl compound; nucleophilic at the α-carbon. Equatorial In the chair conformation of cyclohexane, a bond pointing outwards from the ring, roughly in its mean plane. Formal charge The charge assigned to an atom in a Lewis structure, calculated as valence electrons minus non-bonding electrons minus half the bonding electrons. Functional group A specific arrangement of atoms in a molecule that is responsible for its characteristic reactions. Glycosidic bond The acetal link joining the anomeric carbon of one sugar to an oxygen of another. Grignard reagent An organomagnesium halide, RMgX, which behaves as a carbon nucleophile and strong base. Hemiacetal A compound with an OH and an OR group on the same carbon, formed by adding one molecule of alcohol to an aldehyde or ketone. Heterolysis Breaking of a covalent bond in which one atom takes both electrons, giving ions. Homolysis Breaking of a covalent bond in which each atom takes one electron, giving radicals. Hybridisation The mixing of atomic orbitals on one atom to form hybrid orbitals (sp³, sp², sp) that point in the directions of bonds. Hydrogen bond An attraction between a hydrogen bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on another N, O or F atom. Hyperconjugation Stabilisation of a carbocation or radical by overlap of neighbouring C–H or C–C σ bonds with the empty or half-filled p orbital.

docs.title: I–N
docs.text: Inductive effect The polarisation of σ bonds by an electronegative atom or group, transmitted along a chain and falling off with distance. Intermediate A species formed in one step of a reaction and consumed in a later step, lying in an energy minimum on the reaction profile. Isoelectric point The pH at which an amino acid or protein carries no net charge. Ka and pKa The acid dissociation constant and its negative logarithm; a lower pKa means a stronger acid. Leaving group The atom or group that departs with the bonding electron pair in a substitution or elimination; good leaving groups are weak bases. Lewis acid and base An electron-pair acceptor and an electron-pair donor. Markovnikov's rule In electrophilic addition to an unsymmetrical alkene, the electrophile adds so as to form the more stable carbocation; for HX, the hydrogen adds to the carbon that already has more hydrogens. Mechanism A step-by-step description of a reaction in terms of the movement of electrons and the making and breaking of bonds. Meso compound A compound that has stereocentres but is achiral because of an internal plane of symmetry. Molecular ion The radical cation, M⁺•, formed by removing one electron from a molecule in a mass spectrometer; its m/z gives the molar mass. n + 1 rule In ¹H NMR, a signal from hydrogens with n equivalent neighbouring hydrogens is split into n + 1 lines. Newman projection A drawing of a molecule viewed along a C–C bond, with the front carbon as a point and the back carbon as a circle. Nucleophile A species that donates a pair of electrons to form a new bond to an electron-poor atom, usually carbon; a Lewis base. Nucleophilic acyl substitution The replacement of a leaving group on an acyl carbon by a nucleophile, by addition to give a tetrahedral intermediate followed by elimination.

docs.title: O–R
docs.text: Optical activity The rotation of the plane of plane-polarised light by a chiral substance. Oxidation (organic) An increase in the number of bonds from carbon to more electronegative atoms (O, N, halogens) or a decrease in the number of bonds to hydrogen. Peptide bond The amide link between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of another. Pi (π) bond A bond formed by sideways overlap of p orbitals, with electron density above and below the line joining the nuclei. Polar aprotic solvent A polar solvent without O–H or N–H bonds, such as DMSO or propanone, which speeds SN2 reactions of anions. Polymer A macromolecule made of many repeating monomer units. R/S Descriptors for the configuration of a stereocentre, assigned by ranking the groups with the CIP rules and viewing with the lowest priority away: clockwise is R, anticlockwise S. Racemic mixture A 50:50 mixture of two enantiomers, which is optically inactive. Radical A species with an unpaired electron. Rate-determining step The step of a multistep reaction with the highest-energy transition state, which controls the overall rate. Rearrangement A reaction in which the carbon skeleton or the position of a group changes, such as a hydride or methyl shift in a carbocation. Reduction (organic) An increase in the number of bonds from carbon to hydrogen or a decrease in the number of bonds to more electronegative atoms. Regioselective Describes a reaction that could give two or more constitutional isomers but gives mainly one. Resonance The description of a molecule whose electrons are delocalised by two or more Lewis structures (contributors) that differ only in the positions of electrons; the real molecule is the hybrid. Retention factor (Rf) In chromatography, the distance moved by a spot divided by the distance moved by the solvent front.

docs.title: S–Z
docs.text: Saponification Hydrolysis of an ester by aqueous base, giving a carboxylate salt and an alcohol; used to make soap from fats. Sigma (σ) bond A bond formed by head-on overlap of orbitals, with electron density concentrated along the line joining the nuclei. Skeletal formula A drawing in which carbon atoms are vertices and line ends, hydrogens on carbon are omitted, and other atoms are written in. SN1 and SN2 Nucleophilic substitution mechanisms: SN1 is unimolecular, through a carbocation, with racemisation; SN2 is bimolecular and concerted, with backside attack and inversion. Stereocentre An atom (usually carbon with four different groups) at which interchanging two groups gives a stereoisomer. Stereoisomers Isomers with the same connectivity that differ in the arrangement of their atoms in space. Stereospecific Describes a reaction in which different stereoisomers of the reactant give different stereoisomers of the product. Substitution reaction A reaction in which one atom or group replaces another. Syn addition Addition of two groups to the same face of a double bond, as in catalytic hydrogenation. Tautomers Constitutional isomers that interconvert rapidly by movement of a hydrogen atom and a double bond, such as keto and enol forms. Torsional strain The extra energy of a conformation in which bonds on adjacent atoms are eclipsed. Transition state The arrangement of highest energy on the path of a reaction step, with bonds partly made and partly broken; it cannot be isolated. Zaitsev's rule In eliminations, the more substituted (more stable) alkene is usually the main product. Zwitterion A neutral molecule carrying both a positive and a negative charge, such as an amino acid near neutral pH.

docs.title: Chapter 3: Isomerism and Stereochemistry
docs.text:
Same formula, different molecules

Two compounds can have exactly the same molecular formula and still be different substances, with different boiling points, smells, reactions and effects on the body. Such compounds are isomers. Some isomers differ in which atoms are bonded to which; others have the same connections but a different arrangement in space. The second kind, stereoisomers, can be as subtle as a left hand and a right hand, yet living things tell them apart with great precision. This chapter sorts the kinds of isomerism, shows how to recognise chiral molecules, and teaches the Cahn–Ingold–Prelog rules for naming alkene isomers (E/Z) and stereocentres (R/S).

Learning outcomes

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  • classify a pair of isomers as constitutional isomers, enantiomers or diastereomers;
  • explain why some alkenes have E/Z isomers and assign E or Z using the CIP priority rules;
  • recognise stereocentres and chiral molecules, and use symmetry to spot achiral ones;
  • assign R or S to a stereocentre drawn with wedges and hashes or as a Fischer projection;
  • work out the maximum number of stereoisomers and recognise meso compounds;
  • describe optical activity and racemic mixtures, and explain why chirality matters in biology and medicine.

docs.title: 3.1 Kinds of isomerism
docs.text:
Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures. They fall into two main classes.

Constitutional isomers (structural isomers) differ in the order in which atoms are connected. They may differ in the carbon skeleton (butane and 2-methylpropane, both C₄H₁₀), in the position of a functional group (propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol), or in the functional group itself (ethanol and methoxymethane, both C₂H₆O). Constitutional isomers are simply different compounds with different names.

Stereoisomers have the same connections, atom to atom, but a different arrangement of the atoms in space. They are of two kinds:

  • Enantiomers are stereoisomers that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other.
  • Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images. Cis and trans alkenes are diastereomers, and so are many molecules with two or more stereocentres.
flowchart TD
    I[Isomers: same molecular formula] --> C[Constitutional isomers: different connectivity]
    I --> S[Stereoisomers: same connectivity, different arrangement in space]
    S --> E[Enantiomers: non-superimposable mirror images]
    S --> D[Diastereomers: not mirror images]
    D --> EZ[E/Z isomers of alkenes and rings]
    D --> M[Compounds with two or more stereocentres]
Figure 3.1 The family tree of isomers. Isomers divide first by connectivity, then, for stereoisomers, by whether they are mirror images.

A third kind of difference is not isomerism at all. Conformations are the shapes a single molecule takes as it rotates about its single bonds (Chapter 6). Different conformations interconvert millions of times a second at room temperature and cannot be separated. Stereoisomers, by contrast, can be interconverted only by breaking bonds; they are different compounds that can be isolated and stored.

docs.title: 3.2 E/Z isomerism in alkenes
docs.text:
Rotation about a C=C double bond would break the π bond (Section 1.5), so the groups on a double bond are fixed in place. When each carbon of the double bond carries two different groups, the molecule can exist in two forms. In but-2-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₃, the two methyl groups can be on the same side of the double bond (cis) or on opposite sides (trans). These are diastereomers: cis-but-2-ene boils at about 4 °C and trans-but-2-ene at about 1 °C.

If either carbon of the double bond carries two identical groups, there is no isomerism. But-1-ene, CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃, has two hydrogens on C1, and swapping the "sides" gives the same molecule.

The words cis and trans work well when each carbon carries one hydrogen, but become ambiguous when there are three or four different groups. The general method is the E/Z system, based on the Cahn–Ingold–Prelog (CIP) priority rules.

docs.title: The CIP priority rules
docs.text:
At each carbon of the double bond, rank the two attached groups:

  1. Higher atomic number of the atom directly attached gives higher priority. So Br > Cl > O > N > C > H. (For isotopes, the heavier one wins: D > H.)
  2. If the attached atoms are the same, move outwards one bond at a time. List the atoms attached to each and compare them in order of decreasing atomic number, at the first point of difference. For example, –CH₂OH has the set (O, H, H) and –CH(CH₃)₂ has (C, C, H). Compare the highest first: O beats C, so –CH₂OH wins, even though the isopropyl group has more carbons.
  3. Multiple bonds count as duplicated atoms. A C=O carbon is treated as if it carried two oxygens, and a C≡N carbon as if it carried three nitrogens. So –CHO has the set (O, O, H) and outranks –CH₂OH (O, H, H).

Then:

  • If the two higher-priority groups are on the same side of the double bond, the isomer is Z (from German zusammen, together).
  • If they are on opposite sides, it is E (entgegen, opposite).
Figure 3.2 E and Z isomers. E/Z isomers. In (Z)-but-2-ene the two methyl groups, the higher-priority group on each carbon, are on the same side; in (E)-but-2-ene they are on opposite sides. In 1-bromo-1-chloroprop-1-ene, Br outranks Cl on the left carbon and CH₃ outranks H on the right; with Br and CH₃ on the same side the isomer is Z.

Example 3.1: Assigning E or Z

Assign E or Z to the isomer of 3-methylpent-2-ene, CH₃CH=C(CH₃)CH₂CH₃, in which the hydrogen on C2 and the ethyl group on C3 are on the same side.

C2 carries CH₃ and H. CH₃ wins (C > H).

C3 carries CH₃ and CH₂CH₃. Both attach through carbon. Move outwards: CH₃ has (H, H, H) and CH₂CH₃ has (C, H, H). At the first point of difference C > H, so ethyl wins.

The ethyl group is on the same side as the H of C2, so it is on the opposite side to the CH₃ of C2. The two higher-priority groups are on opposite sides: (E)-3-methylpent-2-ene.

Caution: Z is not always cis

Cis and trans describe particular groups (usually the main chain); Z and E describe the highest-priority groups. They often agree, but not always. In 2-bromobut-2-ene, CH₃CBr=CHCH₃, take the isomer in which the two methyl groups (C1 and C4, the main chain) are on the same side. On C2, Br outranks CH₃, and Br is on the opposite side to the C4 methyl, which is the higher group on C3. So the chain is cis, but the isomer is (E)-2-bromobut-2-ene. Use E/Z in names.

Rings show a similar isomerism. In 1,2-dimethylcyclohexane the two methyl groups can be on the same face of the ring (cis) or on opposite faces (trans). The ring cannot turn inside out by rotation without breaking bonds, so the two are diastereomers.

docs.title: 3.3 Chirality
docs.text:
Hold your hands up, palm to palm. They are mirror images, but you cannot lay one exactly on top of the other: a left glove does not fit a right hand. An object that cannot be superimposed on its mirror image is chiral (from the Greek for hand). An object that can be superimposed on its mirror image, such as a plain mug or a sphere, is achiral.

Molecules can be chiral too. The commonest cause is a carbon atom bonded to four different groups. Such an atom is a stereocentre (also called a stereogenic centre, chiral centre or asymmetric carbon), and is often marked with an asterisk. Butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃, has one: C2 carries H, OH, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃. Its mirror image cannot be superimposed on it, however it is turned.

Figure 3.3 A pair of enantiomers. The enantiomers of butan-2-ol. The two molecules are reflections of each other in the dashed mirror. No rotation will make the left-hand molecule identical with the right-hand one: they are a pair of enantiomers.

docs.title: Symmetry: a quick test
docs.text:
A molecule that has a plane of symmetry, a plane that cuts it into two halves that are mirror images of each other, is achiral. Propan-2-ol, (CH₃)₂CHOH, has two identical methyl groups on the central carbon. A plane through C, O and H divides the molecule into mirror-image halves, so it is achiral, and C2 is not a stereocentre.

To find stereocentres quickly:

  • Ignore CH₂ and CH₃ carbons (two or more identical H atoms) and any sp² or sp carbon (only three or two groups).
  • For each remaining carbon, check whether all four groups are different. Look along each branch until you find a difference: in 3-methylhexane, C3 carries H, CH₃, CH₂CH₃ and CH₂CH₂CH₃, which are four different groups.

Key idea

A molecule with exactly one stereocentre is always chiral. A molecule with two or more stereocentres is usually chiral, but may be achiral if it has an internal plane of symmetry (a meso compound, Section 3.6). The fundamental test is always non-superimposability on the mirror image.

docs.title: 3.4 Naming stereocentres: R and S
docs.text:
Each stereocentre has one of two configurations, labelled R (rectus, right) or S (sinister, left). The procedure uses the same CIP priority rules as for E/Z.

  1. Rank the four groups on the stereocentre from 1 (highest) to 4 (lowest) by the CIP rules.
  2. Orient the molecule so that the lowest-priority group (4) points away from you, behind the page.
  3. Trace the path 1 → 2 → 3. If it runs clockwise, the centre is R; if anticlockwise, it is S.
Figure 3.4 Assigning R or S. Assigning the configuration of butan-2-ol. The groups are ranked OH (1) > CH₂CH₃ (2) > CH₃ (3) > H (4). With H on a hashed wedge, pointing away, the path from 1 to 2 to 3 runs clockwise, so this enantiomer is (R)-butan-2-ol. Think of the molecule as a steering wheel seen by a driver, with the lowest-priority group as the steering column pointing away.

docs.title: Short cuts for drawings
docs.text:
You rarely need to build a model. Two rules handle most drawings:

  • Lowest priority on a hashed wedge (pointing away): read the direction of 1 → 2 → 3 directly from the page.
  • Lowest priority on a solid wedge (pointing towards you): read the direction, then reverse it. Clockwise on the page means S.
  • Lowest priority in the plane of the page: swap it with the group on the hashed wedge. Swapping any two groups inverts the configuration, so assign the new drawing and then reverse your answer.

Example 3.2: Assigning R or S

A drawing of 2-chlorobutane shows C2 with Cl at the top (in the plane), CH₂CH₃ to the lower left (in the plane), CH₃ on a hashed wedge to the lower right and H on a solid wedge to the right. Assign the configuration.

Priorities: Cl (1) > CH₂CH₃ (2) > CH₃ (3) > H (4).

The path Cl (top) → ethyl (lower left) → methyl (lower right): going from top to lower left is anticlockwise, and continuing to the lower right completes an anticlockwise turn. H is on a solid wedge, pointing towards you, so reverse: the true direction is clockwise.

The centre is R: (R)-2-chlorobutane.

Example 3.3: Ranking harder groups

Rank the groups on C2 of 2-hydroxypropanoic acid (lactic acid), CH₃CH(OH)COOH.

The attached atoms are O (of OH), C (of COOH), C (of CH₃) and H. OH is 1 and H is 4. To separate the two carbons, list their substituents: COOH has (O, O, O), counting the C=O oxygen twice, and CH₃ has (H, H, H). So COOH is 2 and CH₃ is 3.

Caution: R/S says nothing about the sign of rotation

R and S are labels from a drawing rule. They do not tell you which way the compound rotates plane-polarised light (Section 3.5). Some R compounds rotate light clockwise and others anticlockwise; the sign must be measured.

docs.title: 3.5 Properties of enantiomers: optical activity
docs.text:
Enantiomers have identical physical properties in an achiral environment: the same melting point, boiling point, density, solubility and spectra. They react at the same rate with achiral reagents. They differ in only two ways:

  1. They rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions. Light whose waves vibrate in a single plane is passed through a solution of the compound in an instrument called a polarimeter. A chiral compound turns the plane by an angle α. One enantiomer turns it clockwise, called dextrorotatory and labelled (+); the other turns it by the same amount anticlockwise, laevorotatory, (−). Because they rotate light, chiral compounds are said to be optically active.
  2. They interact differently with other chiral things, including chiral reagents, chiral catalysts and the enzymes and receptors of living things.

The observed rotation depends on the concentration and the path length, so it is converted into the specific rotation, a property of the compound:

\[ [\alpha] = \frac{\alpha}{l \, c} \]

where \(\alpha\) is the observed rotation in degrees, \(l\) the path length in decimetres and \(c\) the concentration in g mL⁻¹. The temperature and the wavelength of light (usually the sodium D line) are stated with the value.

A 50:50 mixture of two enantiomers is a racemic mixture (or racemate). Its rotation is zero, because the two contributions cancel exactly. A reaction that makes a stereocentre from achiral starting materials, without any chiral influence, always gives a racemic mixture: there is an equal chance of forming each enantiomer. The enantiomeric excess (ee) of a mixture is the excess of one enantiomer over the other, as a percentage of the whole: a mixture of 75% R and 25% S has an ee of 50%.

docs.title: Why chirality matters
docs.text: Enzymes and receptors are built from chiral amino acids and are themselves chiral. They distinguish enantiomers as a right hand distinguishes a right glove from a left. The two enantiomers of carvone smell different: (R)-carvone smells of spearmint and (S)-carvone of caraway seed. Almost all the amino acids in proteins have the same configuration, and almost all natural sugars belong to one series. In medicine, the two enantiomers of a chiral drug can have different activities, different side effects or both, which is why drug regulators require the enantiomers of a new chiral drug to be studied separately. The thalidomide tragedy of the late 1950s and early 1960s made this concern widely known; in that case the enantiomers also interconvert in the body, so even a single pure enantiomer would not have been safe.

docs.title: 3.6 Molecules with more than one stereocentre
docs.text:
Each stereocentre can be R or S, so a molecule with \(n\) stereocentres has at most \(2^n\) stereoisomers. With two stereocentres there are up to four: (R,R), (S,S), (R,S) and (S,R).

  • (R,R) and (S,S) are mirror images: a pair of enantiomers.
  • (R,S) and (S,R) are mirror images: another pair of enantiomers.
  • (R,R) and (R,S) are stereoisomers that are not mirror images: diastereomers.

Unlike enantiomers, diastereomers have different physical properties (melting point, solubility, boiling point), so they can be separated by ordinary methods such as crystallisation, distillation and chromatography.

docs.title: Fischer projections
docs.text:
For molecules with several stereocentres in a chain, such as sugars, chemists often use Fischer projections. The carbon chain is drawn vertically, with the most oxidised carbon at the top. At each stereocentre, the horizontal bonds point towards you and the vertical bonds point away. A Fischer projection may be rotated by 180° in the plane of the page but not by 90°, which would turn horizontal bonds into vertical ones and invert every centre.

To assign R or S in a Fischer projection: if the lowest-priority group is on a vertical bond (pointing away), read 1 → 2 → 3 directly; if it is on a horizontal bond (pointing towards you), as it usually is, read the direction and reverse it.

docs.title: Meso compounds
docs.text:
Tartaric acid, HOOC–CH(OH)–CH(OH)–COOH, has two stereocentres, so up to four stereoisomers are possible, but only three exist. The (2R,3R) and (2S,3S) forms are enantiomers. The (2R,3S) form has an internal plane of symmetry, a mirror plane between C2 and C3, so it is identical with its own mirror image (2S,3R). A compound that has stereocentres but is achiral because of internal symmetry is a meso compound. Meso-tartaric acid is optically inactive, and it is a diastereomer of the other two.

Figure 3.5 The stereoisomers of tartaric acid. Fischer projections of tartaric acid. Horizontal bonds point towards the viewer and vertical bonds away. The (2R,3R) and (2S,3S) forms are non-superimposable mirror images. The (2R,3S) form has a mirror plane (dashed) between the two stereocentres and is the achiral meso form.

Example 3.4: Counting stereoisomers

How many stereoisomers does 2,3-dibromobutane, CH₃CHBrCHBrCH₃, have?

There are two stereocentres (C2 and C3), so at most four. But the molecule is symmetrical: both centres carry the same set of groups (H, Br, CH₃ and the other CHBr unit). As with tartaric acid, the (2R,3S) form has a mirror plane and is meso. So there are three stereoisomers: the enantiomers (2R,3R) and (2S,3S), and meso-(2R,3S).

By contrast, 2-bromo-3-chlorobutane, CH₃CHBrCHClCH₃, is not symmetrical and has all four stereoisomers.

docs.title: Separating enantiomers
docs.text: Because enantiomers have identical physical properties, separating a racemic mixture (called resolution) needs a chiral influence. The classic method reacts the mixture with a single enantiomer of a chiral compound, turning the two enantiomers into two diastereomers. These have different solubilities and can be separated by crystallisation, then converted back. Louis Pasteur achieved the first resolution in 1848 by a rarer route: he noticed that crystals of a salt of racemic tartaric acid came in two mirror-image shapes and separated them by hand. Today chiral chromatography and enzymes are widely used as well.

docs.title: 3.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Constitutional isomers differ in connectivity; stereoisomers differ only in arrangement in space.
  • Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images; diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images.
  • Alkenes with two different groups on each carbon of the C=C show E/Z isomerism. Rank the groups by the CIP rules: Z if the higher-priority groups are on the same side, E if opposite.
  • A carbon with four different groups is a stereocentre. A molecule with a plane of symmetry is achiral.
  • R/S: rank 1 to 4, point 4 away, trace 1 → 2 → 3; clockwise is R, anticlockwise is S. If group 4 points towards you, reverse.
  • Enantiomers have identical properties except the direction in which they rotate plane-polarised light and their interactions with other chiral substances. A racemic mixture is optically inactive.
  • \(n\) stereocentres give at most \(2^n\) stereoisomers; meso compounds reduce the number.

docs.title: 3.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Classify each pair as constitutional isomers, enantiomers, diastereomers or identical: (a) butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol; (b) (R)-butan-2-ol and (S)-butan-2-ol; (c) (Z)-but-2-ene and (E)-but-2-ene; (d) (2R,3R)- and (2R,3S)-2-bromo-3-chlorobutane; (e) (2R,3S)- and (2S,3R)-tartaric acid.

Answer

(a) Constitutional isomers (the OH is in a different position). (b) Enantiomers. (c) Diastereomers. (d) Diastereomers: one centre is the same, the other differs, so they are not mirror images. (e) Identical: this is the meso compound, which is its own mirror image.

Exercise 2

Which of these can show E/Z isomerism? (a) pent-1-ene; (b) pent-2-ene; (c) 2-methylbut-2-ene; (d) 1-chloropropene, ClCH=CHCH₃.

Answer

(a) No: C1 carries two H atoms. (b) Yes: C2 carries CH₃ and H, C3 carries CH₂CH₃ and H. (c) No: C2 carries two CH₃ groups. (d) Yes: C1 carries Cl and H, C2 carries CH₃ and H.

Exercise 3

Rank the following groups by CIP priority, highest first: –CH₂CH₃, –CH=CH₂, –CH₂OH, –CHO, –CH(CH₃)₂.

Answer

Write the set of atoms attached to the first carbon of each: –CHO (O, O, H); –CH₂OH (O, H, H); –CH(CH₃)₂ (C, C, H); –CH=CH₂ (C, C, H), with the duplicated carbon; –CH₂CH₃ (C, H, H).

–CHO > –CH₂OH > then –CH(CH₃)₂ and –CH=CH₂ tie at the first carbon. Go outwards. For isopropyl, the two branches are CH₃ groups, each (H, H, H). For vinyl, one branch is the real CH₂ carbon, with substituents (C, H, H), the C being the duplicate of the first carbon. The duplicate carbon itself counts as carrying three phantom atoms of atomic number zero. The highest-ranked branch of vinyl, (C, H, H), beats the highest-ranked branch of isopropyl, (H, H, H), so vinyl wins.

Order: –CHO > –CH₂OH > –CH=CH₂ > –CH(CH₃)₂ > –CH₂CH₃.

Exercise 4

Mark the stereocentres, if any, in: (a) 3-methylhexane; (b) 3-methylpentane; (c) 2-chlorobutane; (d) 1,2-dichloroethane; (e) 2-aminopropanoic acid (alanine).

Answer

(a) C3 (H, CH₃, ethyl, propyl): one stereocentre. (b) None: C3 carries two identical ethyl groups. (c) C2 (H, Cl, CH₃, ethyl). (d) None: each carbon carries two H atoms. (e) C2 (H, NH₂, CH₃, COOH).

Exercise 5

In a drawing of alanine, H₂N–CH(CH₃)–COOH, the stereocentre has NH₂ at the top (in the plane), COOH to the lower right (in the plane), CH₃ on a solid wedge to the lower left and H on a hashed wedge. Assign R or S.

Answer

Priorities: NH₂ (1, nitrogen) > COOH (2, carbon with O, O, O) > CH₃ (3) > H (4). H points away, so read directly. NH₂ (top) → COOH (lower right) → CH₃ (lower left) is clockwise. The configuration is R. (The alanine found in proteins is S, the mirror image of this drawing.)

Exercise 6

A solution of a pure enantiomer, 0.10 g mL⁻¹, in a 1.0 dm tube gives an observed rotation of +6.0°. (a) What is its specific rotation? (b) What rotation would a racemic mixture give? (c) A sample of the same compound at the same concentration gives +3.0°. What is its enantiomeric excess, and what percentage of each enantiomer does it contain?

Answer

(a) [α] = 6.0 / (1.0 × 0.10) = +60°. (b) 0°. (c) The rotation is half that of the pure enantiomer, so the ee is 50%. The excess is 50% of the (+) enantiomer and the remaining 50% is racemic (25% of each), giving 75% (+) and 25% (−).

Exercise 7

How many stereoisomers are possible for (a) pentane-2,3-diol, CH₃CH(OH)CH(OH)CH₂CH₃; (b) pentane-2,4-diol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH(OH)CH₃? Identify any meso form.

Answer

(a) Two stereocentres (C2 and C3) carrying different sets of groups, so all four stereoisomers exist: two pairs of enantiomers, and no meso form.

(b) Two stereocentres (C2 and C4) with identical sets of groups. The (2R,4R) and (2S,4S) forms are enantiomers; the (2R,4S) form has a mirror plane through C3 and is meso. Three stereoisomers in all.

docs.title: 3.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of stereochemistry

Exercise 1

Stereoisomers that are not mirror images of each other are called

  1. enantiomers
  2. diastereomers
  3. constitutional isomers
  4. conformations
Answer

diastereomers

Exercise 2

Which compound has a stereocentre?

  1. propan-2-ol
  2. butan-2-ol
  3. 2-methylpropan-2-ol
  4. ethanol
Answer

butan-2-ol

Exercise 3

Viewed with the lowest-priority group pointing away, the path 1 → 2 → 3 is anticlockwise. The configuration is

  1. R
  2. S
  3. E
  4. Z
Answer

S

Exercise 4

Which group has the highest CIP priority?

  1. -CH₃
  2. -CH₂OH
  3. -OH
  4. -NH₂
Answer

-OH

Exercise 5

What is the maximum number of stereoisomers for a molecule with three stereocentres?

Answer

8 / eight

Exercise 6

A racemic mixture

  1. rotates plane-polarised light clockwise
  2. contains equal amounts of two enantiomers and shows no rotation
  3. is a single meso compound
  4. can be separated by simple distillation
Answer

contains equal amounts of two enantiomers and shows no rotation

Exercise 7

Match each term to its meaning.

ABchiralhigher priorities on the same sidemeso50:50 mixture of enantiomersZnot superimposable on its mirror imageracematehas stereocentres but is achiral Answer

chiral — not superimposable on its mirror image; meso — has stereocentres but is achiral; Z — higher priorities on the same side; racemate — 50:50 mixture of enantiomers

docs.title: Chapter 16: Laboratory Safety and Green Chemistry
docs.text:
Working safely, and making chemistry cleaner

Organic chemistry is an experimental science. Every reaction in this book was first carried out by someone at a bench, and every structure was confirmed by experiment. Laboratory work brings real hazards: most organic solvents burn, many reagents are corrosive or toxic, and some reactions release heat or gas quickly. Good practice reduces these risks to a very low level. The same habits of thought that make a laboratory safe, asking what could go wrong and how to prevent it, also underlie green chemistry, the effort to design chemical processes that produce less waste, use less hazardous materials and consume less energy. This chapter covers the principles of safe practice, the standard techniques of a teaching laboratory, the measurement of purity and yield, and the principles and metrics of green chemistry.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  • explain the difference between a hazard and a risk, and outline a risk assessment;
  • interpret hazard pictograms and safety data sheets, and choose appropriate protective measures;
