  • describe the purpose and safe use of the common techniques: heating under reflux, distillation, extraction, drying, recrystallisation, filtration, melting-point determination and thin-layer chromatography;
  • dispose of organic waste correctly;
  • calculate percentage yield, atom economy and E-factor, and distinguish them;
  • state the twelve principles of green chemistry and apply them to compare processes.

docs.title: 16.1 Hazard, risk and risk assessment
docs.text:
Two words are often confused:

  • A hazard is something with the potential to cause harm: a flammable liquid, a corrosive acid, a toxic gas, a hot surface.
  • A risk is the likelihood that harm will actually occur, combined with how severe it would be, in a particular situation.

Ethoxyethane is always a hazard (it is extremely flammable). The risk of using it depends on how much is used, whether there are flames or hot surfaces nearby, and whether the work is done in a fume cupboard. Good practice cannot remove hazards, but it can reduce risks to an acceptable level.

Before any practical work, a risk assessment is made, normally by the person in charge and read by everyone who does the experiment. It:

  1. lists every substance used and produced, and every operation (heating, distilling, filtering under vacuum);
  2. identifies the hazards of each, from the supplier's safety data sheet (SDS);
  3. assesses the risks in the planned procedure;
  4. sets out control measures: using smaller quantities or a less hazardous substitute, working in a fume cupboard, wearing protective equipment;
  5. states what to do in an emergency: spills, fires, splashes on skin or in eyes, and how to dispose of waste.

The most effective controls come first: eliminate the hazard if possible, substitute something less hazardous, use engineering controls (fume cupboards, safety screens), then procedures (training, supervision, small scale), and only lastly personal protective equipment, the last line of defence.

docs.title: Basic rules of the teaching laboratory
docs.text:
• Wear safety spectacles or goggles at all times, and a laboratory coat, fastened. Wear suitable gloves when handling corrosive or toxic substances, chosen for the chemicals in use, and remove them before touching door handles, phones or your face.
  • Never eat, drink or apply cosmetics in the laboratory. Never smell chemicals directly or pipette by mouth.
  • Work in a fume cupboard with volatile, toxic or smelly substances, and keep the sash low.
  • Know where the eyewash station, safety shower, fire extinguishers, fire blanket and exits are, and how to use them.
  • Keep flammable solvents away from flames and hot plates. Many organic solvents have vapours denser than air that can travel along a bench to an ignition source.
  • Label every container with its contents and the main hazard. Never return unused reagent to the stock bottle.
  • Never heat a closed system; pressure can build up until the apparatus bursts.
  • Report every accident, spill and breakage, however small. Never work alone.

docs.title: 16.2 Hazard information
docs.text:
Chemicals are classified and labelled internationally under the Globally Harmonised System (GHS). Each label carries pictograms (a black symbol in a red-bordered diamond), a signal word ("Danger" or "Warning"), hazard statements and precautionary statements. The pictograms are:

Pictogram Meaning Organic laboratory examples flame flammable ethanol, propanone, hexane, ethoxyethane flame over circle oxidising potassium manganate(VII), hydrogen peroxide (concentrated) exploding bomb explosive or self-reactive dry diazonium salts, organic peroxides corrosion corrosive to skin, eyes or metals concentrated acids, sodium hydroxide, ethanoyl chloride skull and crossbones acutely toxic methanol (in quantity), bromine, cyanides exclamation mark harmful or irritant many dilute solutions, many organic solids health hazard (silhouette) long-term health hazard: carcinogen, mutagen, reproductive toxin, respiratory sensitiser dichloromethane (suspected carcinogen), chromium(VI) compounds gas cylinder gas under pressure nitrogen, carbon dioxide cylinders environment hazardous to aquatic life many halogenated organic compounds

Table 16.1. GHS hazard pictograms.

The safety data sheet for each substance gives fuller information: physical properties, flash point, exposure limits, first-aid measures, fire-fighting measures, safe storage, and disposal. Reading it is part of planning any experiment.

Caution: solvent flammability

The flash point of a liquid is the lowest temperature at which its vapour can be ignited in air. Ethoxyethane, pentane, hexane and propanone have flash points well below room temperature, so their vapours can ignite at any time if a source of ignition is present. Heat flammable solvents only with a water bath, a heating mantle or a hot plate, never with a naked flame, and in small quantities.

docs.title: 16.3 Standard techniques
docs.text:
Most organic preparations follow the same pattern: carry out the reaction, separate the crude product from the mixture, purify it, and check its identity and purity.

flowchart LR
    R[Reaction: heat under reflux] --> W[Work-up: extract, wash, dry]
    W --> P[Purify: distil or recrystallise]
    P --> A[Analyse: melting or boiling point, TLC, spectra]
    A --> Y[Calculate percentage yield]
Figure 16.1 The stages of a typical organic preparation. Each stage uses one or more standard techniques.

docs.title: Heating under reflux
docs.text: Many organic reactions are slow at room temperature and must be heated for some time. If an open flask were heated, the volatile solvent and reactants would boil away. In heating under reflux, a vertical condenser with cold water flowing through its jacket (in at the bottom, out at the top) is fitted to the flask. Vapour rises into the condenser, condenses and runs back into the flask, so the mixture can be kept boiling at the solvent's boiling point indefinitely without loss. The top of the condenser is left open to the air. Anti-bumping granules are added before heating to promote smooth boiling.

docs.title: Distillation
docs.text: Simple distillation separates a volatile liquid from non-volatile substances, or from liquids whose boiling points differ by more than about 25 °C. The vapour passes through a sloping condenser and is collected as the distillate; a thermometer with its bulb level with the side arm measures the temperature of the vapour. Fractional distillation, with a column packed with glass between the flask and the condenser, separates liquids with closer boiling points: the vapour condenses and re-evaporates many times on the way up the column, becoming richer in the more volatile component. Distillation is used, for example, to collect an aldehyde as it forms (Section 10.5) and to collect cyclohexene from the dehydration of cyclohexanol (Section 10.4).

docs.title: Liquid–liquid extraction
docs.text: A separating funnel is used to separate two immiscible liquids, usually water and an organic solvent. A compound distributes itself between the two layers according to its relative solubility. Acids and bases can be moved between layers by changing the pH (Sections 4.6 and 13.3). When shaking a separating funnel, invert it and open the tap frequently to release pressure, especially when a volatile solvent is used or when sodium hydrogencarbonate solution, which releases CO₂, is present. The organic layer is often washed with water, dilute acid or base, or saturated sodium chloride solution to remove impurities.

docs.title: Drying
docs.text: Organic liquids and solutions that have been in contact with water are dried by swirling with an anhydrous inorganic salt that takes up water to form a hydrate: anhydrous magnesium sulfate, sodium sulfate or calcium chloride. Enough drying agent has been added when some of it remains free-flowing rather than clumped. The drying agent is then removed by filtration or decanting.

docs.title: Recrystallisation
docs.text: Recrystallisation purifies a solid. The impure solid is dissolved in the minimum volume of hot solvent, a solvent in which the compound is very soluble when hot but much less soluble when cold, and in which the impurities either are very soluble (and stay in solution) or are insoluble (and can be filtered off hot). The solution is cooled slowly; crystals of the pure compound form, are collected by suction filtration with a Büchner or Hirsch funnel, washed with a little ice-cold solvent and dried. Some product always remains in the solution, so recrystallisation trades yield for purity.

docs.title: Melting point and boiling point
docs.text: A pure crystalline solid melts sharply, over a range of 1 to 2 °C, at a characteristic temperature. Impurities lower and broaden the melting range. Comparing the melting point of a product with the literature value is a quick test of identity and purity. A mixed melting point helps confirm identity: if a sample is mixed with an authentic sample of the compound it is thought to be and the melting point does not fall, the two are very probably identical. For liquids, the boiling point measured during distillation serves a similar purpose, though less sensitively.

docs.title: Thin-layer chromatography
docs.text:
Thin-layer chromatography (TLC) separates the components of a mixture on a plate coated with a thin layer of a polar solid, usually silica gel (the stationary phase). A small spot of the sample is placed on a baseline drawn in pencil near the bottom, and the plate is stood in a covered jar containing a shallow layer of solvent (the mobile phase), below the baseline. The solvent rises up the plate by capillary action, carrying the components at different rates: less polar compounds, held less strongly by the polar silica, move further. When the solvent front is near the top, the plate is removed, the front is marked, and the spots are made visible, for example under ultraviolet light or with iodine vapour.

Each spot is described by its retention factor, \(R_\mathrm{f}\):

\[ R_\mathrm{f} = \frac{\text{distance moved by the spot}}{\text{distance moved by the solvent front}} \] Figure 16.2 Thin-layer chromatography. A developed TLC plate. Lanes A and B contain pure reference compounds and the third lane contains a mixture, which separates into two spots matching A and B. The retention factor of each spot is the distance it travelled from the baseline divided by the distance travelled by the solvent front.

TLC is quick and needs only a tiny sample. It is used to follow the progress of a reaction (the spot of the starting material fades as a new spot for the product appears), to check the purity of a product (a pure compound gives one spot) and to choose the solvent for larger-scale column chromatography, which uses the same principle to separate gram quantities.

docs.title: 16.4 Waste disposal
docs.text:
Organic waste must never be poured down the sink. Typical arrangements are:

  • non-halogenated organic solvents (ethanol, propanone, hexane, ethyl ethanoate) collected in one labelled container;
  • halogenated solvents (dichloromethane, trichloromethane) collected separately, because they need different treatment;
  • heavy-metal waste (chromium, mercury, silver compounds) collected separately;
  • reactive residues (such as small amounts of sodium metal or LiAlH₄) destroyed by an approved, supervised procedure before disposal;
  • broken glass in a dedicated container.

The volume and hazard of the waste produced by an experiment is itself a measure of how "green" the experiment is, which leads to the second half of this chapter.

docs.title: Percentage yield
docs.text:
The theoretical yield is the amount of product that would form if the limiting reactant reacted completely according to the balanced equation. The percentage yield compares the amount actually obtained with that:

\[ \text{percentage yield} = \frac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}} \times 100 \]

Yields below 100% result from incomplete reactions (including equilibria), side reactions, and losses during transfer and purification.

docs.title: Atom economy
docs.text:
A reaction can have a 100% yield and still produce a great deal of waste, if the by-products are heavy. Atom economy measures how much of the mass of the reactants ends up in the desired product, assuming a 100% yield:

\[ \text{atom economy} = \frac{M_\mathrm{r}\ \text{of desired product}}{\text{sum of}\ M_\mathrm{r}\ \text{of all reactants}} \times 100 \]

using the stoichiometric amounts from the balanced equation.

  • Addition reactions have an atom economy of 100%: every atom of the reactants is in the product. The hydration of ethene, C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH, is an example.
  • Substitution and elimination reactions always produce a by-product and have lower atom economies. Making ethanol from bromoethane, C₂H₅Br + NaOH → C₂H₅OH + NaBr, has an atom economy of only about 31%, because most of the mass of the reactants ends up in sodium bromide.

These calculations are easily automated. The following short Python function computes molar masses from simple formulas and then the atom economy:

import re

MASSES = {"C": 12.011, "H": 1.008, "O": 15.999, "N": 14.007,
          "Na": 22.990, "Cl": 35.45, "Br": 79.904}

def molar_mass(formula):
    """Molar mass of a simple formula such as 'C2H5Br' (no brackets)."""
    total = 0.0
    for symbol, count in re.findall(r"([A-Z][a-z]?)(\d*)", formula):
        total += MASSES[symbol] * (int(count) if count else 1)
    return total

def atom_economy(reactants, product):
    """Percentage of the reactants' mass that ends up in the desired product."""
    return 100 * molar_mass(product) / sum(molar_mass(r) for r in reactants)

print(round(atom_economy(["C2H4", "H2O"], "C2H6O"), 1))         # hydration of ethene
print(round(atom_economy(["C2H5Br", "NaOH"], "C2H6O"), 1))      # substitution
print(round(atom_economy(["C7H6O3", "C4H6O3"], "C9H8O4"), 1))   # aspirin

100.0
30.9
75.0

Example 16.1: Yield and atom economy for aspirin

Aspirin is made from 2-hydroxybenzoic acid (C₇H₆O₃, Mr 138.1) and ethanoic anhydride (C₄H₆O₃, Mr 102.1); the by-product is ethanoic acid:

C₇H₆O₃ + C₄H₆O₃ → C₉H₈O₄ (aspirin, Mr 180.2) + C₂H₄O₂ (Mr 60.1)

Atom economy = 180.2 / (138.1 + 102.1) × 100 = 75.0%.

A student uses 2.00 g of 2-hydroxybenzoic acid (the limiting reactant) and obtains 1.95 g of pure aspirin. Theoretical yield = 2.00 × 180.2 / 138.1 = 2.61 g. Percentage yield = 1.95 / 2.61 × 100 = 74.7%.

The two numbers measure different things. The yield tells you how well the experiment went; the atom economy tells you how wasteful the chosen reaction is, however well it is carried out. The by-product here, ethanoic acid, is at least useful and not very hazardous.

docs.title: The E-factor
docs.text:
Atom economy considers only the balanced equation. The E-factor, introduced by Roger Sheldon, measures the actual waste produced:

\[ \text{E-factor} = \frac{\text{total mass of waste}}{\text{mass of product}} \]

Waste includes by-products, unreacted starting materials, solvent losses and spent reagents and catalysts. An ideal process has an E-factor of zero. Bulk chemical manufacture typically achieves E-factors well below 5, whereas the multistep synthesis of fine chemicals and pharmaceuticals has historically produced tens to hundreds of kilograms of waste per kilogram of product, much of it solvent.

docs.title: 16.6 The principles of green chemistry
docs.text:
Green chemistry is the design of chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate the use and generation of hazardous substances. Its principles were set out as twelve points by Paul Anastas and John Warner in their book Green Chemistry: Theory and Practice (1998). In paraphrase:

  1. Prevent waste rather than treat or clean it up afterwards.
  2. Maximise atom economy: design syntheses so that as much as possible of the starting materials ends up in the product.
  3. Use and generate less hazardous substances wherever practicable.
  4. Design safer chemicals: products should do their job with as little toxicity as possible.
  5. Use safer solvents and auxiliaries, or avoid them.
  6. Design for energy efficiency: run reactions at ambient temperature and pressure where possible.
  7. Use renewable feedstocks rather than depleting ones.
  8. Reduce derivatives: avoid unnecessary protecting groups and temporary modifications, which add steps and waste.
  9. Use catalysts in preference to stoichiometric reagents.
  10. Design for degradation: products should break down into harmless substances after use.
  11. Analyse in real time to monitor and control processes and prevent the formation of pollutants.
  12. Choose inherently safer chemistry to minimise the potential for accidents, explosions and fires.

docs.title: Green chemistry in practice
docs.text:
Many examples in this book can be seen through these principles.

  • Catalysis and atom economy. Catalytic hydrogenation (Section 7.6) adds H₂ with 100% atom economy and a reusable catalyst, while reductions with stoichiometric metal hydrides produce inorganic waste. A well-known industrial example is the manufacture of the painkiller ibuprofen: an older six-step route had an atom economy of about 40%, while a three-step catalytic route introduced in the 1990s raised it to about 77%, with most of the remainder recoverable as ethanoic acid.
  • Safer oxidants. Chromium(VI) oxidations of alcohols (Section 10.5) generate toxic heavy-metal waste; catalytic oxidations using air or hydrogen peroxide produce only water as the by-product.
  • Safer solvents. Benzene and tetrachloromethane, once common solvents, are now avoided because of their toxicity. Water, ethanol, ethyl ethanoate and supercritical carbon dioxide (used, for example, to decaffeinate coffee) are greener choices. Pharmaceutical companies publish solvent-selection guides that rank solvents by safety, health and environmental impact.
  • Renewable feedstocks. Ethanol from fermentation (Section 10.2) and poly(lactic acid) from plant sugars (Section 15.3) are made from renewable resources rather than petroleum.
  • Design for degradation. Biodegradable polyesters, and detergents with unbranched chains that bacteria can break down, are designed with their end of life in mind. The persistence of CFCs (Section 9.1) shows the cost of ignoring this principle.
  • Biocatalysis. Enzymes work in water at room temperature, are highly selective (often producing a single enantiomer, Section 3.5) and are themselves biodegradable.

Key idea

Safety and sustainability are two sides of the same habit: thinking in advance about what each substance and each step will do, not only in the flask but before and after it. The best hazard is the one that is never used, and the best waste is the waste that is never made.

docs.title: 16.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • A hazard can cause harm; a risk is the likelihood and severity of harm in a given situation. A risk assessment identifies hazards and sets control measures, in order: eliminate, substitute, engineer, procedure, protect.
  • Always wear eye protection and a lab coat, use fume cupboards for volatile and toxic substances, keep flammable solvents away from ignition sources and never heat a closed system.
  • GHS pictograms and safety data sheets give hazard information.
  • Standard techniques: reflux (heating without loss), distillation, extraction (vent the funnel), drying with anhydrous salts, recrystallisation, filtration, melting point (sharp if pure), TLC (\(R_\mathrm{f}\)).
  • Organic waste is collected by type, never poured down the sink.
  • Percentage yield measures experimental success; atom economy measures how much of the reactants can end up in the product; the E-factor measures actual waste.
  • The twelve principles of green chemistry aim to prevent waste, use safer substances and solvents, save energy, use renewable feedstocks and catalysts, and design products that degrade.

docs.title: 16.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Explain the difference between a hazard and a risk, using concentrated sulfuric acid as an example.

Answer

Concentrated sulfuric acid is a hazard because it is highly corrosive to skin and eyes and reacts exothermically with water. The risk depends on the situation: transferring a few drops with a dropping pipette while wearing goggles and gloves, with water and a spill kit to hand, is a low risk; pouring a large volume from a heavy bottle without eye protection, or adding water to the acid rather than acid to water, is a high risk.

Exercise 2

Why is a condenser for heating under reflux left open at the top, and why are anti-bumping granules added?

Answer

The apparatus must not be a closed system: as the mixture is heated, the gas inside expands and vapour is produced, and a sealed apparatus could build up pressure and burst. The open top lets the pressure stay at atmospheric while the condenser returns the vapour to the flask. Anti-bumping granules provide sites for bubbles to form, so the liquid boils smoothly instead of superheating and then boiling violently ("bumping").

Exercise 3

A crude solid melts over the range 118 to 124 °C. After recrystallisation it melts at 132 to 133 °C. Explain these observations.

Answer

Impurities lower and broaden the melting range, so the crude product melts over a wide range below its true melting point. After recrystallisation, which removes most of the impurities, it melts sharply at a higher temperature (close to the literature value), indicating a much purer product.

Exercise 4

On a TLC plate the solvent front has moved 6.0 cm. Spot X has moved 4.5 cm and spot Y 1.5 cm. (a) Calculate the \(R_\mathrm{f}\) of each. (b) Which compound is less polar, assuming a silica plate? (c) Why is the baseline drawn in pencil, not ink?

Answer

(a) X: 4.5/6.0 = 0.75; Y: 1.5/6.0 = 0.25. (b) X: it is held less strongly by the polar silica and travels further. (c) Ink contains dyes that would dissolve in the solvent and move up the plate as extra spots; graphite does not.

Exercise 5

Calculate the atom economy for making 1-bromobutane from butan-1-ol and hydrogen bromide: C₄H₉OH + HBr → C₄H₉Br + H₂O. (Mr: C₄H₉OH 74.1, HBr 80.9, C₄H₉Br 137.0.) Then calculate the percentage yield if 7.4 g of butan-1-ol gives 9.6 g of 1-bromobutane.

Answer

Atom economy = 137.0 / (74.1 + 80.9) × 100 = 137.0/155.0 × 100 = 88.4%.

Moles of butan-1-ol = 7.4/74.1 = 0.0999 mol. Theoretical yield = 0.0999 × 137.0 = 13.7 g. Percentage yield = 9.6/13.7 × 100 = 70%.

Exercise 6

Two routes to ethanol are (A) hydration of ethene with steam over a phosphoric acid catalyst and (B) fermentation of glucose: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 C₂H₅OH + 2 CO₂. Calculate the atom economy of each and discuss which is "greener", considering more than atom economy.

Answer

(A) 100%: C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH.

(B) 2 × 46.07 / 180.16 × 100 = 51.1%; the rest of the mass leaves as CO₂.

On atom economy alone, route A is better. But route A uses ethene from petroleum (a non-renewable feedstock) and needs high temperature and pressure (energy), whereas route B uses a renewable feedstock at moderate temperature with a biological catalyst, and the CO₂ released was recently taken from the air by the plants. Route B, however, produces dilute ethanol that must be concentrated by energy-intensive distillation, and growing the crops uses land and water. A full comparison needs a life-cycle assessment; atom economy is only one of the twelve principles.

Exercise 7

For each change, say which green chemistry principle it illustrates: (a) replacing a dichromate oxidation with a catalytic oxidation using air; (b) replacing dichloromethane with ethyl ethanoate as an extraction solvent; (c) avoiding a protecting group by using a more selective reagent; (d) designing a polymer that bacteria can hydrolyse.

Answer

(a) Use catalysts rather than stoichiometric reagents, and use less hazardous substances (no chromium waste). (b) Use safer solvents. (c) Reduce derivatives (fewer steps, less waste). (d) Design for degradation.

docs.title: 16.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of safety and green chemistry

Exercise 1

Which is the most effective way of controlling a risk?

  1. wearing gloves
  2. eliminating or substituting the hazard
  3. putting up a warning sign
  4. working quickly
Answer

eliminating or substituting the hazard

Exercise 2

Why must a separating funnel be vented while shaking?

  1. to let air in so the liquid drains
  2. to release pressure from solvent vapour or gas
  3. to cool the mixture
  4. to mix the layers better
Answer

to release pressure from solvent vapour or gas

Exercise 3

An impure solid compared with the pure compound melts

  1. at a higher temperature over a narrow range
  2. at a lower temperature over a wider range
  3. at exactly the same temperature
  4. not at all
Answer

at a lower temperature over a wider range

Exercise 4

On a TLC plate a spot moves 3.0 cm while the solvent moves 6.0 cm. What is its Rf?

Answer

0.5 / 0.50 / 1/2

Exercise 5

Which type of reaction always has 100% atom economy?

  1. substitution
  2. elimination
  3. addition
  4. condensation
Answer

addition

Exercise 6

The E-factor of a process is

  1. mass of waste divided by mass of product
  2. mass of product divided by mass of reactants
  3. the percentage yield
  4. the energy used per kilogram
Answer

mass of waste divided by mass of product

Exercise 7

Using an enzyme in water at room temperature instead of a metal reagent in an organic solvent best illustrates

  1. design for degradation only
  2. catalysis with safer solvents and energy efficiency
  3. real-time analysis
  4. reducing derivatives
Answer

catalysis with safer solvents and energy efficiency

docs.title: Chapter 15: Polymers and Biomolecules
docs.text:
Large molecules made from small ones, by chemists and by living things

Many of the most important organic substances are enormous molecules built by joining small units again and again. Some are made in factories: poly(ethene) bags, nylon rope, polyester fabric. Others are made by living cells: starch and cellulose from sugars, proteins from amino acids, DNA from nucleotides. Both kinds are built using the reactions of earlier chapters, chiefly additions to alkenes and the formation of esters, amides and acetals. This chapter describes how synthetic polymers are made and how their structures decide their properties, and then introduces three families of biomolecules: carbohydrates, amino acids and proteins, and lipids, with a brief look at nucleic acids.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  • distinguish addition and condensation polymerisation, and draw the repeat unit of a polymer from its monomer(s) and the reverse;
  • write the radical chain mechanism of addition polymerisation;
  • relate the properties of polymers to their structure, and discuss their environmental impact;
  • describe the structures of monosaccharides, including the cyclic forms of glucose and its α and β anomers, and of disaccharides and polysaccharides;
  • describe amino acids as zwitterions, explain the isoelectric point, form peptide bonds and outline the levels of protein structure;
  • describe the structure of fats, oils and phospholipids, and explain how soaps and cell membranes work;
  • outline the structure of nucleic acids.

docs.title: 15.1 Polymers: the basic ideas
docs.text:
A polymer (from the Greek for "many parts") is a very large molecule, a macromolecule, made of many repeating units called monomers joined by covalent bonds. A typical synthetic polymer molecule contains thousands of monomer units and has a molar mass of tens or hundreds of thousands of grams per mole. In a sample, the chains are not all the same length, so polymers are described by an average molar mass.

Polymers are made in two main ways:

  • Addition polymerisation (chain-growth): monomers with a C=C double bond add to the end of a growing chain one at a time, and nothing is lost; the polymer has the same empirical formula as the monomer.
  • Condensation polymerisation (step-growth): monomers with two functional groups each react to form ester or amide links, and a small molecule (usually water) is lost at each link.

docs.title: 15.2 Addition polymers
docs.text:
Ethene, propene, chloroethene, phenylethene and other alkenes polymerise under suitable conditions. The double bond of each monomer opens, and the monomers link into a long saturated chain. The polymer is written as its repeat unit in square brackets with a subscript n:

Figure 15.1 Monomers and repeat units of addition polymers. Three addition polymers. In each, the C=C double bond of n monomer molecules opens to form a long chain of single bonds. The repeat unit, in square brackets, contains the two carbons of the original double bond with their substituents. Monomer Polymer Repeat unit Typical uses ethene, CH₂=CH₂ poly(ethene), polyethylene –CH₂–CH₂– bags, films, bottles, pipes propene, CH₂=CHCH₃ poly(propene), polypropylene –CH₂–CH(CH₃)– containers, ropes, carpets chloroethene, CH₂=CHCl poly(chloroethene), PVC –CH₂–CHCl– window frames, pipes, cable insulation phenylethene, CH₂=CHC₆H₅ poly(phenylethene), polystyrene –CH₂–CH(C₆H₅)– packaging, insulation, disposable cups tetrafluoroethene, CF₂=CF₂ poly(tetrafluoroethene), PTFE –CF₂–CF₂– non-stick coatings, seals methyl 2-methylpropenoate poly(methyl methacrylate), PMMA –CH₂–C(CH₃)(COOCH₃)– shatter-resistant transparent sheets

Table 15.1. Common addition polymers.

To find the monomer from a polymer, identify the two-carbon repeat unit in the main chain and put a double bond between those two carbons.

docs.title: The mechanism: radical chain polymerisation
docs.text:
Many addition polymers are made by a radical chain mechanism, with the same three stages as radical halogenation (Section 6.6):

  1. Initiation. An initiator, such as a peroxide (R–O–O–R), splits on heating into two radicals, RO•. A radical adds to the C=C bond of a monomer, using one π electron of the monomer and forming a new radical on the other carbon: RO• + CH₂=CH₂ → RO–CH₂–CH₂•.
  2. Propagation. The new radical adds to another monomer, and the chain grows by one unit at a time, thousands of times: RO–CH₂CH₂• + CH₂=CH₂ → RO–CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂•, and so on.
  3. Termination. Two growing chains meet and their radicals combine (or one takes a hydrogen atom from the other), ending both chains.

With unsymmetrical monomers such as propene, the radical adds to the CH₂ end so that the new radical is on the more substituted carbon (more stable), which gives a regular "head-to-tail" chain with the substituents on alternate carbons. Poly(ethene) made by radical polymerisation at high pressure has many side branches, which prevent the chains packing closely: this is low-density poly(ethene) (LDPE), soft and flexible. Using metal catalysts (Ziegler–Natta catalysts) at low pressure gives unbranched chains that pack well: high-density poly(ethene) (HDPE), stiffer and stronger. Ziegler–Natta catalysts also control the stereochemistry of poly(propene), placing all the methyl groups on the same side of the chain, which gives a stronger, more crystalline material.

docs.title: 15.3 Condensation polymers
docs.text:
Condensation polymers are made from monomers that each carry two functional groups, so that every reaction leaves a group free at each end for the next step.

Polyesters form from a dicarboxylic acid (or its derivative) and a diol. Poly(ethylene terephthalate), PET, is made from benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid (terephthalic acid) and ethane-1,2-diol. It is used for drinks bottles and, as polyester fibre, for clothing.

Polyamides form from a dicarboxylic acid (or acyl chloride) and a diamine. Nylon-6,6 is made from hexanedioic acid and hexane-1,6-diamine; the numbers give the carbons in each monomer. The amide groups of neighbouring chains hydrogen bond to one another, making nylon strong. Kevlar, an aromatic polyamide made from benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid and benzene-1,4-diamine, has rigid chains held in sheets by hydrogen bonds; it is strong enough to be used in protective clothing.

Figure 15.2 Repeat units of a polyamide and a polyester. Repeat units of two condensation polymers. Nylon-6,6 contains amide links formed between hexane-1,6-diamine and hexanedioic acid. PET contains ester links formed between ethane-1,2-diol and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid. One molecule of water is lost for each link formed.

Example 15.1: Monomers from a repeat unit

Give the monomers of the polymer whose repeat unit is –O–CH₂CH₂CH₂–O–CO–(CH₂)₂–CO–.

The repeat unit contains two ester links. Break each ester link between the C=O carbon and the oxygen, adding OH to the acyl carbon and H to the oxygen. The monomers are propane-1,3-diol, HOCH₂CH₂CH₂OH, and butanedioic acid, HOOC–CH₂CH₂–COOH.

docs.title: Structure and properties
docs.text:
The properties of a polymer depend on the length of its chains, the forces between them and how regularly they pack:

  • Thermoplastics (poly(ethene), PVC, PET, nylon) consist of separate chains held together by intermolecular forces. They soften on heating and can be moulded and remoulded.
  • Thermosets (epoxy resins, melamine resins, vulcanised rubber) have chains linked to one another by covalent cross-links into a network. They do not soften on heating, but char or decompose.
  • Regular chains pack into ordered, crystalline regions, giving stiffer, stronger, more opaque materials; irregular, branched chains give softer, amorphous materials.
  • Stronger forces between chains (hydrogen bonds in nylon, dipole–dipole forces in PVC) give stronger, higher-melting materials than dispersion forces alone (poly(ethene)).

docs.title: Polymers and the environment
docs.text: Most addition polymers have backbones of C–C bonds, which microorganisms cannot break down easily, so plastic waste persists in the environment for a very long time. Possible responses include reduction and reuse; mechanical recycling, in which sorted plastics are melted and reformed; chemical recycling, in which polymers such as PET are broken back down into monomers by hydrolysis or other reactions; incineration with energy recovery, which releases carbon dioxide; and biodegradable polymers. Condensation polymers with ester links in the chain can be hydrolysed, and poly(lactic acid), PLA, a polyester made from lactic acid obtained by fermenting plant sugars, can be composted under industrial conditions. These issues are part of green chemistry (Chapter 16).

docs.title: 15.4 Carbohydrates
docs.text: Carbohydrates (sugars and their polymers) have formulas that can often be written Cₙ(H₂O)ₘ, hence the name "hydrates of carbon". Plants make them from carbon dioxide and water by photosynthesis, and they are the main fuel and an important structural material of living things.

docs.title: Monosaccharides
docs.text:
Monosaccharides are polyhydroxy aldehydes (aldoses) or polyhydroxy ketones (ketoses), usually with five or six carbons. Glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, is an aldohexose (six carbons, an aldehyde group); fructose, its isomer, is a ketohexose.

Glucose has four stereocentres (C2 to C5), so there are sixteen aldohexoses; glucose is one of them. Sugars are drawn as Fischer projections (Section 3.6), with the CHO at the top. In natural sugars, the OH on the stereocentre furthest from the carbonyl group (C5 in glucose) points to the right in the Fischer projection: these are D-sugars. Almost all natural sugars belong to the D series. (The D and L labels refer to this relationship with glyceraldehyde and are not the same thing as R and S or + and −.)

docs.title: Cyclic forms
docs.text:
In solution, glucose exists almost entirely as six-membered rings. The OH group on C5 adds to the C1 aldehyde to form a cyclic hemiacetal (Section 11.4). The ring contains five carbons and one oxygen, and is called a pyranose. The ring closure makes C1 a new stereocentre, called the anomeric carbon, and two forms, the anomers, are possible:

  • α-D-glucopyranose: the OH on C1 is on the opposite face of the ring to the CH₂OH group (down, in the usual Haworth drawing).
  • β-D-glucopyranose: the OH on C1 is on the same face as the CH₂OH group (up).
Figure 15.3 Open-chain and cyclic glucose. D-Glucose as an open-chain Fischer projection and as β-D-glucopyranose in a Haworth projection. In the Haworth projection the ring is drawn flat and seen edge-on, with the ring oxygen at the back right and the thick bonds nearest the viewer. Groups on the right in the Fischer projection point down in the Haworth projection, and in the β anomer the OH on C1 points up, on the same face as CH₂OH.

In water, the two anomers interconvert through the open-chain form, which is present only in a tiny amount. A solution of either pure anomer slowly changes its optical rotation until it reaches an equilibrium mixture of about one-third α and two-thirds β; this change is called mutarotation. The β anomer predominates because in its chair conformation all the substituents, including the C1 OH, are equatorial (Section 6.5).

Because the open-chain form, with its aldehyde group, is always present in equilibrium, glucose gives positive Benedict's and Tollens' tests (Section 11.6); it is a reducing sugar.

docs.title: Disaccharides and polysaccharides
docs.text:
The anomeric OH of one monosaccharide can react with an OH of another to form an acetal link, called a glycosidic bond, with loss of water.

  • Maltose consists of two glucose units joined by an α(1→4) glycosidic bond (from C1 of one, in the α configuration, to the O on C4 of the other). It is a reducing sugar, because the second glucose still has a free hemiacetal.
  • Lactose, milk sugar, links galactose and glucose by a β(1→4) bond.
  • Sucrose, ordinary table sugar, links glucose and fructose through both their anomeric carbons. It has no free hemiacetal and is not a reducing sugar.

Polysaccharides are polymers of monosaccharides:

  • Starch, the main energy store of plants, is a mixture of amylose (unbranched chains of glucose joined by α(1→4) links, which coil into helices) and amylopectin (the same chains with branches joined by α(1→6) links). Glycogen, the energy store of animals, resembles amylopectin but is more highly branched.
  • Cellulose, the main structural material of plants, consists of unbranched chains of glucose joined by β(1→4) links. The β links give straight chains that lie side by side and hydrogen bond into strong fibres. Humans have enzymes that hydrolyse α links but not β links, so we can digest starch but not cellulose; grazing animals rely on microorganisms in their gut to do it.

Key idea

Starch and cellulose are both polymers of glucose. The only difference is the configuration at the anomeric carbon (α in starch, β in cellulose), yet it changes the shape of the chains, the properties of the material and whether we can digest it.

docs.title: Amino acids
docs.text:
The building blocks of proteins are α-amino acids, H₂N–CH(R)–COOH, in which an amino group and a carboxyl group are attached to the same carbon (the α-carbon). Twenty different amino acids, differing in their side chain R, are coded for by genes. The simplest, glycine, has R = H; others have alkyl side chains (alanine, valine, leucine), side chains with OH (serine), SH (cysteine), aromatic rings (phenylalanine, tyrosine), acidic groups (aspartic acid, glutamic acid) or basic groups (lysine, arginine).

Except for glycine, the α-carbon is a stereocentre. Almost all amino acids in proteins have the same configuration, called L, which corresponds to S for all of them except cysteine, whose sulfur atom changes the CIP priorities and makes the L form R.

docs.title: Zwitterions and the isoelectric point
docs.text:
An amino acid contains both an acidic group (COOH, pKa about 2) and a basic group (NH₂, pKa of the conjugate acid about 9 to 10). Near neutral pH, the carboxyl group is ionised and the amino group protonated, so the amino acid exists as a zwitterion, ⁺H₃N–CH(R)–COO⁻ (Example 4.3). This explains why amino acids are crystalline solids with high melting points (they decompose rather than melt) and are more soluble in water than in organic solvents.

The form present depends on pH. In strong acid, both groups are protonated (overall charge +1); in strong base, both are deprotonated (overall charge −1). The pH at which the amino acid carries no net charge is its isoelectric point, pI. For an amino acid with a neutral side chain it lies about halfway between the two pKa values (about 6 for glycine and alanine). At its pI an amino acid does not move in an electric field, which is the basis of separation by electrophoresis.

docs.title: The peptide bond
docs.text:
The carboxyl group of one amino acid can form an amide with the amino group of another, with loss of water. This amide link is the peptide bond. Two amino acids give a dipeptide, several a peptide, and long chains (usually more than about fifty amino acids) a protein. The peptide bond is planar and rigid because of amide resonance (Section 12.6), which strongly influences how protein chains fold.

Figure 15.4 Amino acids and the peptide bond. An α-amino acid and its zwitterion at pH 7, and the formation of a peptide bond. The carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of another form an amide (peptide) bond, shown in red, with loss of a water molecule.

docs.title: Levels of protein structure
docs.text:
• Primary structure: the sequence of amino acids in the chain, written from the N-terminus (free NH₂) to the C-terminus (free COOH).
  • Secondary structure: regular local folding held by hydrogen bonds between the C=O and N–H groups of the backbone: the α-helix (a coil with hydrogen bonds between turns) and the β-pleated sheet (strands lying side by side).
  • Tertiary structure: the overall three-dimensional shape of a chain, held by interactions between side chains: hydrogen bonds, ionic attractions, hydrophobic interactions and covalent disulfide bridges (–S–S–) between cysteine residues.
  • Quaternary structure: the arrangement of several chains in a protein made of more than one, such as haemoglobin, with four chains.

The function of a protein depends on its shape. Enzymes, proteins that catalyse reactions, have active sites shaped to bind particular substrates, often distinguishing between enantiomers (Section 3.5). Heat, extremes of pH and some chemicals disrupt the weak interactions that hold the shape, denaturing the protein and destroying its activity, as when an egg is cooked. Strong acid or base, with heat, hydrolyses the peptide bonds themselves, breaking the protein down into its amino acids.

docs.title: 15.6 Lipids
docs.text: Lipids are the compounds of living things that dissolve in non-polar solvents but not in water. They are a varied group, defined by solubility rather than by structure.

docs.title: Fats and oils
docs.text:
Fats and oils are triglycerides (triacylglycerols): esters of propane-1,2,3-triol (glycerol) with three long-chain fatty acids, usually with even numbers of carbons, typically 12 to 20.

  • Saturated fatty acids, such as hexadecanoic (palmitic) acid and octadecanoic (stearic) acid, have straight, flexible chains that pack closely. Triglycerides rich in them are solid at room temperature: fats, mostly from animals.
  • Unsaturated fatty acids, such as oleic acid (cis-octadec-9-enoic acid), contain one or more C=C bonds, usually cis. Each cis double bond puts a kink in the chain, which stops the molecules packing well and lowers the melting point. Triglycerides rich in them are liquid: oils, mostly from plants and fish.

Hydrogenating some of the double bonds of an oil (Section 7.6) raises its melting point, which is how vegetable oils were traditionally turned into spreads. Saponification of triglycerides with sodium hydroxide gives glycerol and soap (Section 12.5).

docs.title: Phospholipids and membranes
docs.text: In a phospholipid, one fatty acid of a triglyceride is replaced by a phosphate group linked to a small polar or charged molecule. The molecule has a polar, water-loving (hydrophilic) head and two non-polar, water-avoiding (hydrophobic) tails. In water, phospholipids arrange themselves spontaneously into a double layer, a lipid bilayer, with the tails inside and the heads facing the water on both sides. Lipid bilayers form the membranes of all cells, a barrier that keeps the contents of the cell in and most ions and polar molecules out.

docs.title: Steroids
docs.text: Steroids are lipids with a characteristic skeleton of four fused rings (three six-membered and one five-membered). Cholesterol is a component of animal cell membranes and the starting material from which the body makes other steroids, including the sex hormones (testosterone, oestradiol), the corticosteroids and vitamin D.

docs.title: 15.7 Nucleic acids in brief
docs.text:
DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid) store and transmit genetic information. They are condensation polymers of nucleotides. Each nucleotide contains a five-carbon sugar (deoxyribose in DNA, ribose in RNA), a phosphate group and a nitrogen-containing heterocyclic base. The sugars and phosphates alternate along the backbone, joined by phosphate ester links, and a base hangs from each sugar.

DNA contains four bases: adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and thymine (T). Two DNA strands wind around each other in a double helix, held together by hydrogen bonds between bases on opposite strands: A pairs with T (two hydrogen bonds) and G with C (three hydrogen bonds). This complementary base pairing, which depends on the shapes and hydrogen-bonding groups of the bases, allows each strand to serve as a template for copying the other. In RNA, uracil (U) replaces thymine.

docs.title: 15.8 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Polymers are macromolecules of repeating units. Addition polymers form from alkenes with nothing lost; condensation polymers form from bifunctional monomers with loss of a small molecule.
  • Radical addition polymerisation has initiation, propagation and termination steps. Chain structure (branching, regularity, cross-linking, intermolecular forces) decides properties.
  • Polyesters (PET) and polyamides (nylon, Kevlar) contain ester and amide links; they can be hydrolysed. Plastic waste is a major environmental problem.
  • Glucose is an aldohexose; in solution it forms cyclic hemiacetals (α and β anomers) that interconvert by mutarotation. Glycosidic (acetal) links join sugars into disaccharides and polysaccharides; starch has α links, cellulose β links.
  • α-Amino acids exist as zwitterions near pH 7 and have an isoelectric point. Peptide (amide) bonds join them into proteins, whose primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structures determine their function.
  • Triglycerides are esters of glycerol and fatty acids; cis double bonds lower melting points. Phospholipids form membranes. Steroids have four fused rings.
  • DNA and RNA are polymers of nucleotides; base pairing (A–T, G–C) by hydrogen bonds holds the double helix together.

docs.title: 15.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Draw the repeat unit of the polymer formed from (a) phenylethene; (b) propenenitrile, CH₂=CHCN. Give the monomer of the polymer –CH₂–C(CH₃)₂–CH₂–C(CH₃)₂–.

Answer

(a) –CH₂–CH(C₆H₅)–, poly(phenylethene) (polystyrene). (b) –CH₂–CH(CN)–, poly(propenenitrile), used for acrylic fibres. The repeat unit of the last polymer is –CH₂–C(CH₃)₂–, so the monomer is 2-methylpropene, CH₂=C(CH₃)₂.

Exercise 2

Write the initiation, two propagation steps and one termination step for the radical polymerisation of chloroethene initiated by a peroxide RO–OR.

Answer

Initiation: RO–OR → 2 RO• (heat); RO• + CH₂=CHCl → RO–CH₂–C•HCl (the radical forms on the carbon carrying Cl, the more stabilised position). Propagation: RO–CH₂–C•HCl + CH₂=CHCl → RO–CH₂–CHCl–CH₂–C•HCl; the chain then adds further monomers in the same way. Termination: two chain radicals combine, R′–C•HCl + •CHCl–R″ → R′–CHCl–CHCl–R″.

Exercise 3

Explain why nylon-6,6 has a higher melting point than poly(ethene) of similar chain length, and why a PET bottle can, in principle, be broken down into its monomers while a poly(ethene) bag cannot easily be.

Answer

Nylon chains are linked to one another by hydrogen bonds between the N–H of one amide group and the C=O of another, much stronger than the dispersion forces that hold poly(ethene) chains together. PET has ester links in its backbone, which can be hydrolysed (by acid, base or enzymes) back to the diacid and the diol. Poly(ethene) has only C–C and C–H bonds, which have no such reactive site.

Exercise 4

(a) Is glucose a reducing sugar? Is sucrose? Explain. (b) Explain what is meant by mutarotation.

Answer

(a) Glucose is reducing: its cyclic hemiacetal is in equilibrium with the open-chain aldehyde, which reduces Benedict's and Tollens' reagents. Sucrose is not: its glucose and fructose units are joined through both anomeric carbons, so neither has a free hemiacetal that can open to a carbonyl group.

(b) Pure α- or β-D-glucopyranose, dissolved in water, slowly interconverts with the other anomer through the open-chain form. The optical rotation of the solution changes until it reaches the value of the equilibrium mixture (about one-third α, two-thirds β). This change in rotation is mutarotation.

Exercise 5

Both starch and cellulose are polymers of glucose. Explain why cellulose forms strong fibres and is indigestible by humans, while starch is a soft energy store that we digest easily.

Answer

Starch has α(1→4) links, which make the chains coil into helices (and amylopectin is branched); the chains do not pack into fibres. Cellulose has β(1→4) links, which give straight chains that lie side by side and are held together by many hydrogen bonds into strong fibres. Human digestive enzymes are shaped to hydrolyse α-glycosidic links but not β links, so we can digest starch but not cellulose.

Exercise 6

Alanine has pKa values of 2.3 (COOH) and 9.7 (NH₃⁺). (a) Draw the main form of alanine at pH 1, pH 6 and pH 12. (b) Estimate its isoelectric point. (c) Draw the two possible dipeptides formed from one alanine and one glycine.

Answer

(a) pH 1: ⁺H₃N–CH(CH₃)–COOH (charge +1). pH 6: ⁺H₃N–CH(CH₃)–COO⁻ (zwitterion, net charge 0). pH 12: H₂N–CH(CH₃)–COO⁻ (charge −1).

(b) pI ≈ (2.3 + 9.7)/2 = 6.0.

(c) Ala-Gly: H₂N–CH(CH₃)–CO–NH–CH₂–COOH. Gly-Ala: H₂N–CH₂–CO–NH–CH(CH₃)–COOH. They are constitutional isomers.

Exercise 7

Explain why olive oil (rich in oleic acid) is a liquid at room temperature while beef fat (rich in stearic and palmitic acids) is a solid. What is formed when either is boiled with aqueous sodium hydroxide?

Answer

Stearic and palmitic acids are saturated, with straight chains that pack closely, giving strong dispersion forces between triglyceride molecules and a high melting point. Oleic acid has a cis C=C double bond that kinks the chain, preventing close packing, so the forces are weaker and the oil melts below room temperature. Boiling with NaOH saponifies the ester links, giving glycerol and the sodium salts of the fatty acids (soaps).

docs.title: 15.10 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of polymers and biomolecules

Exercise 1

Which polymer is formed by condensation polymerisation?

  1. poly(ethene)
  2. PVC
  3. nylon-6,6
  4. polystyrene
Answer

nylon-6,6

Exercise 2

The repeat unit of poly(propene) is

  1. -CH₂-CH₂-
  2. -CH₂-CH(CH₃)-
  3. -CH₂-CHCl-
  4. -CF₂-CF₂-
Answer

-CH₂-CH(CH₃)-

Exercise 3

In β-D-glucopyranose the OH on C1 is

  1. on the same face as CH₂OH
  2. on the opposite face to CH₂OH
  3. absent
  4. part of an aldehyde group
Answer

on the same face as CH₂OH

Exercise 4

Cellulose differs from starch in having

  1. fructose units
  2. beta(1→4) glycosidic links
  3. peptide bonds
  4. ester links
Answer

beta(1→4) glycosidic links

Exercise 5

At its isoelectric point an amino acid

  1. carries a net positive charge
  2. carries a net negative charge
  3. carries no net charge
  4. is completely un-ionised
Answer

carries no net charge

Exercise 6

The bond that joins amino acids in a protein is

  1. an ester bond
  2. a glycosidic bond
  3. a peptide (amide) bond
  4. a disulfide bond
Answer

a peptide (amide) bond

Exercise 7

Match each DNA base with its partner.

ABadeninecytosineguaninethymine Answer

adenine — thymine; guanine — cytosine

docs.title: About This Book
docs.text:
Who it is for and how to use it

Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds: the fuels we burn, the plastics we wrap things in, the medicines we take, the dyes in our clothes and the molecules of life itself. It has a reputation for being a subject of endless memorisation. It is not. A small number of ideas (where the electrons are, how atoms share them, and how they move when molecules meet) explain nearly every reaction in this book. Learn those ideas properly and the reactions stop being a list and start being a story.

docs.title: Who this book is for
docs.text:
This book is a first course in organic chemistry. It is written for a student in the last years of school or the first year of a university course in chemistry, biology, pharmacy, medicine, chemical engineering or a related subject, and for anyone teaching themselves.

You need school chemistry: atoms with protons, neutrons and electrons, the periodic table, the idea of a chemical bond, balanced equations, moles, and a first acquaintance with acids, bases and equilibrium. Nothing more is assumed. Where a piece of general chemistry is needed (electron shells, electronegativity, logarithms in pH) it is recalled at the point of use.

docs.title: What the book covers
docs.text:
The sixteen chapters fall into four groups.

Part Chapters What you learn Foundations 1 to 5 Bonding and shape, drawing and naming molecules, isomerism and stereochemistry, acids and bases, and the language of mechanisms (curly arrows) Hydrocarbons 6 to 8 Alkanes and their conformations, the addition reactions of alkenes and alkynes, and the special stability and substitution chemistry of benzene Functional groups 9 to 13 Alkyl halides (substitution and elimination), alcohols and ethers, aldehydes and ketones, carboxylic acids and their derivatives, and amines Tools and applications 14 to 16 Spectroscopy (IR, NMR and mass spectrometry), polymers and the molecules of life, and safe and sustainable practice in the laboratory

Table P.1. The plan of the book.

The order matters. Chapters 1 to 5 build the toolkit used everywhere else: by the end of Chapter 5 you will be able to read and draw a reaction mechanism. Chapters 6 to 13 then apply the same few mechanistic patterns to one family of compounds after another. Chapter 14 shows how chemists find out what they have made, and Chapters 15 and 16 connect the subject to materials, biology and the practice of the laboratory.

docs.title: How each chapter is built
docs.text:
Every chapter has the same parts, so you always know where you are.

  • Learning outcomes at the top say what you should be able to do at the end.
  • Numbered sections explain the ideas, moving from a picture to a precise statement.
  • Figures show structures and mechanisms. Structures are drawn as skeletal formulas (Chapter 1 explains how to read them), and curly arrows in mechanisms are drawn in red.
  • Boxes pick out what matters: a key idea box holds the one thing to remember from a section, a note adds detail, and a caution box marks a common mistake.
  • Worked examples solve a problem step by step.
  • A summary lists the main points.
  • Exercises follow, each with its answer folded underneath. Try the exercise on paper before you open the answer.
  • A short quiz at the end checks your understanding. You can answer it on the page and see at once whether you were right.

At the back are a glossary of the terms used in the book and a list of further reading.

docs.title: How to use the book
docs.text:
Organic chemistry is learned with a pencil. Read a section, then close the book and draw the structures and mechanisms yourself. When a mechanism appears, do not try to memorise the picture: ask, for each arrow, where the electrons come from and why they go where they go. If you can answer that question, you will be able to work out mechanisms you have never seen.

Three habits will help more than anything else:

  1. Count electrons and check charges. Every structure you draw should have the right number of bonds to each atom and the right formal charges. Most errors in mechanisms are errors of bookkeeping.
  2. Draw molecules as skeletal formulas. They are faster, clearer and closer to how chemists think. Chapter 1 shows you how.
  3. Look for patterns. A nucleophile attacking a carbonyl group in Chapter 11 is the same event as a nucleophile attacking an alkyl halide in Chapter 9, seen in a different setting. The book points these links out; notice them.

Safety first

This book describes reactions to explain how molecules behave. It is not a laboratory manual. Laboratory work must be done only under supervision, in a properly equipped laboratory, following a risk assessment and the local safety rules. Chapter 16 explains the principles of safe practice.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text: Names follow the current IUPAC recommendations (propan-2-ol, ethanoic acid), with common names given where they are still widely used (isopropyl alcohol, acetic acid). Formulas are written with subscripts (CH₃CH₂OH). Energies are in kilojoules per mole (kJ mol⁻¹), bond lengths in picometres (pm) and acidities as pKₐ values. In figures, a solid wedge is a bond coming towards you out of the page, a hashed wedge is a bond going away from you behind the page, and a plain line lies in the page.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Reaction Mechanisms and Curly Arrows
docs.text:
How and why bonds break and form

A balanced equation tells you what goes in and what comes out. A mechanism tells you how: which bonds break, which form, in what order, and through which short-lived species. Mechanisms are the grammar of organic chemistry. Once you can read and write them, the hundreds of reactions in this book reduce to a handful of patterns, and you can predict the products of reactions you have never met. This chapter introduces the language of mechanisms (nucleophiles, electrophiles and curly arrows), the reactive intermediates that appear in them, and the energy ideas that decide whether and how fast a reaction goes.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  • distinguish homolytic and heterolytic bond cleavage and draw full and fish-hook arrows correctly;
  • identify nucleophiles and electrophiles and the atoms through which they react;
  • draw curly arrows following the rules, and check every structure for correct charges;
  • recognise the four basic arrow patterns of polar mechanisms;
  • rank the stability of carbocations, carbanions and radicals and explain the order;
  • read a reaction energy profile, distinguishing transition states, intermediates and the rate-determining step;
  • classify reactions as additions, eliminations, substitutions or rearrangements, and as oxidations or reductions.

docs.title: 5.1 What a mechanism is
docs.text:
A mechanism is a step-by-step description of a reaction at the level of electrons. Each step shows bonds breaking and forming, and the structures between steps are real species, however short-lived. A mechanism is a theory: it is proposed to explain the experimental facts (the products, the effect of changing the reactants, the rate, the stereochemistry) and it is accepted when it explains them all.

Why bother? Because a mechanism is transferable. Learn how hydroxide reacts with bromomethane and you know how cyanide reacts with iodoethane, how water reacts with a tertiary bromide (by a different route, for reasons you will understand) and how an amine attacks an alkyl halide in a drug synthesis.

docs.title: 5.2 Breaking bonds: homolysis and heterolysis
docs.text:
A covalent bond holds two electrons. When it breaks, those electrons can be shared out in two ways.

  • In homolysis (homolytic cleavage) each atom takes one electron. The products are radicals, species with an unpaired electron, written with a dot: Cl•. Homolysis usually needs light or heat, and happens most easily for weak, non-polar bonds such as Cl–Cl, Br–Br and O–O.
  • In heterolysis (heterolytic cleavage) one atom takes both electrons. The products are a cation and an anion. Heterolysis is favoured for polar bonds in polar solvents, where the ions are stabilised.

The movement of a pair of electrons is drawn with a full-headed curly arrow. The movement of a single electron is drawn with a fish-hook arrow (half-headed).

Figure 5.1 Homolysis and heterolysis. Homolysis and heterolysis. In homolysis of chlorine, two fish-hook arrows send one electron of the bond to each atom, giving two chlorine radicals. In heterolysis of a C–Br bond, one full curly arrow sends both electrons to bromine, giving a carbocation and a bromide ion.

Most reactions in this book are polar reactions, in which bonds break and form heterolytically and electron pairs move from electron-rich to electron-poor sites. Radical reactions, such as the chlorination of alkanes (Chapter 6) and many polymerisations (Chapter 15), form a second group. A third group, pericyclic reactions, in which bonds reorganise in a single cyclic step, is beyond a first course, apart from a mention in Chapter 7.

docs.title: 5.3 Nucleophiles and electrophiles
docs.text:
Polar reactions happen between an electron-rich species and an electron-poor one.

A nucleophile ("nucleus-loving") is a species with a pair of electrons that it can donate to form a new bond. It is a Lewis base. Nucleophiles have:

  • a lone pair, often on a negatively charged atom: HO⁻, CH₃O⁻, CN⁻, Br⁻, I⁻, or on a neutral atom: H₂O, NH₃, CH₃OH;
  • or a π bond: alkenes, alkynes and benzene rings donate their π electrons;
  • or, more rarely, a polarised σ bond, as in the C–Mg bond of a Grignard reagent or the B–H bond of borohydride (Chapter 11).

An electrophile ("electron-loving") is a species that can accept a pair of electrons to form a new bond. It is a Lewis acid. Electrophiles have:

  • an empty orbital: H⁺, carbocations, BF₃, AlCl₃;
  • or an atom made δ+ by a polar bond, usually with a group that can leave: the carbon of C–Br in a haloalkane, the carbon of C=O in a carbonyl group, the hydrogen of H–Br.

Key idea

Almost every polar reaction step is a nucleophile giving a pair of electrons to an electrophile. When you meet a new reaction, first find the nucleophile (where are the most available electrons?) and the electrophile (where is the electron-poor atom?). The first curly arrow runs from one to the other.

The same species can be described as a base or a nucleophile depending on what it attacks. Hydroxide acting on a proton is a base; hydroxide acting on a carbon is a nucleophile. Basicity is a thermodynamic property (the position of an equilibrium with H⁺, measured by pKa), while nucleophilicity is a kinetic one (how fast the species attacks carbon). They usually run in parallel, but not always: iodide is a very weak base yet a good nucleophile, and the bulky tert-butoxide ion is a strong base but a poor nucleophile. These differences matter in Chapter 9.

docs.title: 5.4 The rules for curly arrows
docs.text:
A curly arrow shows the movement of one pair of electrons. Follow these rules and your mechanisms will be correct in form, even before they are correct in chemistry:

  1. The tail starts at the electrons: a lone pair, a negative charge or a bond (σ or π). Never start an arrow at an atom with no lone pair, at a positive charge, or at a hydrogen atom.
  2. The head points to where the electrons go: to an atom (to become a lone pair) or to the space between two atoms (to become a new bond).
  3. Arrows run from nucleophile to electrophile, from electron-rich to electron-poor.
  4. Atoms never exceed their limits. If an arrow brings a new bond to an atom that already has a full octet (such as carbon with four bonds), another arrow must take a pair of electrons away from that atom in the same step.
  5. Charge is conserved. The total charge on each side of every step must be the same.
  6. Check formal charges after every step. An atom that gains a bond by donating a lone pair becomes more positive; an atom that receives a lone pair by losing a bond becomes more negative.

Caution: the commonest arrow errors

  • Drawing an arrow from an H⁺ to a lone pair ("the proton attacks"). The arrow goes the other way: from the lone pair to the H.
  • Making a five-bonded carbon. If a nucleophile adds to a saturated carbon, a bond to that carbon must break at the same time.
  • Losing track of charges: a neutral water molecule that uses a lone pair to form a bond becomes H₂O⁺–R, a positively charged oxonium ion.

docs.title: 5.5 The four basic patterns
docs.text:
Polar mechanisms are built from a small set of steps. Learn to recognise these four and you can read almost any mechanism in the book.

  1. Loss of a leaving group. A polar bond breaks heterolytically and the electronegative atom leaves with the electron pair. A good leaving group is a stable, weakly basic species: Br⁻, I⁻, Cl⁻, H₂O, a sulfonate ion.
  2. Nucleophilic attack. A nucleophile donates a pair of electrons to an electrophilic atom, forming a new bond.
  3. Proton transfer. A base removes a proton (Chapter 4). Proton transfers often start or finish a sequence, to make a better leaving group or to neutralise a charged product.
  4. A π bond attacks an electrophile. The π electrons of an alkene or arene form a new σ bond to an electrophile, leaving a positive charge on the other carbon.

A fifth pattern, rearrangement, moves a group from one atom to a neighbour, usually to turn a carbocation into a more stable one (Section 5.6).

Several patterns can happen together in one step. In the SN2 reaction of Chapter 9, nucleophilic attack and loss of the leaving group occur simultaneously: one arrow from the nucleophile to the carbon, and one from the C–leaving group bond to the leaving group.

Figure 5.2 The basic arrow patterns. The four basic arrow patterns. (a) The C–Br bond of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane breaks with both electrons going to bromine. (b) A lone pair of water attacks the carbocation. (c) A second water molecule removes a proton from the oxonium ion. (d) The π electrons of ethene attack the hydrogen of H–Br, and the H–Br bonding pair leaves with bromine. Steps (a) to (c) together are the mechanism of a substitution reaction; step (d) is the first step of an addition reaction.

Example 5.1: Reading a mechanism

The reaction of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane with water gives 2-methylpropan-2-ol and HBr. The mechanism in Figure 5.2 (a), (b), (c) has three steps.

Step 1. The C–Br bond breaks heterolytically. Bromine, more electronegative, leaves as Br⁻; carbon, which has lost a bond and its share of the electrons, becomes a carbocation, (CH₃)₃C⁺. Charges: 0 → (+1) + (−1). Balanced.

Step 2. Water is the nucleophile (lone pair on O); the carbocation is the electrophile (empty p orbital). The arrow runs from the oxygen lone pair to the carbon. Oxygen now has three bonds and one lone pair, so it carries a +1 formal charge: (CH₃)₃C–OH₂⁺.

Step 3. A second water molecule acts as a base. Its lone pair takes a proton from the oxonium ion, and the O–H bonding pair returns to the oxygen, which becomes neutral. Products: (CH₃)₃COH and H₃O⁺.

Overall: (CH₃)₃CBr + 2 H₂O → (CH₃)₃COH + H₃O⁺ + Br⁻, which is the stated equation with the HBr ionised in water.

docs.title: 5.6 Reactive intermediates
docs.text: Many reactions pass through species that are too reactive to be isolated under normal conditions but live long enough to take part in later steps. These reactive intermediates are local energy minima on the path from reactants to products.

docs.title: Carbocations
docs.text:
A carbocation has a carbon with only three bonds and six valence electrons, carrying a positive charge. The carbon is sp² hybridised and trigonal planar, with an empty p orbital perpendicular to the plane. Carbocations are strong electrophiles.

Their stability increases with the number of alkyl groups attached to the positive carbon:

Figure 5.3 Carbocation stability. The order of carbocation stability. Each alkyl group attached to the positive carbon donates electron density, through the inductive effect and through hyperconjugation, spreading the positive charge. A tertiary cation, with three alkyl groups, is much more stable than a methyl cation, which has none.

Two effects explain the order. Alkyl groups are weakly electron-donating by the inductive effect. More importantly, the electrons of C–H (and C–C) σ bonds on neighbouring carbons can overlap with the empty p orbital and spread the charge. This delocalisation of σ electrons is called hyperconjugation; the more neighbouring C–H bonds there are, the greater the stabilisation.

Resonance is even more powerful. A carbocation next to a C=C double bond (an allylic cation, CH₂=CH–CH₂⁺) or next to a benzene ring (a benzylic cation, C₆H₅CH₂⁺) shares its charge over several carbons. Even a primary allylic or benzylic cation is about as stable as a simple secondary cation. A neighbouring atom with a lone pair (O or N) stabilises a carbocation strongly by resonance as well: CH₃O–CH₂⁺ ↔ CH₃O⁺=CH₂.

Because they are so eager to become more stable, carbocations can rearrange. A hydrogen (with its bonding pair, a hydride shift) or an alkyl group (a methyl shift) moves from a neighbouring carbon to the positive carbon, if this converts a less stable cation into a more stable one: for example, a secondary cation next to a tertiary carbon becomes a tertiary cation. Rearrangements explain some unexpected products in Chapters 7, 9 and 10.

docs.title: Carbanions
docs.text: A carbanion has a carbon with three bonds and a lone pair, carrying a negative charge. Carbanions are strong bases and strong nucleophiles. Their stability follows the opposite order to carbocations, because alkyl groups donate electrons and destabilise a negative charge: methyl > primary > secondary > tertiary. Like other anions, carbanions are stabilised by resonance (as in the enolate ions of Chapter 11, where the charge is shared with a carbonyl oxygen), by electronegative groups nearby and by greater s character (the ethynide ion, HC≡C⁻).

docs.title: Radicals
docs.text:
A carbon radical has three bonds and one unpaired electron, seven valence electrons in all. It is neutral but very reactive, because it needs one more electron to complete its octet. Radical stability follows the same order as carbocation stability, for similar reasons: tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl, with allylic and benzylic radicals stabilised further by resonance. This order explains why radical bromination prefers tertiary C–H bonds (Chapter 6).

Intermediate Electrons on carbon Charge Shape Stabilised by carbocation 6 + trigonal planar (sp²) alkyl groups, resonance, adjacent lone pairs radical 7 0 nearly planar alkyl groups, resonance carbanion 8 − pyramidal (sp³) unless conjugated resonance, electronegative groups, s character

Table 5.1. The three carbon-centred reactive intermediates.

docs.title: 5.7 Energy: will it go, and how fast?
docs.text: Two separate questions decide the outcome of a reaction. Thermodynamics asks whether the products are more stable than the reactants: where does the equilibrium lie? Kinetics asks how fast equilibrium is reached. A reaction can be strongly favourable yet immeasurably slow; a mixture of methane and air can stand for years at room temperature until a spark supplies the energy to start it.

docs.title: Thermodynamics
docs.text:
The position of an equilibrium is set by the standard Gibbs energy change, \(\Delta G^\circ\):

\[ \Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ = -RT \ln K \]

A negative \(\Delta G^\circ\) means that products are favoured (\(K > 1\)). At 298 K, every 5.7 kJ mol⁻¹ of \(\Delta G^\circ\) changes \(K\) by a factor of ten. In many organic reactions the entropy term is small and \(\Delta H\) gives a good guide. Bond energies let you estimate \(\Delta H\): add the energies of the bonds broken and subtract those of the bonds formed.

Example 5.2: Estimating ΔH from bond energies

For CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl, using bond dissociation energies (kJ mol⁻¹): C–H in methane 439, Cl–Cl 242, C–Cl in CH₃Cl 350, H–Cl 431.

Bonds broken: 439 + 242 = 681. Bonds formed: 350 + 431 = 781.

ΔH = 681 − 781 = −100 kJ mol⁻¹. The reaction is strongly exothermic; yet methane and chlorine do not react in the dark at room temperature, because the first step (breaking a bond) has a high energy barrier. Light provides the energy to split Cl₂ into radicals and start the reaction (Chapter 6).

docs.title: Kinetics and energy profiles
docs.text:
A reaction energy profile plots energy against the reaction coordinate, a measure of how far the reaction has progressed. Reactants must pass over an energy barrier to become products. The top of the barrier is the transition state, marked ‡: the arrangement of highest energy along the path, in which old bonds are partly broken and new bonds partly formed. A transition state lasts no longer than a single molecular vibration and cannot be isolated. The height of the barrier from the reactants is the activation energy, \(E_\mathrm{a}\). The larger \(E_\mathrm{a}\), the slower the reaction.

Figure 5.4 Reaction energy profiles. Reaction energy profiles. (a) A one-step reaction passes through a single transition state; the activation energy is the height of the barrier and ΔH is the energy difference between products and reactants. (b) A two-step reaction passes through an intermediate, which sits in a shallow energy well between two transition states. The step with the highest transition state, here the first, is the rate-determining step.

In a reaction of several steps, an intermediate lies in a dip between two transition states. It is a real species with a finite lifetime, and it can sometimes be detected or trapped. The overall rate is controlled by the step with the highest transition state, the rate-determining step. Only the species involved up to and including that step appear in the rate equation, which is one of the main experimental tests of a mechanism.

Reaction rates increase with temperature, because a larger fraction of molecules then has enough energy to cross the barrier; as a rough rule of thumb, many reactions near room temperature go about two to three times faster for a 10 °C rise. A catalyst speeds up a reaction by providing a different path with a lower activation energy. It is not consumed, and it does not change the position of the equilibrium: it speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally.

The Hammond postulate links the two kinds of picture: a transition state resembles the species (reactant, intermediate or product) closest to it in energy. For an endothermic step that forms a carbocation, the transition state resembles the carbocation, so anything that stabilises the carbocation also lowers the barrier. This is why reactions that pass through more stable carbocations are faster.

docs.title: 5.8 Kinds of reaction
docs.text:
Most organic reactions belong to one of four types:

  • Addition: two reactants combine into one product. Alkenes add HBr: CH₂=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CH₂Br (Chapter 7). Carbonyl groups add nucleophiles (Chapter 11).
  • Elimination: one reactant splits into two products, usually forming a π bond. Bromoethane loses HBr with a strong base to form ethene (Chapter 9). Elimination is the reverse of addition.
  • Substitution: one group replaces another. Hydroxide replaces bromide: CH₃Br + OH⁻ → CH₃OH + Br⁻ (Chapter 9). Benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition (Chapter 8).
  • Rearrangement: the atoms of one molecule reorganise into a constitutional isomer.

docs.title: Oxidation and reduction in organic chemistry
docs.text:
In organic chemistry it is usually easier to judge oxidation and reduction by counting bonds than by electron transfer. A carbon is oxidised when it gains bonds to more electronegative atoms (O, N, halogens) or loses bonds to hydrogen; it is reduced when it gains bonds to hydrogen or loses bonds to electronegative atoms. The series

\[ \mathrm{CH_4 \;\rightarrow\; CH_3OH \;\rightarrow\; H_2C{=}O \;\rightarrow\; HCOOH \;\rightarrow\; CO_2} \]

is a sequence of increasing oxidation of carbon: zero, one, two, three and four bonds to oxygen. The addition of H₂ to an alkene is a reduction; the conversion of an alcohol into a ketone is an oxidation (Chapter 10).

docs.title: 5.9 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • A mechanism describes a reaction step by step in terms of electron movement.
  • Homolysis gives radicals (fish-hook arrows); heterolysis gives ions (full arrows).
  • Nucleophiles donate electron pairs (lone pairs, π bonds); electrophiles accept them (empty orbitals, δ+ atoms with leaving groups).
  • A curly arrow moves one electron pair from its tail (lone pair or bond) to its head (atom or new bond). Never exceed an octet; conserve charge.
  • Four basic patterns: loss of a leaving group, nucleophilic attack, proton transfer, and a π bond attacking an electrophile. Rearrangements are a fifth.
  • Carbocation and radical stability: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl, increased further by resonance (allylic, benzylic). Carbanions follow the reverse order.
  • ΔG° decides the position of equilibrium; the activation energy decides the rate. Intermediates sit in energy wells; transition states sit at energy maxima. The highest barrier is the rate-determining step.
  • Reactions are additions, eliminations, substitutions or rearrangements. Gaining bonds to O, N or halogen is oxidation; gaining bonds to H is reduction.

docs.title: 5.10 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Classify each species as a nucleophile, an electrophile or both: (a) CN⁻; (b) H₃O⁺; (c) CH₃CH₂⁺; (d) NH₃; (e) BF₃; (f) CH₂=CH₂; (g) the carbon of CH₃–Br; (h) H₂O.

Answer

Nucleophiles: (a) CN⁻, (d) NH₃, (f) ethene (through its π bond). Electrophiles: (b) H₃O⁺ (delivers H⁺), (c) the carbocation, (e) BF₃, (g) the δ+ carbon of bromomethane. (h) Water is a nucleophile through its oxygen lone pairs and a weak electrophile (as an acid) through its hydrogens; in most reactions it acts as a nucleophile or a base.

Exercise 2

Find the error in each description and correct it. (a) "In the reaction of H–Cl with water, an arrow is drawn from H⁺ to the oxygen lone pair." (b) "Hydroxide adds to the carbon of bromomethane, giving a carbon with five bonds, which then loses bromide." (c) "Cl₂ splits in light: one curly arrow from the Cl–Cl bond to one chlorine."

Answer

(a) The arrow must start at the electrons: from the oxygen lone pair to the H, with a second arrow from the H–Cl bond to Cl. (b) Carbon cannot have five bonds. The C–Br bond breaks as the O–C bond forms, in a single step: one arrow from the hydroxide lone pair to the carbon, and one from the C–Br bond to Br. (c) Homolysis is shown with two fish-hook arrows, one from the bond to each chlorine. A single full arrow would describe heterolysis into Cl⁺ and Cl⁻.

Exercise 3

Draw the products and assign formal charges for each step: (a) the lone pair of ammonia attacks the carbon of the methyl cation, CH₃⁺; (b) the π bond of propene attacks H⁺ so that the new C–H bond forms at C1.

Answer
