(a) CH₃–NH₃⁺: nitrogen now has four bonds and no lone pair, formal charge +1. Overall charge +1 is conserved.

(b) The π electrons form a C–H bond to C1, so C1 becomes CH₃ and C2 loses its share of the π pair: CH₃–C⁺H–CH₃, the propan-2-yl (isopropyl) cation, a secondary carbocation. Total charge +1 is conserved.

Exercise 4

Rank in order of increasing stability, and explain: (a) CH₃⁺, (CH₃)₂CH⁺, CH₃CH₂⁺, (CH₃)₃C⁺; (b) CH₃CH₂CH₂⁺ and CH₂=CHCH₂⁺.

Answer

(a) CH₃⁺ < CH₃CH₂⁺ < (CH₃)₂CH⁺ < (CH₃)₃C⁺. Each additional alkyl group stabilises the positive carbon by hyperconjugation and by its weak inductive donation.

(b) CH₃CH₂CH₂⁺ < CH₂=CHCH₂⁺. The allylic cation is stabilised by resonance: the charge is shared between C1 and C3 (CH₂=CH–CH₂⁺ ↔ ⁺CH₂–CH=CH₂).

Exercise 5

Use bond energies to estimate ΔH for the addition of HBr to ethene, CH₂=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CH₂Br. Take: C=C 610, H–Br 366, C–C 350, C–H 410, C–Br 285 (all kJ mol⁻¹).

Answer

The C=C becomes C–C, and one C–H and one C–Br bond are formed, while H–Br is broken. Bonds broken: C=C (610) + H–Br (366) = 976. Bonds formed: C–C (350) + C–H (410) + C–Br (285) = 1045. ΔH ≈ 976 − 1045 = −69 kJ mol⁻¹. Additions to alkenes are usually exothermic, because a π bond and a σ bond are replaced by two stronger σ bonds.

Exercise 6

On an energy profile for a two-step reaction in which the second transition state is higher than the first: (a) which step is rate-determining? (b) Where is the intermediate? (c) If the overall reaction is exothermic, are the products above or below the reactants?

Answer

(a) The second step, because its transition state is the highest point on the profile. (b) In the energy well between the two transition states. (c) Below the reactants.

Exercise 7

Classify each change as oxidation, reduction or neither for the carbon shown in bold: (a) CH₃CH₂OH → CH₃CHO; (b) CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃CH₃; (c) CH₃CH₂Br → CH₃CH₂OH; (d) CH₃COCH₃ → CH₃CH(OH)CH₃.

Answer

(a) Oxidation: the carbon loses a C–H bond and gains a second bond to oxygen. (b) Reduction: each carbon gains a bond to H. (c) Neither: one bond to an electronegative atom (Br) is replaced by another (O). (d) Reduction: the carbon gains a C–H bond and loses one of its two bonds to oxygen.

docs.title: 5.11 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of mechanisms

Exercise 1

A fish-hook (half-headed) arrow shows the movement of

  1. a pair of electrons
  2. a single electron
  3. a proton
  4. a whole atom
Answer

Exercise 2

Which is NOT a nucleophile?

  1. CH₃O⁻
  2. NH₃
  3. BF₃
  4. CH₂=CH₂
Answer

Exercise 3

The tail of a curly arrow must start at

  1. a positive charge
  2. a hydrogen atom
  3. a lone pair or a bond

Exercise 4

Which carbocation is the most stable?

  1. CH₃⁺
  2. CH₃CH₂⁺
  3. (CH₃)₂CH⁺
  4. (CH₃)₃C⁺

Exercise 5

The rate-determining step of a multistep reaction is the step

  1. that comes first
  2. with the highest-energy transition state
  3. that releases the most energy
  4. that forms the products
Answer

with the highest-energy transition state

Exercise 6

A catalyst

  1. shifts the equilibrium towards products
  2. lowers the activation energy
  3. raises ΔG
  4. is used up in the reaction
Answer

lowers the activation energy

Exercise 7

Match each reaction to its type.

ABCH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → BrCH₂CH₂BrsubstitutionCH₃CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂OH + Br⁻eliminationCH₃CH₂Br → CH₂=CH₂ + HBraddition Answer

CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → BrCH₂CH₂Br — addition; CH₃CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂OH + Br⁻ — substitution; CH₃CH₂Br → CH₂=CH₂ + HBr — elimination

docs.title: Chapter 14: Spectroscopy: IR, NMR and Mass Spectrometry
docs.text:
How chemists find out what they have made

Until the middle of the twentieth century, working out the structure of an unknown compound could take years of chemical tests, degradations and syntheses. Today a few milligrams of sample and an hour of instrument time usually suffice. Three techniques do most of the work. Infrared spectroscopy identifies functional groups. Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy maps the carbon–hydrogen framework. Mass spectrometry gives the molar mass and clues from the way the molecule breaks apart. This chapter explains what each technique measures, how to read the spectra, and how to combine the evidence to solve a structure.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  • relate the energy, frequency, wavelength and wavenumber of electromagnetic radiation;
  • explain why bonds absorb infrared radiation at characteristic wavenumbers, and identify the main functional groups from an IR spectrum;
  • predict the number of signals in ¹H and ¹³C NMR spectra from molecular symmetry;
  • use chemical shift, integration and splitting (the n + 1 rule) to interpret ¹H NMR spectra;
  • identify the molecular ion in a mass spectrum, use isotope patterns for chlorine and bromine, and explain common fragment ions;
  • combine the molecular formula, degree of unsaturation and spectra to deduce the structure of a simple unknown.

docs.title: 14.1 Light and molecules
docs.text:
Spectroscopy studies how matter absorbs or emits electromagnetic radiation. Radiation can be described by its wavelength λ, its frequency ν (with \(c = \lambda u\)), or its wavenumber \( ilde{ u} = 1/\lambda\), usually given in cm⁻¹. The energy of one photon is

\[ E = h u = rac{hc}{\lambda} = hc ilde{ u} \]

where \(h\) is Planck's constant. Molecules can absorb a photon only if its energy matches the gap between two of their energy levels. Different regions of the spectrum probe different kinds of motion:

Region Typical wavelength What it excites Technique radio waves metres nuclear spin in a magnetic field NMR infrared 2.5 to 25 μm (4000 to 400 cm⁻¹) bond vibrations IR spectroscopy ultraviolet and visible 200 to 800 nm electrons in π systems UV–visible spectroscopy

Table 14.1. Regions of the electromagnetic spectrum used in organic chemistry.

Mass spectrometry is not, strictly, spectroscopy: it does not involve absorption of light but separates ions by their mass. It is always used alongside the spectroscopic methods.

docs.title: Why bonds absorb infrared light
docs.text:
Chemical bonds are not rigid. They stretch and bend, like springs joining balls, at frequencies in the infrared range. A bond absorbs infrared radiation of the same frequency as its vibration, provided that the vibration changes the dipole moment of the molecule. The frequency depends on two things, as for a spring:

\[ \tilde{\nu} \propto \sqrt{\frac{k}{\mu}} \]

where \(k\) is the force constant (the stiffness of the bond) and \(\mu\) the reduced mass of the two atoms. So:

  • Stronger bonds vibrate faster. C≡C (about 2150 cm⁻¹) > C=C (about 1650 cm⁻¹) > C–C (about 1200 cm⁻¹).
  • Bonds to light atoms vibrate faster. C–H, O–H and N–H stretches all appear at high wavenumbers, between 2850 and 3600 cm⁻¹.

An IR spectrum plots the percentage of light transmitted against wavenumber, decreasing from left to right; absorptions appear as dips ("bands" or "peaks") pointing down.

Figure 14.1 An infrared correlation chart. Characteristic infrared absorptions of the main bonds. Stretches of bonds to hydrogen appear above 2500 cm⁻¹, triple bonds near 2100 to 2260 cm⁻¹, and double bonds, including the strong carbonyl band, between 1500 and 1800 cm⁻¹. Below about 1500 cm⁻¹ lies the fingerprint region, which is complex but characteristic of each compound.

docs.title: Reading an IR spectrum
docs.text:
Focus on the region above 1500 cm⁻¹ and ask a few questions in turn:

  1. Is there a strong band at 1680 to 1750 cm⁻¹? That is a C=O stretch, usually the strongest band in the spectrum. Within this range, esters (about 1735 to 1750) tend to be higher than aldehydes (about 1725) and ketones (about 1715), and amides lower (about 1650 to 1690). Conjugation with a C=C or a benzene ring lowers the wavenumber by about 20 to 30 cm⁻¹.
  2. Is there a broad band at 3200 to 3550 cm⁻¹? That is an O–H stretch of an alcohol or phenol, broadened by hydrogen bonding. A carboxylic acid O–H is even broader, spreading from about 2500 to 3300 cm⁻¹ and overlapping the C–H bands, together with a C=O band.
  3. Are there one or two sharper bands at 3300 to 3500 cm⁻¹? That is N–H: primary amines and amides (NH₂) show two bands, secondary ones (NH) one.
  4. Where are the C–H stretches? Below 3000 cm⁻¹ means sp³ C–H (alkyl); just above 3000 means sp² C–H (alkene or arene); a sharp band near 3300 means a terminal alkyne ≡C–H.
  5. Is there a band at 2100 to 2260 cm⁻¹? C≡N (sharp, about 2250) or C≡C.
Bond Wavenumber (cm⁻¹) Appearance O–H (alcohol, phenol) 3200–3550 strong, broad O–H (carboxylic acid) 2500–3300 very broad N–H (amine, amide) 3300–3500 medium, sharper; NH₂ gives two bands C–H (sp³) 2850–2960 medium to strong C–H (sp²) 3000–3100 medium ≡C–H (sp) about 3300 strong, sharp C≡N about 2250 medium, sharp C≡C 2100–2260 weak to medium C=O 1680–1750 strong, sharp C=C (alkene) 1620–1680 variable C=C (aromatic ring) about 1450–1600 several bands C–O 1000–1300 strong

Table 14.2. Characteristic infrared absorptions.

Figure 14.2 IR spectra of an alcohol and a ketone. Schematic infrared spectra of ethanol and propanone. Ethanol shows a broad, strong O–H band centred near 3350 cm⁻¹ and a strong C–O band near 1050 cm⁻¹, but no carbonyl band. Propanone shows no O–H band but a very strong, sharp C=O band near 1715 cm⁻¹.

The fingerprint region below 1500 cm⁻¹ contains many overlapping bands from bending vibrations and C–C and C–O stretches. It is hard to interpret band by band, but it is unique to each compound: if the spectrum of an unknown matches that of a known compound exactly in this region, the two are the same.

Example 14.1: Using IR to follow a reaction

A student oxidises propan-2-ol to propanone. How would IR spectroscopy show that the reaction is complete?

The starting alcohol has a broad O–H band at about 3300 cm⁻¹ and no C=O band. The product ketone has a strong C=O band at about 1715 cm⁻¹ and no O–H band. The reaction is complete when the O–H band has disappeared and the C=O band is present.

docs.title: 14.3 NMR spectroscopy: principles
docs.text: Some atomic nuclei, including ¹H and ¹³C (but not ¹²C or ¹⁶O), behave like tiny magnets because they have a property called nuclear spin. In a strong external magnetic field, such a nucleus can line up with the field (lower energy) or against it (higher energy). Radio waves of exactly the right frequency make it flip from the lower to the higher state: the nucleus is in resonance. An NMR spectrometer places the sample, dissolved in a solvent without ordinary hydrogen (usually CDCl₃, deuterochloroform), in a powerful magnet and measures the frequencies at which the nuclei absorb.

docs.title: Chemical shift
docs.text:
If every hydrogen absorbed at the same frequency, NMR would be useless. It is useful because the electrons around each nucleus shield it slightly from the external field. A nucleus surrounded by more electron density feels a smaller field and resonates at a lower frequency (it is shielded, or upfield); a nucleus near electronegative atoms has less electron density around it, feels more of the field and resonates at a higher frequency (it is deshielded, or downfield).

The position of a signal is reported as its chemical shift, δ, in parts per million (ppm) relative to a reference compound, tetramethylsilane, (CH₃)₄Si (TMS), which is set at δ = 0. Using ppm makes δ independent of the strength of the magnet. Most ¹H signals fall between 0 and 13 ppm.

Figure 14.3 ¹H chemical shifts. Approximate ¹H chemical shifts. Hydrogens on sp³ carbon far from electronegative atoms appear at 0.8 to 1.8 ppm. A neighbouring carbonyl group or benzene ring moves them to about 2.0 to 2.7 ppm, and an attached oxygen or halogen to 3.3 to 4.5 ppm. Alkene hydrogens appear at 4.5 to 6.5 ppm, aromatic hydrogens at 6.5 to 8.5 ppm, aldehyde hydrogens at 9 to 10 ppm and carboxylic acid hydrogens at 10 to 13 ppm. O–H and N–H signals vary widely.

Two effects explain the chart. Electronegative atoms pull electron density away and deshield nearby hydrogens, and the effect falls off with distance: in 1-bromopropane, the CH₂ next to Br is at about 3.4 ppm, the middle CH₂ at about 1.9 and the CH₃ at about 1.0. π electrons circulating in the applied field create local fields that strongly deshield hydrogens on alkenes, on aromatic rings (the ring current) and on aldehyde carbonyl carbons.

docs.title: 14.4 Reading a ¹H NMR spectrum
docs.text: A ¹H NMR spectrum gives four pieces of information.

docs.title: 1. The number of signals: equivalent hydrogens
docs.text:
Hydrogens in identical chemical environments (related by the symmetry of the molecule or by fast rotation) are chemically equivalent and give a single signal. To count the environments, imagine replacing each hydrogen in turn by another group: hydrogens that give the same compound are equivalent.

  • Ethane, CH₃CH₃: all six H are equivalent: one signal.
  • Propane, CH₃CH₂CH₃: the six CH₃ hydrogens are equivalent, the two CH₂ hydrogens another set: two signals.
  • Ethyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃: three signals (CH₃CO, OCH₂ and the CH₃ of the ethyl group).
  • Methylbenzene: the CH₃ gives one signal; the aromatic hydrogens fall into ortho, meta and para sets that often overlap near 7.2 ppm.

docs.title: 2. The chemical shift: what kind of hydrogen
docs.text: The position of each signal tells you its environment (Figure 14.3).

docs.title: 3. The integration: how many hydrogens
docs.text: The area under each signal is proportional to the number of hydrogens producing it. The instrument prints an integral trace or values; these give the ratio of hydrogens, which must be scaled to the molecular formula. Ethyl ethanoate gives integrals in the ratio 2 : 3 : 3.

docs.title: 4. The splitting: how many neighbours
docs.text:
Hydrogens on adjacent carbons interact through the bonding electrons (spin–spin coupling), and their signals split into several lines. For hydrogens with \(n\) equivalent neighbouring hydrogens (usually on the next carbon, three bonds away), the signal is split into n + 1 lines: the n + 1 rule.

Neighbouring H (n) Lines (n + 1) Name Relative intensities 0 1 singlet (s) 1 1 2 doublet (d) 1 : 1 2 3 triplet (t) 1 : 2 : 1 3 4 quartet (q) 1 : 3 : 3 : 1 4 5 quintet 1 : 4 : 6 : 4 : 1 6 7 septet 1 : 6 : 15 : 20 : 15 : 6 : 1

Table 14.3. Splitting patterns from the n + 1 rule. The intensities follow Pascal's triangle.

The spacing between the lines, the coupling constant \(J\), is measured in hertz (about 7 Hz for neighbouring hydrogens on freely rotating sp³ carbons). Two groups that are coupled to each other show the same \(J\), which helps match them up. Equivalent hydrogens do not split each other, and hydrogens on O and N usually appear as broad singlets because they exchange rapidly between molecules.

Figure 14.4 The ¹H NMR spectrum of ethyl ethanoate. Schematic ¹H NMR spectrum of ethyl ethanoate. The OCH₂ group, deshielded by oxygen, appears at 4.1 ppm as a quartet (three neighbouring H on CH₃). The CH₃ of the ethyl group appears at 1.2 ppm as a triplet (two neighbours on CH₂). The CH₃C=O group, next to the carbonyl and with no neighbouring H, appears at 2.0 ppm as a singlet. The areas are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 3.

Key idea

A quartet (2H) and a triplet (3H) with the same coupling constant mean an ethyl group, CH₃CH₂–. A septet (1H) and a doublet (6H) mean an isopropyl group, (CH₃)₂CH–. A singlet (9H) near 1 ppm means a tert-butyl group. Learning to spot these patterns speeds up every problem.

Example 14.2: Ethyl ethanoate or methyl propanoate?

Two isomeric esters, C₄H₈O₂, are ethyl ethanoate (CH₃COOCH₂CH₃) and methyl propanoate (CH₃CH₂COOCH₃). One gives signals at δ 3.7 (s, 3H), 2.3 (q, 2H), 1.1 (t, 3H). Which is it?

Both have an ethyl group (quartet + triplet) and a methyl singlet. The difference is where the groups are attached. In this spectrum the singlet is at 3.7 ppm, typical of CH₃ on oxygen, and the quartet at 2.3 ppm, typical of CH₂ next to C=O. So the methyl is on oxygen and the ethyl on the carbonyl: methyl propanoate. (Ethyl ethanoate has the reverse: a singlet at 2.0 and a quartet at 4.1.)

docs.title: Identifying O–H and N–H signals
docs.text: Because O–H and N–H hydrogens exchange with deuterium, adding a drop of D₂O to the sample and shaking replaces them with D, which does not appear in a ¹H spectrum. The signal that disappears is the O–H or N–H.

docs.title: 14.5 ¹³C NMR spectroscopy
docs.text:
Only about 1.1% of carbon atoms are ¹³C, the isotope with nuclear spin, so ¹³C spectra are weaker and take longer to record. They are normally run with proton decoupling, which removes the splitting by hydrogens, so each kind of carbon gives a single line. Two pieces of information are used:

  • The number of signals equals the number of different carbon environments. Propan-1-ol gives three signals; propan-2-ol, which is symmetrical, gives two. Benzene gives one; methylbenzene gives five (CH₃ and four kinds of ring carbon).
  • The chemical shift, which spans about 0 to 220 ppm: sp³ carbons at about 0 to 50 ppm (higher, about 50 to 90 ppm, when bonded to O or N), alkene and aromatic carbons at about 100 to 150 ppm, and carbonyl carbons at about 160 to 220 ppm (esters, acids and amides about 160 to 185; aldehydes and ketones about 190 to 220).

Peak areas in routine ¹³C spectra are not reliably proportional to the number of carbons, so integration is not used.

docs.title: 14.6 Mass spectrometry
docs.text:
In the commonest method, electron ionisation, the vaporised sample is bombarded with high-energy electrons, which knock an electron out of each molecule to give a radical cation, the molecular ion, M⁺•:

\[ \mathrm{M + e^- \rightarrow M^{+\bullet} + 2\,e^-} \]

The ions are accelerated and separated according to their mass-to-charge ratio, m/z. Since nearly all ions carry a single charge, m/z is the mass of the ion. The mass spectrum plots the relative abundance of each ion against m/z, with the most abundant ion (the base peak) set to 100.

docs.title: The molecular ion
docs.text: The peak of highest m/z (ignoring small isotope peaks) is usually the molecular ion, and it gives the relative molecular mass. With high-resolution instruments, masses are measured to four or more decimal places, which is enough to decide the molecular formula: CO, N₂ and C₂H₄ all have nominal mass 28, but their exact masses differ in the third decimal place.

docs.title: Isotope peaks
docs.text:
Elements with more than one common isotope give characteristic patterns:

  • Carbon: about 1.1% of carbon is ¹³C, so a molecule with \(n\) carbons shows a small M + 1 peak about \(1.1n\)% the height of M.
  • Chlorine: ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl occur in a ratio of about 3 : 1, so a compound with one chlorine shows peaks at M and M + 2 in the ratio 3 : 1.
  • Bromine: ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br are nearly equal in abundance, so one bromine gives M and M + 2 of nearly equal height.

The nitrogen rule is a further check: a compound containing C, H, O and an odd number of nitrogen atoms has an odd molecular mass; with no nitrogen (or an even number), the mass is even.

docs.title: Fragmentation
docs.text:
The molecular ion has excess energy and often breaks into a cation and a neutral radical. Only the charged fragment is detected. Bonds break preferentially where they give stable cations:

  • next to a carbonyl group, giving a resonance-stabilised acylium ion, R–C≡O⁺;
  • at branch points, giving more substituted carbocations;
  • at a benzylic position (C₆H₅CH₂⁺, m/z 91, is common in compounds with a benzyl group).

Differences between peaks correspond to the neutral pieces lost: 15 (CH₃), 29 (C₂H₅ or CHO), 18 (H₂O, typical of alcohols), 28 (CO or C₂H₄).

Figure 14.5 The mass spectrum of butanone. A schematic mass spectrum of butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃ (Mr 72). The molecular ion appears at m/z 72. Cleavage of the bonds on either side of the carbonyl group gives the acylium ions CH₃CO⁺ (m/z 43, here the base peak) and CH₃CH₂CO⁺ (m/z 57), and the ethyl cation (m/z 29).

docs.title: 14.7 UV–visible spectroscopy in brief
docs.text: Molecules with conjugated π systems absorb ultraviolet or visible light, which promotes a π electron to a higher, empty orbital. The more extended the conjugation, the smaller the energy gap and the longer the wavelength absorbed. Ethene absorbs at about 170 nm in the far ultraviolet; buta-1,3-diene at about 217 nm. A molecule with a long chain of alternating double bonds, such as β-carotene (eleven conjugated C=C bonds), absorbs blue light in the visible region and appears orange. Azo dyes (Section 13.5) owe their colours to the same effect. UV–visible spectroscopy is used mainly to measure concentrations (via the Beer–Lambert law) and to study conjugated systems.

docs.title: 14.8 Solving structures: putting it together
docs.text:
A systematic approach works best:

  1. Molecular formula (from mass spectrometry or analysis). Calculate the degree of unsaturation (Section 2.6).
  2. IR: which functional groups are present, and which are absent?
  3. ¹³C NMR: how many carbon environments? Is there a C=O, aromatic or alkene carbon?
  4. ¹H NMR: how many kinds of H; how many of each (integration); what environments (shift); which groups are neighbours (splitting)?
  5. Assemble fragments, and check that the proposed structure accounts for every signal and for the formula.

Example 14.3: An unknown ketone

Compound X, C₄H₈O, shows a strong IR band at 1715 cm⁻¹ and no band above 3100 cm⁻¹ except C–H. Its ¹H NMR spectrum has δ 2.45 (q, 2H), 2.14 (s, 3H), 1.06 (t, 3H). The mass spectrum shows peaks at m/z 72, 57, 43 and 29. Identify X.

Formula: DBE = (8 + 2 − 8)/2 = 1, one ring or π bond.

IR: 1715 cm⁻¹ is a C=O (ketone or aldehyde); no O–H. The π bond is the C=O.

¹H NMR: a quartet (2H) and triplet (3H) form an ethyl group; the CH₂ at 2.45 ppm is next to C=O. A singlet (3H) at 2.14 is a CH₃ next to C=O with no neighbouring H. No signal at 9 to 10 ppm, so not an aldehyde.

Structure: CH₃–CO–CH₂CH₃, butanone. The mass spectrum agrees: M⁺ at 72 and acylium ions at 43 (CH₃CO⁺) and 57 (C₂H₅CO⁺) (Figure 14.5).

docs.title: 14.9 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • \(E = h\nu = hc/\lambda\). IR excites bond vibrations; NMR flips nuclear spins in a magnetic field; UV–visible excites π electrons.
  • IR: stronger bonds and lighter atoms absorb at higher wavenumber. Key bands: O–H 3200–3550 (broad), acid O–H 2500–3300, N–H 3300–3500, C=O 1680–1750 (strong), C≡N about 2250.
  • ¹H NMR: number of signals = number of environments; chemical shift = environment (δ relative to TMS); integration = relative number of H; splitting = n + 1 lines for n neighbouring H.
  • ¹³C NMR: one line per carbon environment (proton-decoupled), δ 0 to 220; C=O 160 to 220.
  • Mass spectrometry: M⁺• gives the molar mass; Cl gives M : M+2 = 3 : 1, Br gives 1 : 1; fragments form stable cations such as acylium ions.
  • Solve structures by combining the formula, DBE, IR, ¹³C and ¹H NMR, and MS, and check every signal.

docs.title: 14.10 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

How would you distinguish by IR spectroscopy alone between: (a) cyclohexanol and cyclohexanone; (b) propanoic acid and propan-1-ol; (c) hex-1-yne and hex-2-yne?

Answer

(a) Cyclohexanol shows a broad O–H band near 3300 cm⁻¹ and no C=O; cyclohexanone shows a strong C=O near 1715 cm⁻¹ and no O–H. (b) Propanoic acid shows a very broad O–H from about 2500 to 3300 cm⁻¹ and a C=O near 1710 cm⁻¹; propan-1-ol shows a narrower O–H near 3300 cm⁻¹ and no C=O. (c) Hex-1-yne, a terminal alkyne, shows a sharp ≡C–H stretch near 3300 cm⁻¹ and a C≡C band near 2100 cm⁻¹; hex-2-yne has no ≡C–H, and its C≡C band is weak or absent because the nearly symmetrical bond hardly changes the dipole moment as it vibrates.

Exercise 2

How many signals would you expect in the ¹H NMR spectrum and in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of: (a) propanone; (b) butanone; (c) 1,4-dimethylbenzene; (d) 2-methylpropan-2-ol?

Answer

(a) ¹H: 1 (six equivalent H); ¹³C: 2 (CH₃ and C=O). (b) ¹H: 3; ¹³C: 4. (c) ¹H: 2 (CH₃ and the four equivalent ring H); ¹³C: 3 (CH₃, the two ring carbons bearing CH₃, and the four ring CH carbons). (d) ¹H: 2 (nine CH₃ H and the OH); ¹³C: 2 (CH₃ and the central carbon).

Exercise 3

Predict the ¹H NMR spectrum (shift, integration, splitting) of 1-chloropropane, CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl.

Answer

Three signals: CH₂Cl at about 3.5 ppm (2H, triplet, two neighbours on the middle CH₂); middle CH₂ at about 1.8 ppm (2H, a sextet, five neighbours, 3 + 2, if the coupling constants are similar); CH₃ at about 1.0 ppm (3H, triplet).

Exercise 4

A compound C₃H₇Br has a ¹H NMR spectrum with a doublet at δ 1.7 (6H) and a septet at δ 4.2 (1H). Its mass spectrum shows two peaks of equal height at m/z 122 and 124. Identify it.

Answer

The two molecular ion peaks of equal height, two mass units apart, show one bromine atom. A doublet (6H) and a septet (1H) indicate an isopropyl group, (CH₃)₂CH–; the CH at 4.2 ppm is deshielded by the attached Br. The compound is 2-bromopropane, (CH₃)₂CHBr. (C₃H₇⁷⁹Br = 122, C₃H₇⁸¹Br = 124.)

Exercise 5

A compound has a molecular ion at m/z 78 and an M + 2 peak at m/z 80 one-third as high. Its ¹H NMR spectrum shows a doublet (6H) and a septet (1H). Suggest a structure.

Answer

An M : M + 2 ratio of 3 : 1 indicates one chlorine. Subtracting ³⁵Cl (35) from 78 leaves 43, which is C₃H₇. The isopropyl pattern (doublet 6H, septet 1H) gives 2-chloropropane, (CH₃)₂CHCl.

Exercise 6

Compound Y, C₈H₈O, has IR bands at 3060 cm⁻¹ and 1690 cm⁻¹. Its ¹H NMR spectrum shows δ 7.4 to 8.0 (m, 5H) and 2.6 (s, 3H). Identify Y and explain the C=O wavenumber.

Answer

DBE = (16 + 2 − 8)/2 = 5: a benzene ring (4) plus one C=O. The 5H multiplet at 7.4 to 8.0 is a monosubstituted benzene ring (C₆H₅–); the band at 3060 cm⁻¹ is aromatic C–H. The singlet (3H) at 2.6 is a CH₃ next to C=O. Y is 1-phenylethanone (acetophenone), C₆H₅COCH₃. The C=O band (1690 cm⁻¹) is lower than for a simple ketone (1715) because the carbonyl is conjugated with the benzene ring, which lowers its bond order slightly.

Exercise 7

An alcohol C₄H₁₀O shows only two signals in its ¹H NMR spectrum: a singlet at δ 1.3 (9H) and a broad singlet at δ 2.0 (1H) that disappears on shaking with D₂O. Its ¹³C NMR spectrum has two lines. Identify it.

Answer

The 9H singlet is a tert-butyl group; the 1H broad singlet that exchanges with D₂O is the OH. Two carbon environments fit (CH₃)₃C–OH: 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

docs.title: 14.11 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of spectroscopy

Exercise 1

A strong, sharp IR band at about 1715 cm⁻¹ indicates

  1. an O-H group
  2. a C=O group
  3. a C≡N group
  4. an aromatic ring
Answer

a C=O group

Exercise 2

In ¹H NMR, the area under a signal tells you

  1. the number of neighbouring H
  2. the relative number of H producing it
  3. the type of carbon
  4. the molar mass
Answer

the relative number of H producing it

Exercise 3

A CH₂ group next to a CH₃ group (and no other H neighbours) appears as a

  1. singlet
  2. doublet
  3. triplet
  4. quartet
Answer

quartet

Exercise 4

How many signals are there in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of propan-2-ol?

Answer

2 / two

Exercise 5

A mass spectrum shows M and M + 2 peaks of nearly equal height. The compound contains

  1. one chlorine atom
  2. one bromine atom
  3. one nitrogen atom
  4. one sulfur atom
Answer

one bromine atom

Exercise 6

TMS is used in NMR as

  1. the solvent
  2. the reference with δ = 0
  3. a source of deuterium
  4. a catalyst
Answer

the reference with δ = 0

Exercise 7

Which ¹H chemical shift is typical of an aldehyde CHO hydrogen?

  1. 1.0 ppm
  2. 3.5 ppm
  3. 7.3 ppm
  4. 9.7 ppm
Answer

9.7 ppm

docs.title: Chapter 1: Structure and Bonding
docs.text:
Electrons, shapes and the ways we draw molecules

Everything in organic chemistry follows from the way carbon shares its electrons. A carbon atom forms four bonds, it bonds strongly to other carbon atoms, and it does so in three distinct geometries. Those three facts allow an almost unlimited number of stable molecules. This chapter builds the picture of bonding that the rest of the book relies on: how to count electrons and draw correct structures, how electronegativity makes bonds polar, how hybridisation explains molecular shape, and how resonance describes molecules that a single drawing cannot capture.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  • draw correct Lewis structures for organic molecules and ions, and assign formal charges;
  • predict bond polarity from electronegativity and recognise polar molecules;
  • state the hybridisation (sp³, sp² or sp) of carbon, nitrogen and oxygen atoms and predict bond angles and shapes;
  • distinguish σ and π bonds and explain why a double bond does not rotate;
  • read and draw full, condensed and skeletal formulas;
  • draw resonance contributors with curly arrows and judge which contributes most;
  • relate boiling point and solubility to intermolecular forces.

docs.title: 1.1 What organic chemistry is about
docs.text:
Organic chemistry is the chemistry of compounds of carbon. The name is historical: early chemists believed that compounds from living things contained a "vital force" and could not be made from minerals. In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made urea, a compound found in urine, by heating ammonium cyanate, a salt that could be prepared without any living source. Over the following decades the idea of a vital force faded, and the name "organic" stayed for the chemistry of carbon.

Why does one element deserve its own branch of chemistry? Carbon sits in the middle of the second row of the periodic table, with four valence electrons. It neither gives these electrons away easily (as sodium does) nor takes four more easily (as fluorine takes one). Instead it shares them, forming four covalent bonds. Carbon–carbon bonds are strong, so carbon atoms link into chains, branches and rings of any size. Carbon also bonds well to hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulfur and the halogens. The result is many millions of known compounds, more than for all the other elements combined.

Most organic molecules have a skeleton of carbon and hydrogen atoms that is fairly unreactive, decorated with small groups of other atoms that react in predictable ways. These groups are called functional groups (Chapter 2). Learning organic chemistry is largely learning how each functional group behaves, and why.

docs.title: 1.2 Atoms, electrons and the covalent bond
Electron configuration
docs.text:
A carbon atom has six electrons: two in the 1s orbital and four in the second shell, arranged as 2s² 2p². Only the second-shell electrons, the valence electrons, take part in bonding. The number of valence electrons is the group number in the main-group table: hydrogen has 1, carbon 4, nitrogen 5, oxygen 6 and the halogens 7.

Atoms of the second row (carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine) have room for eight electrons in their valence shell, one s orbital and three p orbitals with two electrons each. Bonded atoms tend to arrange themselves so that each has a full shell: eight electrons for second-row atoms (the octet rule) and two for hydrogen.

docs.title: The covalent bond
docs.text:
A covalent bond is a pair of electrons shared between two nuclei. Both nuclei attract the shared pair, and that mutual attraction holds the atoms together. When one atom shares a pair with another, both count the pair towards their octet.

The number of bonds an atom normally forms follows from how many electrons it needs to complete its shell:

Atom Valence electrons Usual number of bonds Lone pairs (neutral) H 1 1 0 C 4 4 0 N 5 3 1 O 6 2 2 F, Cl, Br, I 7 1 3

Table 1.1. Valence and bonding of the common atoms of organic chemistry.

Memorise the last two columns. When you draw a structure, a neutral carbon has four bonds, a neutral nitrogen three bonds and a lone pair, a neutral oxygen two bonds and two lone pairs. Any atom that does not fit this pattern carries a formal charge (Section 1.3).

Key idea

Carbon forms four bonds. In every structure you draw, check that each carbon has exactly four bonds (counting a double bond as two and a triple bond as three) unless it is deliberately shown as a cation, anion or radical.

docs.title: 1.3 Lewis structures and formal charge
docs.text:
A Lewis structure shows every valence electron: bonding pairs as lines and non-bonding pairs (lone pairs) as pairs of dots. To draw one:

  1. Add up the valence electrons of all the atoms. Add one for each negative charge and subtract one for each positive charge.
  2. Connect the atoms with single bonds. (The connectivity usually comes from the formula or the name.)
  3. Use the remaining electrons as lone pairs to complete the octets, starting with the most electronegative atoms.
  4. If an atom still lacks an octet, turn a lone pair on a neighbouring atom into a second (or third) bond.

docs.title: Formal charge
docs.text:
Some atoms in a correct Lewis structure have more or fewer bonds than usual. Such an atom carries a formal charge, worked out by comparing the electrons it "owns" in the structure with the valence electrons of the free atom:

\[ \text{formal charge} = V - N - \frac{B}{2} \]

where \(V\) is the number of valence electrons of the free atom, \(N\) the number of non-bonding electrons on the atom in the structure, and \(B\) the number of bonding electrons around it. Each bond line counts as two bonding electrons.

Example 1.1: Formal charges in the hydroxide and hydronium ions

Hydroxide, OH⁻. Oxygen has one bond (B = 2) and three lone pairs (N = 6). Formal charge = 6 − 6 − 1 = −1. The negative charge sits on oxygen.

Hydronium, H₃O⁺. Oxygen has three bonds (B = 6) and one lone pair (N = 2). Formal charge = 6 − 2 − 3 = +1.

Ammonium, NH₄⁺. Nitrogen has four bonds and no lone pair: 5 − 0 − 4 = +1.

The formal charges in each ion add up to the overall charge, as they always must.

With practice you will not need the formula, because the patterns are few. For the atoms you meet most often:

  • Carbon with four bonds is neutral; with three bonds and no lone pair it is a carbocation (+1); with three bonds and one lone pair it is a carbanion (−1); with three bonds and one unpaired electron it is a radical (neutral).
  • Nitrogen with four bonds is +1; with two bonds and two lone pairs it is −1.
  • Oxygen with three bonds (one lone pair) is +1; with one bond (three lone pairs) it is −1.

Caution: formal charge is bookkeeping

A formal charge tells you which atom has more or fewer electrons than it would in a neutral, normal bonding pattern. It does not always say where the electron density really is. In the hydronium ion, the "+" is written on oxygen, yet oxygen is still the most electron-rich atom: much of the positive charge is actually carried by the hydrogens. Use formal charges to check structures and to follow electrons in mechanisms, not as measured charges.

docs.title: 1.4 Electronegativity and polar bonds
docs.text:
Electronegativity is the tendency of an atom in a molecule to attract the electrons of a bond towards itself. On the Pauling scale the values that matter most in organic chemistry are:

Atom H C N O F Cl Br I Electronegativity 2.2 2.5 3.0 3.4 4.0 3.2 3.0 2.7

Table 1.2. Pauling electronegativities, rounded.

Electronegativity rises across a row (C < N < O < F) and falls down a group (F > Cl > Br > I). When two bonded atoms differ in electronegativity, the shared pair lies closer to the more electronegative atom. The bond is then polar: one end carries a partial negative charge (δ−) and the other a partial positive charge (δ+).

  • The C–H bond is nearly non-polar (difference 0.3). This is why hydrocarbons dissolve poorly in water and are relatively unreactive.
  • C–O, C–N and C–halogen bonds are polar, with carbon δ+. That δ+ carbon is a target for electron-rich reagents, a theme that runs through the whole book.
  • O–H and N–H bonds are strongly polar, with hydrogen δ+. Such hydrogens can be lost as protons (Chapter 4) and can take part in hydrogen bonding (Section 1.8).

A molecule is polar overall when its bond polarities do not cancel. Water is polar because its two O–H bonds point in different directions at an angle. Tetrachloromethane (CCl₄) has four polar C–Cl bonds, but they point to the corners of a regular tetrahedron and cancel, so the molecule has no overall dipole.

docs.title: Shapes from electron pairs
docs.text:
The simplest way to predict shape is valence-shell electron-pair repulsion (VSEPR): the groups of electrons around a central atom (bonds and lone pairs) get as far apart as possible. A double or triple bond counts as one group.

  • Four groups point to the corners of a tetrahedron, 109.5° apart (methane, CH₄). With one lone pair among the four groups the shape is trigonal pyramidal (ammonia, angle about 107°); with two lone pairs it is bent (water, about 104.5°).
  • Three groups lie in a plane at 120° (trigonal planar), as at each carbon of ethene.
  • Two groups lie in a straight line at 180° (linear), as at each carbon of ethyne.

docs.title: Hybrid orbitals
docs.text:
Why does carbon form four equal bonds, when its valence orbitals are one 2s and three 2p orbitals of different shapes? The answer chemists use is hybridisation: the atomic orbitals mix to form new hybrid orbitals, which point in the directions of the bonds.

  • sp³ hybridisation. The 2s and all three 2p orbitals mix to give four equivalent sp³ orbitals pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron. Each overlaps with an orbital of another atom to make a bond. A carbon with four single bonds is sp³.
  • sp² hybridisation. The 2s and two of the 2p orbitals mix to give three sp² orbitals in a plane at 120°. The third 2p orbital is left unchanged, perpendicular to the plane. A carbon with one double bond is sp².
  • sp hybridisation. The 2s and one 2p orbital mix to give two sp orbitals pointing in opposite directions (180°). Two 2p orbitals remain, perpendicular to each other and to the axis. A carbon with a triple bond, or with two double bonds (as in carbon dioxide), is sp.
Figure 1.1 Shapes of methane, ethene and ethyne. The three hybridisation states of carbon. In methane the four bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron; the wedged bond comes towards the reader and the hashed bond goes away. In ethene each carbon is trigonal planar; in ethyne the molecule is a straight line.

A quick rule: count the groups (atoms plus lone pairs) around the atom. Four groups means sp³, three means sp², two means sp. The rule applies to nitrogen and oxygen too. The nitrogen of ammonia has three bonds and a lone pair, four groups, so it is sp³.

docs.title: σ and π bonds
docs.text:
A bond formed by orbitals that overlap head-on, along the line between the two nuclei, is a σ (sigma) bond. Every single bond is a σ bond. Its electron density is concentrated between the nuclei, and rotating one end of the bond does not change the overlap, so groups joined by a single bond rotate freely.

In ethene each carbon uses its three sp² orbitals for σ bonds: one to the other carbon and two to hydrogens. The unhybridised p orbitals on the two carbons are parallel and overlap side by side, above and below the plane of the molecule. This side-on overlap is a π (pi) bond. A double bond is therefore one σ bond plus one π bond, and a triple bond is one σ bond plus two π bonds.

Figure 1.2 σ and π bonds in ethene. The bonding in ethene. The σ framework of C–C and C–H bonds lies in one plane. The two p orbitals, one on each carbon, stand perpendicular to that plane and overlap side by side to form the π bond, with electron density above and below the plane.

Two consequences follow, and both matter later in the book:

  1. A double bond does not rotate. Twisting one end of ethene by 90° would turn the p orbitals perpendicular to each other and break the π bond. This costs a lot of energy, so at room temperature the groups on a double bond keep their positions. That is why cis and trans isomers of alkenes exist (Chapter 3).
  2. π electrons are exposed and reactive. The π electrons lie further from the nuclei than σ electrons and are held less tightly. Alkenes react with electron-seeking reagents by using their π electrons (Chapter 7).
Bond Example Hybridisation of C Length (pm) Approximate bond energy (kJ mol⁻¹) C–C ethane sp³ 154 350 C=C ethene sp² 134 610 C≡C ethyne sp 120 835

Table 1.3. Carbon–carbon single, double and triple bonds. More bonds make the link shorter and stronger, but a π bond is weaker than a σ bond: the second bond adds less than the first.

Example 1.2: Hybridisation in ethanenitrile (acetonitrile), CH₃C≡N

The CH₃ carbon has four σ bonds: four groups, sp³, tetrahedral. The carbon of the C≡N group has two groups (the CH₃ carbon and the nitrogen): sp, linear. The nitrogen has the triple bond and one lone pair: two groups, sp. So the C–C≡N unit is a straight line, and the angles around the methyl carbon are about 109.5°.

docs.title: 1.6 Drawing organic molecules
docs.text:
Organic chemists draw structures all day, so they use short-hand. You must be able to read and write three styles.

  • A full structural formula shows every atom and every bond. It is clear but slow to draw for anything bigger than a few atoms.
  • A condensed formula writes each carbon with its hydrogens, in order along the chain: CH₃CH₂CH₂OH. Branches are put in brackets: (CH₃)₂CHOH is propan-2-ol.
  • A skeletal formula (line drawing) draws only the bonds of the carbon skeleton as a zigzag of lines.
Figure 1.3 Three ways of drawing the same molecule. Propan-1-ol drawn three ways. The full structural formula shows every atom and bond; the condensed formula writes the atoms in sequence; the skeletal formula shows only the zigzag of carbon–carbon bonds, with the OH group written out.

The rules for skeletal formulas are short:

  1. Each end of a line and each corner (vertex) is a carbon atom.
  2. Hydrogens on carbon are not drawn. Each carbon has as many hydrogens as it needs to make four bonds.
  3. All atoms other than carbon and hydrogen are written in, together with any hydrogens attached to them (OH, NH₂).
  4. Chains are drawn as zigzags, with angles of about 120°, which matches the real shape of a chain of sp³ carbons.

Example 1.3: Reading a skeletal formula

In the skeletal formula of propan-1-ol in Figure 1.3 there are three carbons: the left end of the line, the corner, and the corner where the OH is attached. The left carbon has one bond drawn, so it carries three hydrogens (CH₃). The middle carbon has two bonds drawn, so it has two hydrogens (CH₂). The right carbon has two bonds (one to carbon, one to oxygen), so it also has two hydrogens. The formula is C₃H₈O, which you can check against the condensed formula CH₃CH₂CH₂OH.

Caution: hidden hydrogens still count

A frequent error is to forget the implied hydrogens when writing a molecular formula or when looking for a hydrogen that a reaction removes. Always count them. A carbon at a corner with two lines has two hydrogens; at a corner with three lines, one; at a corner with four lines, none.

To show three dimensions, a solid wedge is a bond coming out of the page towards you, a hashed wedge is a bond pointing behind the page, and a plain line lies in the plane of the page. Methane in Figure 1.1 is drawn this way: two bonds in the plane, one wedge and one hash.

docs.title: 1.7 Resonance
docs.text:
Some molecules cannot be described by a single Lewis structure. The ethanoate ion (acetate, CH₃CO₂⁻) is the classic example. One Lewis structure puts a C=O double bond to the upper oxygen and the negative charge on the lower oxygen; an equally good structure swaps them. Experiment shows that the two carbon–oxygen bonds are the same length, between a typical C=O and a typical C–O. Neither drawing is right on its own.

The answer is resonance. The real ion is a single structure, a resonance hybrid, that is a blend of the two drawings, which are called resonance contributors (or resonance forms). The negative charge is spread equally over both oxygens and each C–O bond has a bond order of about one and a half.

Figure 1.4 Resonance in the ethanoate ion. Resonance in the ethanoate ion. A lone pair on the negatively charged oxygen of contributor A moves to form a C=O π bond, while the original π bond moves onto the other oxygen, giving contributor B. The double-headed arrow links the contributors. The hybrid has two equivalent C–O bonds, each with partial double-bond character (dashed line), and half a negative charge on each oxygen.

docs.title: Rules for resonance contributors
docs.text:
• Contributors differ only in the positions of electrons (π electrons and lone pairs). The atoms do not move and σ bonds do not break.
  • Contributors are linked by a double-headed arrow (↔). This is not an equilibrium: the molecule does not flip between the forms. A mule is not sometimes a horse and sometimes a donkey; it is a hybrid all the time.
  • Every contributor must be a valid Lewis structure, with the same total charge and the same number of electrons, and no second-row atom with more than eight.
  • Curly arrows show how one contributor is turned into another. Each curly arrow moves a pair of electrons from where its tail is (a lone pair or a bond) to where its head points (an atom or the position between two atoms). You will use exactly the same arrows for reaction mechanisms in Chapter 5.

docs.title: Which contributors matter most?
docs.text:
Not all contributors are equal. The hybrid resembles most closely the contributors that are most stable, judged by these criteria in order:

  1. Full octets. Structures in which every second-row atom has an octet are better.
  2. Fewest formal charges. Structures with less separation of charge are better.
  3. Negative charge on the more electronegative atom (and positive charge on the less electronegative atom).

When two or more contributors are equivalent, as in ethanoate, the delocalisation is especially effective. Spreading charge over several atoms lowers the energy of the molecule. This extra stability, the resonance stabilisation, explains why carboxylic acids are much more acidic than alcohols (Chapter 4) and why benzene is unusually unreactive (Chapter 8).

Example 1.4: Resonance in the carbonyl group

Methanal (formaldehyde, H₂C=O) can be drawn with a second contributor in which the π electrons have moved onto oxygen: H₂C⁺–O⁻. The first contributor has full octets and no charges, so it is by far the major one. The second is minor, but not useless: it shows that the carbonyl carbon is electron-poor (δ+) and the oxygen electron-rich (δ−). This polarity is the key to the chemistry of aldehydes and ketones in Chapter 11.

Key idea

Resonance is a way of describing delocalised electrons with the localised language of Lewis structures. When you see a lone pair or a negative charge next to a π bond, or a positive charge next to a π bond or a lone pair, look for resonance.

docs.title: 1.8 Intermolecular forces and physical properties
docs.text:
Covalent bonds hold atoms together within a molecule. Much weaker intermolecular forces hold molecules to one another. They decide whether a compound is a gas, liquid or solid at room temperature, and what it dissolves in.

  • London dispersion forces act between all molecules. Momentary uneven distributions of electrons create temporary dipoles that attract one another. They grow with the size and surface area of the molecule. This is why boiling points rise along the alkanes: methane boils at −162 °C, while octane boils at about 126 °C. A long, unbranched molecule has more surface contact than a compact, branched one, so pentane boils at 36 °C and its branched isomer 2,2-dimethylpropane at about 10 °C.
  • Dipole–dipole forces act between polar molecules, whose permanent dipoles line up end to end.
  • Hydrogen bonds are the strongest of the three. A hydrogen attached to O, N or F is strongly δ+, and it is attracted to a lone pair on another O, N or F atom.

The effect of hydrogen bonding is dramatic. Ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) and methoxymethane (dimethyl ether, CH₃OCH₃) have the same formula, C₂H₆O. Ethanol molecules hydrogen bond to each other and it boils at 78 °C; the ether has no O–H bond, cannot hydrogen bond to itself, and boils at about −24 °C.

Solubility follows the rule "like dissolves like". Polar molecules, especially those that can hydrogen bond, dissolve in water; non-polar molecules dissolve in non-polar solvents such as hexane. Small alcohols such as methanol and ethanol mix with water in all proportions, but as the hydrocarbon part grows the molecule becomes more oil-like: butan-1-ol is only partly soluble in water, and octan-1-ol is nearly insoluble.

docs.title: 1.9 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Carbon forms four covalent bonds, links to itself in chains and rings, and bonds well to H, O, N, S and the halogens.
  • Neutral C has four bonds; N three bonds and one lone pair; O two bonds and two lone pairs; halogens one bond and three lone pairs. Departures from this pattern carry a formal charge: \(V - N - B/2\).
  • Differences in electronegativity make bonds polar. Carbon bonded to O, N or a halogen is δ+.
  • Count the groups around an atom: four groups is sp³ (109.5°), three is sp² (120°), two is sp (180°).
  • A single bond is a σ bond; a double bond is σ + π; a triple bond is σ + 2π. The π bond prevents rotation about a double bond.
  • Skeletal formulas show only the carbon framework; every vertex and line end is a carbon with enough hydrogens to make four bonds.
  • Resonance contributors differ only in the positions of electrons. The real molecule is the hybrid, and delocalisation stabilises it.
  • Dispersion forces, dipole–dipole forces and hydrogen bonds govern boiling point and solubility.

docs.title: 1.10 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Draw a Lewis structure for methanamine, CH₃NH₂, showing all lone pairs. What is the hybridisation of the nitrogen, and the approximate H–N–H angle?

Answer

Carbon has three H atoms and a bond to N; nitrogen has two H atoms, the bond to C and one lone pair. Total valence electrons: 4 + 5 + 5 × 1 = 14, which is six bonds (12 electrons) and one lone pair (2 electrons). Nitrogen has four groups (three bonds and a lone pair), so it is sp³ and the shape about it is trigonal pyramidal, with angles of about 107°, a little less than 109.5° because the lone pair repels more strongly than a bonding pair.

Exercise 2

Calculate the formal charge on each atom other than hydrogen in (a) the methoxide ion, CH₃O⁻; (b) the nitrogen of the tetramethylammonium ion, (CH₃)₄N⁺; (c) the carbon of the methyl cation, CH₃⁺.

Answer

(a) Carbon: four bonds, formal charge 4 − 0 − 4 = 0. Oxygen: one bond and three lone pairs, 6 − 6 − 1 = −1.

(b) Nitrogen: four bonds, no lone pair, 5 − 0 − 4 = +1.

(c) Carbon: three bonds, no lone pair, 4 − 0 − 3 = +1. It has only six electrons around it, which is why carbocations are so reactive.

Exercise 3

State the hybridisation of each carbon in propene, CH₂=CH–CH₃, and in buta-1,3-diene, CH₂=CH–CH=CH₂.

Answer

Propene: the two carbons of the double bond are sp²; the CH₃ carbon is sp³. Buta-1,3-diene: all four carbons are sp², because each one is part of a double bond.

Exercise 4

How many hydrogens are attached to each carbon in the skeletal formula of cyclohexene (a six-membered ring with one double bond)? Write its molecular formula.

Answer

The two carbons of the double bond each have three bonds drawn (two to the ring neighbours counted as one each, plus the extra π bond), so each has one H. The other four ring carbons have two bonds drawn and so two H each. Total: 2 × 1 + 4 × 2 = 10 hydrogens. The formula is C₆H₁₀.

Exercise 5

Draw the second resonance contributor of the nitromethane molecule, CH₃–NO₂, given that one contributor is CH₃–N⁺(=O)–O⁻. Show the curly arrows that relate them. Are the two N–O bonds the same length?

Answer

A lone pair on the singly bonded O⁻ moves in to form an N=O π bond, and at the same time the π electrons of the existing N=O bond move onto the other oxygen, which becomes O⁻. The second contributor is CH₃–N⁺(–O⁻)=O, equivalent to the first. Because the two contributors are equivalent, the real molecule has two identical N–O bonds, intermediate between a single and a double bond, with half a negative charge on each oxygen. The nitrogen keeps its +1 formal charge in both.

Exercise 6

Arrange in order of increasing boiling point, and explain: butane, propan-1-ol, methoxyethane (CH₃OCH₂CH₃). All three have similar molar masses (58, 60 and 60 g mol⁻¹).

Answer

Butane (about −1 °C) < methoxyethane (about 7 °C) < propan-1-ol (97 °C). Butane is non-polar and has only dispersion forces. Methoxyethane is polar and adds dipole–dipole attraction, but has no O–H bond and cannot hydrogen bond to itself. Propan-1-ol forms hydrogen bonds between molecules through its O–H group, so far more energy is needed to separate the molecules.

Exercise 7

Explain why a C=C double bond, with a total bond energy of about 610 kJ mol⁻¹, is not twice as strong as a C–C single bond (about 350 kJ mol⁻¹).

Answer

The double bond is one σ bond plus one π bond. The π bond is formed by side-on overlap of p orbitals, which is less effective than the head-on overlap of a σ bond. So the π bond contributes only about 610 − 350 = 260 kJ mol⁻¹, less than the σ bond. This weaker π bond is also why alkenes are much more reactive than alkanes.

docs.title: 1.11 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of bonding

Exercise 1

What is the hybridisation of the carbon atom in carbon dioxide, O=C=O?

  1. sp
  2. sp2
  3. sp3
Answer

sp

The carbon has two groups around it (two double bonds), so it is sp and the molecule is linear.

Exercise 2

An oxygen atom with three bonds and one lone pair has a formal charge of

  1. -1
  2. 0
  3. +1
  4. +2
Answer

+1

6 valence electrons - 2 non-bonding - 6/2 = +1.

Exercise 3

How many hydrogen atoms are on a carbon at a corner of a skeletal formula where three lines meet (all single bonds)?

Answer

1 / one

Three bonds are drawn, so one hydrogen is needed to make four.

Exercise 4

Which statement about resonance contributors is correct?

  1. The molecule flips rapidly between them.
  2. They differ only in the positions of electrons, not atoms.
  3. They may have different numbers of electrons.
  4. The least stable contributor resembles the real molecule most.
Answer

They differ only in the positions of electrons, not atoms.

Exercise 5

Which bond is the most polar?

  1. C-H
  2. C-C
  3. C-O
  4. C-I
Answer

C-O

The electronegativity difference is largest for C-O (2.5 against 3.4).

Exercise 6

Match each molecule to the shape about its central atom.

ABmethanebentammonialinearwatertetrahedralethynetrigonal pyramidal Answer

methane — tetrahedral; ammonia — trigonal pyramidal; water — bent; ethyne — linear

Exercise 7

Ethanol boils at 78 °C and methoxymethane at about -24 °C. The main reason is

  1. ethanol has a larger molar mass
  2. ethanol molecules form hydrogen bonds to one another
  3. methoxymethane is non-polar
  4. methoxymethane has a double bond
Answer

ethanol molecules form hydrogen bonds to one another
